body_md: To more than one person, a command ends in **-en** for -ar verbs and in **-an** for the rest: **pasen**, **esperen**, **vengan**, **traigan**. A pronoun sticks to the end: **siéntense**.

Two more conditions that take the subjunctive: **con tal de que me lo devuelvas** — *on condition you give it back*; **salvo que lo necesite** — *unless I need it*. Lending to a friend in Buenos Aires comes with both.
title_en: Con tal de que, salvo que

body_md: Learn these two whole — they are in the past, which the course teaches later. **Me perdí** — *I got lost*; right now you are **perdido** or **perdida**. **Me robaron** — *I got robbed*: *me robaron el celu*.

On a vos command both pronouns join the end, person first, and the stress gets a written accent: **devolvémelo** — *give it back to me*; **pasámelo** — *send it to me*; **decímelo** — *tell me*. To him or her, *le* turns into *se* again: **mandáselo**.
A porteño host says **pasen, pasen** at the door, **pónganse cómodos**, and **no se preocupen** when you apologize for being late. **Están en su casa** — *make yourselves at home*.

Put *el* or *la* in front of *más* and you have the top of the list: **el barrio más tranquilo**, **la calle más ruidosa** — and **menos** for the bottom: *la calle menos ruidosa*. The group comes after **de**, not *in*: **el mejor del mundo**, **la más linda de la ciudad**.
**Me da miedo** is *it scares me* in general; **me dio miedo** is one scare, over and done. The thing that scares you is the subject: **me dan miedo los perros**.
**Boludo** is common between close friends and an insult to anyone else — say it only to friends you know well. **Quilombo** means a mess; it's informal, not rude, but keep it out of formal settings.

The *e* of *pedir* turns into *i* in **pido**, **pide**, and in the past for *él* and *ellos*: **pidió**, **pidieron**. *Nosotros* keeps its *e* — and **pedimos** is both *we order* and *we ordered*: **anoche pedimos empanadas**.
*de + el* always becomes **del**, and *a + el* becomes **al**: *la parada del bondi*, *de acá al kiosco*. With *la* nothing joins: *a la parada*.
People say **la engañó** — *he cheated on her* — and in gossip even more often **le metió los cuernos**, literally *put the horns on*. **Engañar** is also plain *to trick, to fool*.

**Opinar** is having a view: **¿vos qué opinás?** — *what do you think?*; **opino lo mismo**. But **yo opino que…** sounds formal, like a TV panel: in daily speech porteños start with **para mí** or **me parece que**: **para mí, depende del tema**; **me parece que tenés razón**.
For more than one person: **pasen** — *come in*; **vengan** — *come*; **siéntense** — *sit down*; **pónganse cómodos** — *make yourselves comfortable*; **no se preocupen** — *don't worry*.
The word for *that* matches the thing: **esa campera**, **ese buzo**, **esas zapatillas**. When you point without naming it, **eso** never changes.
To say who you are, use **soy**: *Soy Sofi.* One word carries "I am". The word for "I" (**yo**) is usually left out; add it only to stress or contrast: *Yo soy Martín.*

Three people, three forms of *ser*:

| yo | **soy** |
| vos | **sos** |
| él, ella | **es** |

The verb already tells you who, so *él* or *ella* is usually dropped: *Es de Rosario* — he's (or she's) from Rosario.

**Su** is *his*, *her* or *their* (and *your* for *ustedes*); with more than one it is **sus**: *su mamá*, *sus hijos*. *Our* matches the thing, not the people: **nuestro** papá, **nuestra** familia, **nuestros** abuelos, **nuestras** hermanas.

A strike is named after who stops: **paro docente** — *the teachers*; **paro de colectivos** — the **colectiveros**; **paro general** — everyone. The **gremio** — *the union* — **anunció un paro** for Thursday, and the news calls it a **medida de fuerza**.

| **Tendría que haber** ido. | I should have gone. |
| **Tendrías que haber** avisado. | You should have let us know. |
| **Me arrepiento.** | I regret it. |

**Tendría que haber** + participle: how porteños say *should have*. **Debería haber ido** is also correct, but sounds more formal.

**Acabo de** + infinitive is *I just did it*: **acabo de comer**, **acaba de salir**. Porteños mostly say **recién** + the past instead: **recién llegué**, **recién salió** — it means the same. **Volví a** is *I did it again*: **volví a llamar**. Or just **de nuevo** or **otra vez** — *again*.

One person **ceba** — pours the water from the **termo** — and passes the mate around the **ronda**. You drink it all, through the **bombilla**, and hand it back to the **cebador**, the person who pours.

Same order as *te lo devuelvo* — person first, thing second — with new verbs: **te lo presto** — *I'll lend it to you*; **te lo guardo** — *I'll keep it for you*; **te lo muestro** — *I'll show you*. The thing decides lo or la: *¿la bici?* **te la presto**.
**Me siento mal** — *I feel bad*. **Lo siento** — *I'm sorry*, for real bad news. For bumping into someone, say **perdón**.

You meet the **-ra** form (*tuviera*, *pudiera*) after *si* (if) and after *ojalá* (I wish), and almost nowhere else at this level. Mind the difference: **ojalá llueva** — *I hope it rains* (it can happen); **ojalá pudiera ir** — *I wish I could go* (it is not real).

| hacer | **hará** | ¿Qué hará a esta hora? |
| venir | **vendrá** | Vendrá más tarde. |
| poder | **podrá** | ¿Podrá venir? |
| querer | **querrá** | ¿Qué querrá? |
| costar | **costará** | ¿Cuánto costará? |
| estar | **estarán** | Estarán en el bar. |
| ser | **serán** | Serán las ocho. |

Regular verbs just add **-á** to the infinitive (*costar* → **costará**); the irregular ones squeeze it (*hacer* → **hará**, *venir* → **vendrá**). For them, it's **-án**; for vos, **-ás**: *¿estarás cansado?*

At the table the host never stops: **coman**, **prueben**, **tomen algo**, **agarren pan**. Same rule as *pasen*: -ar verbs end in **-en**, the rest in **-an** — **coman**, **hagan** lugar, **vayan** sentándose.

A **final** that ends in a tie goes to the **alargue** — *extra time* — and then to **penales**: the **arquero atajó** one and somebody **metió** the last. **Salir campeón** is *to win the title*. **¡Aguante!** shows love for your team, win or lose: *¡Aguante Argentina!*
Habits from back then are imperfect: **los domingos nos juntábamos**, **festejábamos Reyes**. One night that went wrong is preterite: **el bondi tardó una hora y no te avisé**.

| yo, él, ella | **hubiera** | sabido, venido, ido |
| vos | **hubieras** | llamado, avisado, pensado |

For what didn't happen, both halves: **Si hubiera sabido, te hubiera avisado.** *If I'd known, I'd have told you.* You will also hear **habría** in the second half: *te habría avisado*. Same meaning. Compare *si supiera* — if I knew (now).
**Si hubiéramos salido antes, no hubiéramos perdido el vuelo** — *we* and *they* take **hubiéramos, hubieran**, in both halves.

The reply has its own verbs: **te reenvío el mail** — *I'm forwarding you the email*; **te paso el link**; **te pongo en copia** — *I'm cc'ing you*. **Revisé la planilla** — *I went through the spreadsheet*.

| | ir, ser | estar | tener |
| yo | **fui** | **estuve** | **tuve** |
| vos | **fuiste** | **estuviste** | **tuviste** |
| él, ella | **fue** | **estuvo** | **tuvo** |
| nosotros | **fuimos** | **estuvimos** | **tuvimos** |
| ellos | **fueron** | **estuvieron** | **tuvieron** |

No accents here. *Fui a la cancha* is *went*; *fue bárbaro* is *was*.
The feeling verbs keep their pronoun in the past too: **me enojé**, **te asustaste**, **se preocupó**.
**Quiero ir** — *I want to go*. **Quiero que vayas** — *I want you to go*. When the wish is about someone else, the second verb turns subjunctive.

| what he said | what you tell |
| «Voy.» | Dijo que **iría**. |
| «Vengo mañana.» | Dijo que **vendría** mañana. |
| «Te llamo.» | Dijo que me **llamaría**. |

A promise told later goes into *would*. In everyday speech porteños mostly say **dijo que iba a venir**; the *-ría* form sounds more careful.

The **calesita** in the plaza, **golosinas** from the kiosco, a **barrilete** on a windy day, and the **álbum** of **figuritas** you filled for every **Mundial** — **lo llenábamos entre todos** — *we used to fill it together*.

The rules for the person who pours: **calentá el agua** in the pava — *heat the water* — but **no la hiervas**: water that **hierve** burns the yerba. **Yo cebo**, you drink. When there's no taste left, **el mate está lavado** — *washed out* — and it's time to change the yerba.
title_en: Calentá el agua, no la hiervas

body_md: Something does it *to* you: **me dejó pensando** — *it got me thinking*; **me partió el alma** — *it broke my heart*. And you end up frozen: **me quedé helado** — *I froze, I was stunned*. A woman says **me quedé helada**. The good ones: **me hace bien**, **me da ternura**, and **¡qué alivio!**
**Facturas** are the pastries you buy by the dozen at the bakery — *medialunas* are the best known. Nothing to do with bills.

**Ando buscando laburo** — *I've been looking for work*: **ando** + *-ando* is these days. **Estamos por arrancar** — *we're about to start*. **Le cae bien a todo el mundo** — *everybody likes him*; **a ese no lo aguanto** — *I can't stand that guy*.
With a vos command the pronoun joins the end: **ayudame**, **alcanzame** — *help me*, *hand me*. No written accent: the stress stays on **-da-** and **-za-**, so not *ayúdame*.

From 21 to 29 the number is one word: **veintiuno**, **veintidós**, **veinticinco**. From **treinta** on it is three words joined by **y**: *Tengo treinta y cuatro años.* The same pattern works for **cuarenta**, **cincuenta** and all the way up to **noventa**. Before *años*, **uno** becomes **un**: *veintiún años*, *treinta y un años*.

| | -ar | -er, -ir |
| yo | labur**é** | com**í**, sal**í** |
| vos | labur**aste** | com**iste**, sal**iste** |
| él, ella | labur**ó** | com**ió**, sal**ió** |
| nosotros | labur**amos** | com**imos**, sal**imos** |
-er and -ir share one set of endings. *Salimos* is both *we go out* and *we went out* — *anoche* or *ayer* tells you which.

For paperwork, **demorar** is how long something takes: **¿cuánto demora la residencia?** The honest answer is *depende*. For a person or a bus porteños say **tardar**: *Lucía tardó media hora*, *el bondi tardó un montón*. You **presentás** the papers, and when they finally **atienden** you, it's over in five minutes.

The little word changes with the people who like it: **nos** gusta — we like it; **les** gusta — they like it, or you all do. The verb still matches the food: *nos gusta el pollo*, *nos gust**an** los fideos*.

| to me | **se me** cayó | I dropped it |
| to you | **se te** cayó | you dropped it |
| to him, her | **se le** cayó | he dropped it |

Same with *rompió, perdió, pasó*: **se me pasó** — *I forgot*. The middle word says who it happened to.
title_en: Se me, se te, se le

body_md: **Si** is *if* — no accent, unlike *sí*. After it comes the plain present: **Si querés, vamos al cine.** **Si podés, salimos a la noche.**
**No sabía** — the state, imperfect. **Me di cuenta** — the moment, preterite. **¿Qué significa *garpar*?** — *to pay*, in lunfardo.
**Poner** makes feelings too: **me pone nervioso que llegue tarde**, **me pone de mal humor que cancele**. Same shape as *me da bronca*: the feeling, then **que** + subjunctive.
When it happened to all of you, the middle word is **nos**: **se nos acabó el café** — *we ran out of coffee*; **se nos rompió la heladera**. To a friend: **¿se te pasó?** — *did you forget?*
The whole family of soft advice: **deberíamos juntarnos más** — *we should get together more*; **deberían pagarte más** — *they ought to pay you more*. Advice to *us* is the gentlest of all.
A strike is a **paro**: **hay paro de subte**, **paro de colectivos**. When protesters block a street it's a **piquete** or a **corte**, and the street **está cortada**. A **marcha** is a march.
A reaction to someone else's news takes the subjunctive: **qué bueno que estés acá**, **me alegro que te vaya bien**, **qué lástima que no puedas venir**.

| | regular | shortened |
| yo, él, ella | comprar**ía**, ir**ía** | **tendría**, **podría**, **haría**, **diría** |
| vos | ir**ías** | |
The ending goes on the whole infinitive: *comprar* → **compraría**. **Yo que vos** + would is advice: *yo que vos, esperaría*. **Tendría que** is *should* — *tendría que ir* — and **podría** is *could*.

The old neighbor is **don José** or **doña Rosa** — first name, with respect. A **persona mayor**, a **jubilado**, still gets **vos**, plus a **cómo no** (*of course*) and a **permiso** when you need to get past — *con permiso* exists, but porteños mostly say just **permiso**, and you **pedís permiso** before going in: *entró sin pedir permiso*.

**Te aconsejo que lleves efectivo** — *my advice: bring cash*. **Conviene que** and **es importante que** work like *te recomiendo que*: the advice lands in the subjunctive — **conviene que busques un depto cerca del subte**.

| Te presto **la bici**. | Te **la** presto. |
| Te guardo **el cargador**. | Te **lo** guardo. |
| Te paso **las fotos**. | Te **las** paso. |
| Le digo **el secreto**. | **Se lo** digo. |
| ¿Me mostrás **el depto**? | ¿Me **lo** mostrás? |

Any verb works the same way: the person first, the thing second, and *le* before *lo, la* becomes **se**.
title_en: Te lo presto, se lo digo

body_md: For someone else it's **se siente**: **mi abuela no se siente bien**. Where it hurts is **dolor de** — **tengo dolor de cabeza** — *I've got a headache*, the same as **me duele la cabeza**.

Three words that need nothing after them: **arriba** (up, upstairs), **abajo** (down, downstairs), **adentro** (inside). *Estoy abajo* is what a porteño texts from the street when they're at your door. The fourth one is **afuera** — *outside*: *mi auto está afuera*.

*Tener* — to have — is how you give your age: Spanish *has* years.
| yo | **tengo** | Tengo veinte años. |
| vos | **tenés** | ¿Cuántos años tenés? |
| él, ella | **tiene** | Tiene doce años. |
The *e* of *tener* becomes *ie* in *tiene* — but never in the vos form: **tenés**. Before a noun, *uno* is **un**: *tiene un año*.

16 to 19 are **dieci** + the number: *dieciséis*, *diecisiete*, *dieciocho*, *diecinueve*.
Before, the **campaña**, the **debate** on TV and the **encuestas** — *the polls* — that always get it wrong. After, the **resultado**. The course stays out of who won.

**Merecerse** keeps its pronoun for every person: **me lo merezco**, **te lo merecés**, **se lo merece** — *she deserves it* — **nos lo merecemos** — *we deserve it*. A **gerente** who sees your **responsabilidad** grow should hear it: **se merece el ascenso**.
title_en: Se lo merece, nos lo merecemos

body_md: Most of the family comes in *-o / -a* pairs: **tío, tía** — **primo, prima** — **sobrino, sobrina** — **nieto, nieta**. *Mi* stays the same for all of them.
**Hay** for something new: *hay una estación por acá*. **Está** for the one you already mean: *la estación está en la avenida*.

Porteños are direct, but they soften it first: **sin ofender** — *no offense*; **te lo digo con cariño**; **no es nada personal**. A **crítica** goes down better that way, above all on a **tema delicado**.
Argentines buy almost anything **en cuotas** — in installments — and the first question at the register is **¿en cuántas cuotas?**
**Mañana** on its own is *tomorrow*: *Hoy laburo, mañana no.* With **la** it is *the morning*, and porteños say **a la mañana** for *in the morning*. So *tomorrow morning* is **mañana a la mañana**.

An argument in Buenos Aires is a sport, not a fight: **discutimos** a lot and stay friends. To reject a point, say **¡nada que ver!** — *not at all!* (it can also mean *nothing alike* or *nothing to do with it*). If the other person won't listen: **no seas cabeza dura** — *don't be so stubborn*.
**Hacer** + infinitive works with any verb: **me hizo sentir como en casa**, **te hace pensar**, **nos hizo llorar a todos**. And people too: **vos me hacés reír**.
Advice to the group uses *we*: **es mejor que salgamos temprano**, **conviene que lo hagamos mañana**. *Salir* keeps its *g*: *salgo* → **salgamos**.

*Estar* says how something is right now, and the word matches the thing:

| el bar | está cerrad**o** | la plaza | está llen**a** |
| mis hermanos | están apurad**os** | la cerveza | está calient**e** |

| ¿Por qué estás apurada? | **Porque** el bondi está lleno. |

*Caliente* and *libre* only add *-s*: *libres*, *calientes*.
The pronoun comes along into the wish: **que te mejores** — *get well soon*; **que te diviertas** — *have fun*; **que lo disfrutes** — *enjoy it*. The same *que* + subjunctive as *que te vaya bien*.
title_en: Que te mejores, que te diviertas

body_md: **Hacer** + infinitive is *to make someone do*: **me hizo reír**, **me hizo llorar**, **nos hizo esperar**. **Me hace acordar** — *it reminds me*: *esta canción me hace acordar a vos*.

Colors match their noun like any adjective: *un pantalón negro*, *una remera negra*, *zapatillas negras*. Ones ending in *-e* or a consonant only change for more than one: *verde* → **verdes**, *azul* → **azules**. The color comes after the noun.
*Your* is **tu**, and it takes an *-s* with more than one: **tu** hermano, **tus** hermanos. *My* works the same way: *mi* gato, **mis** gatos.

| | él, ella | ellos |
| ser | sea | **sean** |
| estar | esté | **estén** |
| tener | tenga | **tengan** |
| poder | pueda | **puedan** |
| llegar | llegue | **lleguen** |
For *they*, add **-n**. **Puede ser que** and **es posible que** take the subjunctive like *no creo que*: *puede ser que estén cerrados*. The same form is *you* for a group: *que tengan buen finde, chicos*.
It comes right after *¿de dónde sos?*: **¿Dónde naciste?** — **Nací en Rosario, pero vivo acá.** And when you didn't catch what someone said, it's the past too: **perdón, no entendí**.
**A la vuelta** is *around the corner* — on the next street, not this one. **En la otra vereda** is *across the street*: *la panadería está en la otra vereda*.

Put **lo** in front of an adjective and it becomes *the … thing*: **lo lindo** — *the nice thing*; **lo feo** — *the ugly part*; **lo difícil** — *the hard part*; **lo único** — *the only thing*: **lo único que extraño es el mar**.
**Entre nos** — *between you and me* — is where porteño gossip starts. **Sin querer** — *by accident*: **te pisé sin querer**.
**¿De qué cuadro sos?** — and the answer is for life.

**Aunque sea** — *at least, even if it's only* — is the deal you make with yourself: *hoy no tengo ganas, pero **aunque sea** un rato voy*. And the other half of it: **aunque no me dé el tiempo** — *even if I don't have the time*.

Life's big steps take the pronoun, like **se casó**: **me recibí** — *I graduated*; mi hermano **se recibió** de abogado; mi tía **se jubiló** — *retired*. Ask **¿de qué te recibiste?** — *what did you graduate in?* **Se murió** — *died* — is for talking among friends; to the family you say **falleció** — *passed away*.
**Era otra época** — *it was a different time*. The **inmigrantes** who arrived around 1900 packed into the city's **conventillos** and shaped its tango and its accent.
**Ponerse a** + a verb is *to start doing*: **nos pusimos a bailar** — *we started dancing*; **me puse a laburar** — *I got down to work*.
-er and -ir verbs only differ for **vos** and **nosotros**: *vendés, vendemos* but *compartís, compartimos*. Everywhere else they match: *come, comparte*; *comen, leen, escriben*.

| a habit — normal verb | not yet — subjunctive |
| Cuando **llego**, tomo mate. | Avisame cuando **llegues**. |
| Cuando **termino**, salgo. | Cuando **termines**, llamame. |

About the future, *cuando* and **apenas** take the subjunctive: *apenas puedas*.

The porteño exit starts long before the door: **bueno, me voy yendo** — *well, I'd better get going* — and then twenty minutes of talk. On the way out, love for whoever isn't there: **saludos a tu vieja**, **mandale saludos a Juan**. *Tu vieja* / *tu viejo* is only for friends your age; to anyone else, *saludos a tu mamá*.
*Me levanto, te levantás, se levanta* — the pronoun comes before the verb and matches the person. **Los sábados** means *on Saturdays*.

**Emocionarse** in every person: **me emocioné**, **¿te emocionaste?**, **mi viejo se emocionó**, **nos emocionamos todos**. It was **emotivo** — *moving* — and **se me hizo un nudo en la garganta** — *I got a lump in my throat*.

For machines, porteños say **anda** — *it works*: **no anda el wifi**, **¿anda el ascensor?**. *Funciona* means the same and is just as common. The other ways things fail: **se rompió**, **está roto**, **no prende** — *it won't turn on*; **se colgó** — *it froze*; **pierde agua** — *it's leaking*.

Any verb goes into *would* the same way — the infinitive plus **-ía**: *pasar* → **dijo que pasaría**; *devolver* → **me juró que me la devolvería**. A few change the stem: *poner* → **pondría**, like *tener* → *tendría*.

The verb matches the thing you like, not you: *Me **gusta** el mate*, but *Me **gustan** las facturas*. The little word in front says who likes it: **me**, **te**, **le**. With a name, add **a** and keep **le**: *A Lucía le gusta el mate.*
**Trucho** — *fake, dodgy*: *un billete trucho*. **Zarpado** — *over the top*, for good or bad. **Bardo** — *a mess, trouble*: *se armó un bardo*.
The shortest way to order anything: name it and add **por favor**. *Un café, por favor.* *Una medialuna, por favor.* No verb needed.
The porteño sign-off, in emails and out of them: **cualquier cosa, avisame** — *if anything comes up, let me know*. A **consulta** is a question you send; a **respuesta**, the reply.
**Enterarse** is *to find out, to hear about*: **me enteré ayer**, **¿te enteraste?**, **se enteró todo el mundo**.
One thing **está**, more than one **están**: *¿Dónde está mi celu?* — *¿Dónde están mis anteojos?* The answer drops the thing you're looking for: **Están en la mochila.**

| yo, él, ella | **había** | probado, estado, empezado |
| vos | **habías** | terminado, escuchado |
| nosotros | **habíamos** | llamado, avisado |
| ellos | **habían** | **escrito**, hecho, dicho, visto |

Any participle goes with any person: **habíamos probado**, **habías escrito**. **Nunca había probado algo así** — never, up to a moment in the past. **Ya habíamos terminado cuando llegaste** — done before the other thing happened.
**Sé** (with an accent) is *I know*. **¿Sabés?** — *do you know?* And the porteño *I have no idea*: **ni idea**.

| **Acabo de** llegar. | I just got here. |
| **Suelo** almorzar tarde. | I usually have lunch late. |
| **Volví a** perder las llaves. | I lost my keys again. |

All three take an infinitive. **Soler** has a past too, **solía** — *solía almorzar tarde* — but *antes almorzaba tarde* says the same.
**Caliente** is for things: *el café está caliente*. Said about a person it means angry — or something ruder — so for yourself use *tengo calor*, and for the weather *hace calor*.

**¡Buen provecho!** — *enjoy!* — is said when you serve food, or when you pass people who are eating, even coworkers or strangers. The answer is **gracias**. And when the host says **sírvanse** — *help yourselves* — everybody starts right away.
**El mejor** and **el peor** need no *más*: **el mejor asado del barrio**, **el peor día de mi vida**. Everything else takes *el más*: **el más tranquilo**, **la más difícil**.

**Me siento mal** — *I feel sick*; **¿cómo te sentís?** — *how do you feel?* The vowel changes with *yo*, not with *vos*: **me siento**, but **te sentís**. *Dormir* does the same: **duermo**, but **dormís**; **dormí** is the past, *I slept*. On its own, **lo siento** is *I'm sorry*.

| straight out | softer |
| Probá el flan. | Te recomiendo que **pruebes** el flan. |
| Pedí un taxi. | Es mejor que **pidas** un taxi. |

**Te recomiendo que** and **es mejor que** take the subjunctive. *Probar* → **pruebes**, *pedir* → **pidas**.
Carlos **Gardel** died in 1935, and porteños still say he **canta mejor cada día**. A tango's **letra** — *lyrics* — is usually about **nostalgia**: the barrio, the mother, the woman who left.
**Quería que vinieras** puts the wish in the past, so the second verb follows it. **Aunque** takes the subjunctive only for a maybe: *aunque llueva*.

A word ending in a vowel adds **-s**: *galletita → galletitas*, *chicle → chicles*. One ending in a consonant adds **-es**: *alfajor → **alfajores***. With a number, *un* and *una* drop out: *dos paquetes*. Containers take **de**: *una botella de agua*, *un paquete de chicles*.
**Recorrer** is *to travel around, to go all over*: **recorrimos la Patagonia**. The road is the **ruta** — *la ruta 40* runs the length of the country.

One past behind another: **había** + a participle. **Cuando llegué, ya habían comido** — *when I got there, they'd already eaten*. Yo, él and ella take **había**; vos, **habías**; ellos, **habían**. Pronouns go in front: **ya se había ido**, **no me habían dicho nada**. *Hecho, dicho, visto* are the irregular ones.
**No hace falta** — *there's no need*. **Conviene** is the advice: **conviene ir temprano** — *it's best to go early*.

A chance you let go: **dejé pasar la oportunidad** — *I let the chance go*. To someone who didn't come: **te lo perdiste** — *you missed out*. **Lamentablemente** — *unfortunately* — you can't **volver atrás** — *go back* — so you drop it with **ya fue**.
On its own, **es que…** is the start of every porteño excuse: **—¿No venís? —Es que laburo temprano.**

Day to day porteños soften a request with **quería**: **quería un turno para mañana**, **te quería pedir algo**. **Quisiera** — *I would like* — is the formal one, for the phone or an office: **quisiera un turno**; nobody orders food with it. To ask a stranger for something, add **no** and the future: **¿no tendrás hora?** — *you wouldn't happen to have the time?*

| **Cuanto más** practicás, | The more you practice, |
| mejor hablás. | the better you speak. |
| Avisame **cuanto antes**. | Let me know as soon as you can. |
**Cuanto más** + one thing, then the other with **más**, **menos**, **mejor**. **Cuanto menos** — *the less*: **cuanto menos dormís, peor te sentís**.

**Estoy al horno** — *I'm in big trouble*. **Qué bajón** — *what a shame*. **Al pedo** — *for nothing, doing nothing*: **fui al pedo**, **estoy al pedo**. And the flat *no way*: **ni en pedo**. The other *pedo* phrases: **estar en pedo** — *to be drunk*; **de pedo** — *by pure luck*: *llegué de pedo*. Among friends only.
**Bondi** is the everyday word for the city bus; *colectivo* is the neutral one. The **subte** is the Buenos Aires underground.
Apartments are sized in **ambientes** — rooms, not counting the kitchen and bathroom. *Un dos ambientes* has a living room and one bedroom.
The story moves on with **así que** — *so* — and explains itself with **por eso** — *that's why*: **Perdí el bondi, así que llegué tarde.** **Llovió; por eso no fui.**

Take the *ellos* preterite and swap **-ron** for **-ra**: *salieron* → **saliera**, *volvieron* → **volviera**, *dijeron* → **dijera**. With vos add an **-s**: **estudiaras, dijeras, fueras**. For *ellos*: **querían que vinieran todos**.

*Doler* has a past too, and it stays glued to its *me*: **me dolió la cabeza** — *my head hurt*, **¿te dolió?**, **a mi viejo le dolió la rodilla**. When more than one thing hurt, it's **dolieron**, just like *me duelen*: **me dolieron los ojos** — *my eyes hurt*.
*Estar* and the describing word after it match the person: *estamos cansad**os***. An -ar verb takes the person's ending: *practic**amos***. *Gustar* matches the thing: *nos gust**an** los fideos*.

Stuck on a word: **¿cómo se dice…?** — *how do you say…?* — and **¿qué significa?** — *what does it mean?* Too fast: **más despacio, por favor**. And the line that makes people slow down and help: **hablo un poco** — *I speak a little*. Argentines call the language **castellano**.

To say how clothes fit, use **me queda**: *Esta camisa me queda bien* — *this shirt fits me well*. *Me queda chico* — *it's too small for me*. *El vestido me queda grande* — *the dress is too big for me*.
**Yo que vos** — *if I were you* — is how a porteño gives advice, and the conditional follows: **yo que vos, iría**, **yo que vos, no diría nada**.
**La verdad** opens an honest answer: **la verdad, no sé** — *honestly, I don't know*. **La verdad que sí** — *yeah, really*.

**Dejar de** + infinitive is *to stop, to quit*: **dejé de fumar**, **¿dejaste de ir al gimnasio?**, **¡dejá de quejarte!** Its opposite is **volver a**: **volvió a fumar** — *he started smoking again*. **Ponerse a** is *to start doing*: **me puse a estudiar** — *I started studying*.
The imperfect paints the scene, the preterite is what happens in it: **Estaba en el subte cuando me llamó Sofi** — *I was on the subway when Sofi called me*.
**Sin que** works the same way: **cerrá la puerta sin que se escape el gato** — *without the cat getting out*. And **antes de que vuelva** — *before I'm back* — hasn't happened yet.
Every *don't* grows from the *yo* of the present: *dejo* → **no dejes**, *cuento* → **no cuentes**. *Saco* gives **no saques**: the *c* turns *qu* to keep its sound.

| they say | you answer |
| ¿Me ayudás con las bolsas? | **Cómo no**, **te doy una mano**. |
| Gracias, querido. | **No es nada.** / **Faltaba más.** |
| No, no, yo puedo. | **Dejá, dejá**, que te las llevo. |

Respect for **don José** and **doña Rosa** comes from the tone, not from usted.
**Me morí de risa**, **¿de qué te reís?**, **me hizo sentir…** — and **cuanto antes lleguemos, mejor**. **A la larga** — *in the long run*: **a la larga, el esfuerzo rinde**.
**No me alcanza** — *it's not enough (for me)*. It works for money, time, anything: **no me alcanza la plata**, **no me alcanza el tiempo**.

**Hinchar por** runs in the family: **en casa hinchamos todos por el mismo cuadro**; **de chico hinchaba por otro, pero mi viejo no me dejó**. A fan **de toda la vida** never changes club — changing wife is easier, they say. Day to day, people simply say **somos del mismo cuadro**.

**Fue clausurado** is the event — *it got closed down*; **está clausurado** is the result — *it is closed now*. The ending agrees with the thing: **el boliche fue clausurado**, **la obra fue clausurada**, **la cancha está clausurada**.

More verbs that take a **la** pointing at nothing: **me la juego** — *I'll go for it*; **la pifié** — *I blew it* — and its opposite, **la pegaste** — *you got it right*; **la rompe** — *she's amazing at it*; **se la agarró conmigo** — *he took it out on me* (he got angry at me, though it wasn't my fault). **Me las tomo** — *I'm out of here*. And to make someone stop: **¡cortala!** — *cut it out!*
title_en: Me la jugué, la pifié, la rompe

body_md: Someone new in town gets a **¡bienvenido!** — or **¡bienvenida!** for a woman. The end of the word matches the person.

Travel stories run on the preterite: **acampamos** — *we camped* — **hicimos dedo** — *we hitchhiked* — **¿recorriste el norte?**, **mis viejos recorrieron la costa**. Distances are in **kilómetros**, and in the south there are always more than you thought.

**Cené, cenaste, cenó, cenamos, cenaron**; **viví, viviste, vivió, vivimos, vivieron**. Two sets of endings, and every regular verb takes one of them: -ar verbs go like *cenar*; -er and -ir verbs go like *vivir*.

**Se me** + verb says it happened *to* you, by accident — you didn't do it on purpose: **no fue mi culpa, se me cayó** — *it wasn't my fault, I dropped it*. And the excuse every porteño has ready when they're late: **se me hizo tarde** — *it got late*.
Use **estar** for how you are right now: *estoy cansado*, *¿estás nerviosa?* To ask why: **¿por qué?** — two words. The answer is **porque**, one word: *Porque Sofi está enferma.*
**Creo que viene** — the indicative, because you believe it. **No creo que venga** — the subjunctive, because you doubt it.

**Te debo diez mil pesos** — *I owe you*; **me debés la mitad** — *you owe me half*. Friends split the bill **a medias**. A **deuda** is what you owe; if you are short, say **te pago a fin de mes** — when you get paid.

**Facu** is short for *facultad* — university. For jobs, Spanish drops the article: **Soy profesora**, not *soy una profesora*. Jobs change for a woman: *profesor* → **profesora**, *médico* → **médica**, *jefe* → **jefa**.
**Me preocupa que trabajes tanto**, **qué suerte que estemos todos**, **me sorprende que no sepa** — a reaction + *que* keeps the subjunctive, for any person.
**Para** + an infinitive when it's the same person: *estudio para aprender*. **Para que** + the subjunctive when it's someone else: **te lo mando para que lo leas**.

Stuck on a word: **¿cómo se dice…?** — *how do you say…?* — and **¿qué significa?** — *what does it mean?* Too fast: **¿me repetís?** or **más despacio, por favor**. **No entendí** is *I didn't get that*. And the line that buys you patience: **hablo un poco de castellano** — Argentines call the language *castellano*.

**Me la banco** — *I can handle it*; **se la bancó** — *she put up with it*. To say you can't stand something, drop the **la** and name it: *no me banco este frío* — *I can't stand this cold*; *no me banco a mi jefe* — *I can't stand my boss*.

Words ending in *-r*, *-n*, *-e* take **-cito**: **calor → calorcito**, **café → cafecito**. Short *sol* does too: **solcito**. Words in *-o* just swap it for **-ito**, and a *c* turns *qu*: **fresco → fresquito**; a *z* turns *c*: **pedazo → pedacito**. Porteños love diminutives for nice weather: **hace fresquito**, **qué lindo calorcito**.

In a café nobody orders one slice: ask for **tostadas** — *Un café y tostadas, por favor.* **Un tostado** is something else: a toasted ham-and-cheese sandwich, the classic café lunch. *Una tostada* is one slice, at home: *¿Otra tostada?*

| | now | yesterday |
| yo | labur**o** | labur**é** |
| vos | labur**ás** | labur**aste** |
| él, ella | labur**a** | labur**ó** |

*Laburo* is *I work*; **laburó** is *he worked*. Only the stress, and the accent that marks it, tells them apart. Every regular -ar verb works like this: *hablé, llegaste, compró*.
**Aunque llueve, vamos** — it's raining, and we're going. **Aunque llueva, vamos** — whether it rains or not. A fact takes the normal verb; a maybe takes the subjunctive.
title_en: Aunque: a fact, or a maybe

body_md:
| not found yet — subjunctive | already found — normal verb |
| Busco un depto que **tenga** balcón. | Encontré un depto que **tiene** balcón. |
| Busco algo que **quede** cerca. | Vivo en un depto que **queda** cerca. |
| ¿Hay un dueño que **acepte** mascotas? | Mi dueño **acepta** mascotas. |

If it might not even exist, the verb after **que** goes into the subjunctive.
Something you're looking for but haven't found yet takes the subjunctive: **busco un depto que tenga balcón**. Once you've found it, it doesn't: *encontré un depto que tiene balcón*.
English says *used to*; Spanish just uses the imperfect. **Jugábamos en la calle** — *we used to play in the street*. **Siempre**, **a veces** and **de chico** go with it.
**Tengo que** is *I have to*; put **voy a** in front for later: **voy a tener que laburar** — *I'm going to have to work*. It works for everyone: **vas a tener que**, **vamos a tener que**.
An argument in Buenos Aires is a sport, not a fight: **discutimos** a lot and stay friends. **Me convenciste** — *you've convinced me*; **cambié de idea** — *I changed my mind*.
Money talk goes lunfardo fast: **¿quién garpa?** — *who's paying?*; **¡es un afano!** — *it's a rip-off!*; **berreta** — *cheap, shoddy*. And food is **el morfi**.
The verb already says who: *soy* is only ever "I am", *sos* only "you are". So **Soy de acá** and *Yo soy de acá* are both right, and the short one is what people say.
Spanish says you *have* years: **Tengo veinte años** — I'm twenty. *Tenés* is the vos form, *tiene* is for him or her.
**Nos conocemos**, **nos escribimos** — each other, us. **Se separaron**, **se pelean** — each other, them.

The news opens with **hubo**: **hubo un incendio**, **hubo un accidente en la avenida**, **hubo dos heridos** — who then **fueron trasladados al hospital**. At the kitchen table the same story loses the passive: *trasladaron a los heridos*.

| | ponerse | enojarse |
| yo | **me puse** | **me enojé** |
| vos | **te pusiste** | **te enojaste** |
| él, ella | **se puso** | **se enojó** |

The pronoun stays in the past. **Ponerse** + a feeling is *to get*: *me puse nervioso* — *I got nervous*.

**Ayudar → ayudes**, **esperar → esperes**, **mandar → mandes**, **avisar → avises**. *Poner* and *traer* keep the *g* of their *yo*: **pongo → pongas**, **traigo → traiga**. The same form, with **no** in front, tells someone not to: *esperame* — **no me esperes**; *llamame* — **no me llames**. The pronoun jumps to the front.
title_en: -ar takes e, the rest take a

body_md: Other verbs work like *me llamo, te llamás*: **hablo**, **¿hablás?** — **entiendo**, **¿entendés?** The *I* form ends in **-o**; the vos form is stressed on the end. Lost? *Perdón, no entiendo. **Despacio**, por favor.*

**Hace un año que vivo acá** — *I've been living here for a year*: Spanish stays in the present. **Llevar** + time + *-ando / -iendo* says the same: **llevo un año viviendo acá**. Or just a place: **lleva un año acá**. With **sin**: **llevás tres días sin dormir**. To ask: **¿hace cuánto que vivís acá?** Day to day porteños say **hace… que**.

| Mi prima **se casó** el sábado. | got married |
| **Nos casamos** en marzo. | we got married |
| El bebé **nació** ayer. | was born |
| ¿Dónde **naciste**? | were you born |

**Casarse** takes its pronoun; **nacer** doesn't. **Nos casamos** is also the present: *nos casamos en julio* — *we're getting married in July*. The wedding is a **casamiento**; the legal one is **por civil**, or just **el civil**. Before it, **se comprometieron** — *they got engaged*; after it, the **luna de miel**. **Está embarazada** is *she's pregnant*.

**Ya no** is *not anymore*: **ya no vivo ahí**. Porteños say it even more with **no … más**: *no vivo más ahí*. The opposite is **sigue** — *still*: *sigue roto*, *sigue lloviendo*. **Cada vez más** — *more and more*: *cada vez más caro*; **cada vez menos** — *less and less*.

The tip is **la propina**, usually 10 percent and in cash. The bill may also have a small charge per person, the *cubierto*: it is not the tip. **¿Compartimos?** — *shall we share?* — is how two people order one enormous *bife*.

**Novedades** is news about people and plans: **¿hay novedades de Juan?**, **todavía no hay novedades**. **Noticias** works too, and is also the news on TV; **una noticia** is one piece of news. Good news gets **¡buenísimo!**; bad news **¡qué mal!**

Going somewhere takes **a** — *to* — every time: *Voy a la plaza.* The question word has that **a** built in: **¿adónde vas?** is *where are you going to?* English often drops the *to*; Spanish never drops the **a**. **A + el** becomes **al**: *voy al kiosco*, but *vas a la estación*.

Election day is a Sunday, and everyone asks **¿dónde votás?** — usually at a school near home: **votamos en la misma escuela**. Your **mesa** is the numbered table where you vote. Before it there is **veda**: campaigning stops 48 hours before the vote, and from the night before nobody can sell alcohol.

| yo | **estoy** |
| vos | **estás** |
| él, ella | **está** |

Two verbs mean *to be*. **Ser** says who or what something is, and where it's from: *Soy de Rosario.* **Estar** says where it is right now: *Estoy en Buenos Aires.*
**¿Cuánto sale?** is the everyday Argentine way to ask a price — **¿cuánto cuesta?** works too and means the same. For more than one thing the verb changes: **¿cuánto salen?**, **¿cuánto cuestan?**
**Llevarse bien** is *to get along*: **me llevo bien con mi hermana**, **nos llevamos re mal**.

The other persons follow: **nos pidió que llegáramos temprano** — *she asked us to get there early*; **les dijo que trajeran algo** — *he told them to bring something*. **Encargar** is to give someone an errand: **me encargó que le llevara el pan** — *she asked me to bring her the bread*.

**Al horno** — *in trouble*; **qué bajón** — *what a shame*; **ni en pedo** — *no way*; **rata** — *stingy*; **manija** — *very excited*; **guita** — *money*; **hacer la gamba** — *to help someone out or keep them company*. All among friends.

**Venga**, **vaya**, **haga** are both *I* and *he/she*: *quiere que venga* — *he wants me/him to come*. Context, or an added **yo** or **él**, tells you who: *quiere que vaya yo*. On its own, **que** + this form is *let him* or *tell him to*: *dale, que venga*.
title_en: One word for yo and él

body_md: **Con tal de que me lo devuelvas** — *as long as you give it back* — and **salvo que lo necesite** — *unless I need it* — take the subjunctive. On the door: **se aceptan tarjetas**, **se hacen envíos**.
title_en: Con tal de que, se aceptan

body_md: Plural things take the plural verb: **se aceptan tarjetas**, **se hacen envíos**, **se arreglan bicis**. One thing, the singular: **se busca perro** — with a **recompensa** if you're lucky.

**Por más que** — *no matter how much* — is a stronger *aunque*: **por más que me cueste, sigo** — *however hard it is, I keep going*. A maybe takes the subjunctive, a fact doesn't: *por más que **entreno**, engordo* — I do train; it just doesn't show.

| **Acabamos de** llegar. | We just got here. |
| Los porteños **suelen** cenar tarde. | Porteños usually have dinner late. |
| **Volvió a** fumar. | He started smoking again. |
| **Dejé de** fumar. | I quit smoking. |
| **Me puse a** estudiar. | I started studying. |

All five take an infinitive straight after: *acabar de, soler, volver a, dejar de, ponerse a*.
**Disculpá** gets a stranger's attention: *Disculpá, ¿sos Martín?* **Permiso** is what you say to get past someone, on a full bus or in a doorway.
**Fue** + participle, agreeing: **fue construido**, **fue inaugurada**, **fueron detenidos**.

After **no es que**, every verb goes subjunctive: **no es que no me interese** — *it's not that I'm not interested*; **no es que no me importe** — *it's not that I don't care*; **no es que me caiga mal** — *it's not that I don't like him*; **no es que no queramos / podamos** — *it's not that we don't want to / can't*. The real reason follows with **es que** + a normal verb: *es que no llego* — *I just can't make it*.
**Se me cayó el vaso** — the glass fell, and it happened to me. No blame: that is why every porteño story of a mishap starts with **se me**.

The card for the bus and the subte is **la SUBE**: you **cargás** it at a kiosco — the same verb as charging **el celu**, the phone (short for **celular**). *Celular* is also the phone number: *pasame tu celular* — *give me your number*.
**Donde** with no accent joins a place to the rest of the sentence: **el bar donde nos conocimos** — *the bar where we met*. The question keeps its accent: *¿dónde?*
On a command it goes on the end, as before: **mostrame las fotos**, **buscame a las ocho**. The stress doesn't move from *mostrá*, *buscá*: *mos-TRA-me*, *bus-CA-me*.

The conditional takes the edge off a request: *¿me das una mano?* becomes **¿me darías una mano?**, *¿me ayudás?* becomes **¿me ayudarías?**. **¿Te molestaría…?** — *would you mind…?* — works like *me gustaría*. With friends the plain *¿me ayudás?* is already polite; the **-ía** form is for bigger favors or people you don't know.
Report what someone said and the tense steps back: **viene** becomes **dijo que venía**. If it is still true now, the present can stay: **me preguntó dónde queda**.

Most swearing is aimed at the situation, not at a person: **¡la puta madre!**, **¡la concha de la lora!**, **¡mierda!**, **¡carajo!**, **¡qué cagada!** A bad day is *un día de mierda*. **Me chupa un huevo** is *I don't give a shit*. Two are not insults, just very informal: **una boludez** is something silly or small, and **me cagué de risa** means *I laughed my ass off* — I laughed a lot.

| | hacer | ver | decir | venir | poder |
| yo | hice | vi | dije | vine | pude |
| vos | hiciste | viste | dijiste | viniste | pudiste |
| él, ella | hizo | vio | dijo | vino | pudo |
| nosotros | hicimos | vimos | | | |
A new stem, then *-e, -iste, -o*, with no accent — *hizo* is spelled with a *z*. *Ver* keeps it short: *vi, viste, vio*.
Nobody says *quisiera*: **dame un kilo de papas** — *give me a kilo of potatoes* — is polite enough with a *por favor*.

| | ser | tener | vivir | ir |
| yo, él, ella | era | tenía | vivía | iba |
| vos | eras | tenías | vivías | ibas |
| nosotros | éramos | teníamos | vivíamos | íbamos |
| ellos, ustedes | eran | tenían | vivían | iban |

*Ellos* just adds **-n**. **Quería** and **podía** work the same way: *de chico quería ser maestro, pero no podía salir solo.*

**Insistió en que fuera** — *she insisted I go*. **Me sugirió que la llamara** — *he suggested I call her*. As in *me pidió que trajera*, the verb after **que** is in the past subjunctive (*fuera, llamara*).

| the one + a place or a detail | **el de** la vidriera, **la de** la izquierda |
| the one + a verb | **el que** quieras, **la que** te probaste |
| more than one | **los de** allá, **las que** prefieras |

Not chosen yet, so the subjunctive: **el que elijas**; to a group, **elijan los que quieran**. Don't mind? **Como quieras.**

For the table there's the **parrillada** — *a mixed grill* on its own little grill: chorizo, morcilla, **mollejas** — *sweetbreads: a soft gland, not bread* — **chinchulines** and a **tira de asado**. On your own: a **bife de chorizo** or an **entraña**. The classic start is a **provoleta para compartir**; the prized cuts are **ojo de bife** and **lomo**, with *papas fritas* or *ensalada* on the side.

| Acá **se cena** tarde. | People eat late here. |
| **Se saluda** con un beso. | You greet with a kiss. |

**Se** + the *él* form talks about everyone in general, no one in particular.

**En lo de mi abuela** — *at my grandma's (place)*; **vamos a lo de Juan** — *let's go to Juan's*. Sunday lunch there meant **ravioles con tuco**, and a **sobremesa** that ran until the *mate* came out.
**Estar por** + infinitive is *to be about to*: **estoy por salir** — *I'm just about to leave*. A porteño's *I'm on my way* is often **ya salgo**, which may mean in an hour.
**Prohibido estacionar** — *no parking*; **prohibido fumar** — *no smoking*. The sign itself is a **cartel**.

For *ellos* and *ustedes* the imperfect just adds an **-n**: **eran**, **tenían**, **vivían**, **iban**. For *nosotros* it's **-íamos**: **teníamos**, **vivíamos**. *Mis abuelos vivían en el campo y nosotros íbamos en enero.*

**¿Conocés a alguien que arregle bicis?** — don't know if they exist, subjunctive. **No hay nadie que cocine así** — they don't, subjunctive again. **Me pone nervioso que cancele** — a feeling about it, subjunctive too.
**Boludo** is common between close friends and an insult to anyone else — understand it, don't use it yet. **Quilombo** means a mess; it's informal, not rude, but keep it out of formal settings.

Prices in Argentina run to thousands: **dos mil**, **quince mil**, **cien mil** — *mil* never takes an *s*. A **millón** does: *dos millones* — and takes **de** before the thing: *un millón de pesos*.

When you want *someone else* to do something, the second verb changes: **quiero que vengas** — *I want you to come*. This form is the **subjunctive**. **No hace falta que** — *there's no need to* — takes it too: *no hace falta que traigas nada*.
title_en: Quiero que + a new verb form

body_md: **Me toca a mí** — *it's my turn*. **¿A quién le toca?** — *whose turn is it?* The chore follows in its basic form (*lavar*, *sacar*, *limpiar*): **te toca lavar los platos**. Add *a mí* / *a vos* for stress: **hoy te toca a vos**.
The same guess in the present: **a lo mejor** — *maybe*; **supongo que sí** — *I suppose so*; **probablemente** — *probably*.

People get labels: a **rata** never pays; a **careta** is fake or uptight (or someone who doesn't drink or party); **grasa** is tacky (a snobbish word: fine as a joke about a shirt, rude about a person). **Estar manija** is to be very excited about something: **estoy manija con el recital**. The **cana** is the police. A friend who backs you **te hace la gamba**; one who talks nonsense **manda fruta**.
*Ser de* works for a country, a city or one corner of it: **Soy de un pueblo de Córdoba.** **Soy de zona sur.** *Zona norte*, *zona sur* and *zona oeste* go straight after *de* — no *la*.
title_en: De, for any size of place

body_md:
| what was said | what you tell |
| «¿Venís?» | Te preguntó **si venías**. |
| «No puedo.» | Me dijo **que no podía**. |
| «No podés.» | Te dijo **que no podías**. |
Reported, the present steps back: *venís* → **venías**, *podés* → **podías**.

Looking back, a finished thing takes the preterite: **al principio me costó** — *it was hard at first* — **pero me adapté** — *I adapted*. How things were takes the imperfect: *al principio era raro*. Now **me siento como en casa**. Say it **de corazón**.
The softest porteño suggestion is **estaría bueno** — *it would be nice*: **estaría bueno juntarnos**, **estaría bueno que vengas**. **Habría que** is *we ought to*: *habría que avisarle*.
In Buenos Aires **911** is the police and **107** is the ambulance. In the street, shout **¡ayuda!** and tell someone what to do: **llamá a la policía**, *llamá una ambulancia*. *Es urgente.*
**Acabo de** — just now; **suelo** — usually; **volví a** — again.

Day to day an opinion starts with **para mí**: *para mí, está cerrado* — *if you ask me, it's closed*. **Para mí que** + a normal verb is a guess: *para mí que hoy llueve*. And **no me parece que** takes the subjunctive, like *no creo que*: *no me parece que haya mucha gente*.

News starts with **¿escuchaste…?** or **¿te enteraste?** — *did you hear?*: *¿escuchaste lo de Pablo?* The answer is **me enteré** — *I found out*: *me enteré ayer*. A useful piece of news is **un dato**: *gracias por el dato*.
One pair of pants is **un pantalón** — singular: *Mi pantalón es nuevo.* *Los pantalones* works too. The same goes for **un jean**. And **ropa** — *clothes* — is always singular: *Mi ropa es nueva.*
**Hoy laburo**, **ayer laburé**. The same verb: the ending changes and the stress jumps to it. *la-BU-ro* is now, *la-bu-RÉ* is done. Say it out loud and the past is already right.
title_en: Today or yesterday: the stress tells

body_md: Two more with their own stem and no accent: **traje, trajiste, trajo** (brought) and **quise, quisiste, quiso** (wanted, tried). **Quise** is about one moment: *I wanted to* (and tried). **No quise**: *I didn't want to* (and didn't). **Quise venir, pero no pude** — *I wanted to come but couldn't* — is the porteño apology for a missed asado.
A machine that fails on its own: **se** + preterite. **Se colgó la compu**, **se apagó el celu**, **se quedó sin batería**.
**Buscar** is *to look for* — *tengo que buscar laburo* — and also *to pick someone up*: *tengo que buscar a mi hijo*, *tienen que buscar a sus hijos*.

**Me prometiste que ibas a venir** — *you promised me you'd come* (more careful: *que vendrías*). And the classic ending: **al final no vino** — *in the end he didn't come*. If he did, he **cumplió** — *kept his word*: *prometió llamar y cumplió*.
Right now: **estar** + the verb in *-ando* (for -ar verbs) or *-iendo* (for -er and -ir): *estoy cocin**ando***, *está escrib**iendo***. Two to learn by ear: **leyendo**, **durmiendo**.
For what didn't happen: **si hubiera sabido, te hubiera avisado** — *if I'd known, I'd have told you*. Porteños use **hubiera** + a participle in both halves.

**A ver** — *let's see* — slows an argument down. **Pensándolo bien** — *on second thought* — is how you change sides: *pensándolo bien, me convenciste* — *on second thought, you convinced me*. To heat it up again: **sos un exagerado** — *you're being dramatic*.
**¿Tenés la tarjeta? Sí, la tengo.** The pronoun stands for the thing and goes before the verb: *lo* and *los* for masculine words, *la* and *las* for feminine ones.

**Me robaron el celu** — *my phone got stolen*, literally *they stole the phone from me*. The thief is a **chorro** in lunfardo, a **ladrón** in the news. On the subte it is usually a **punga** — *a pickpocket* — and you notice later. **Me asaltaron** is worse: they robbed you face to face.
On the 29th of every month many families eat **ñoquis** with a banknote under the plate, for luck. A **feriado** is a public holiday, and there are plenty of them.
**Crecer** is *to grow* — a city, a kid, a tree: **el barrio creció**, **crecí en Rosario** — *I grew up in Rosario*. Porteños also say **me crié**: *me crié en Flores* — *I grew up in Flores*.

*Avisar* in the past is plain -ar: **avisé**, **avisaste**, **avisó**. The text at eight-forty: **¿Dónde estás? Te esperaba a las ocho.** And the answer, always: **ya salgo**. The other classics: **estoy llegando** (still ten minutes away), **estoy en camino** — *I'm on my way* — and **llego en diez**.

A porteño story wanders, so it has signposts: **como te decía** — *like I was saying* — brings it back; **el tema es que** — *the thing is* — gets to the point; **a todo esto** — *by the way* — goes off on a side road; **hablando de** jumps to the next story.
You send **el currículum**; they ask about your **experiencia** and tell you about the **puesto** — *the position*. **Pagan bien** — *they pay well* — is what everyone wants to hear.

**Macanudo** is the old-school *great guy* — you will hear it from older people; under fifty it is **copado** or **piola**, and **es una genia** for a woman who is great at what she does; **trabajador** is *hard-working*. **Agrandado** is *full of himself*, **egoísta** *selfish* — and *egoísta* is the same for him and for her, like *inteligente*.
Buenos Aires is a grid of streets cut by wide **avenidas** — Corrientes, Santa Fe, 9 de Julio. On an avenida almost every corner has a **semáforo**. Cross when it's green: **cruzá**.

At the **fiambrería** you buy by weight: **cien gramos de jamón**, cut in **fetas** — *slices*. The classic order is **un cuarto** — 250 grams: *un cuarto de jamón cocido*. **Jamón cocido** is plain ham; **jamón crudo** is the cured one.

The *I* form ends in **-o**: **hablo**, **entiendo**. The vos form is stressed on the end: **hablás**, **entendés**, **repetís**. One verb is different: *I know* is just **sé**, and the vos form is **sabés**. **Me** (*me*) and **te** (*you*) go before the verb: *No te entiendo. ¿Me entendés?* *No entiendo. ¿Hablás inglés?* — *No sé.*

Take off *-ar* and add the ending for the person:

| yo | labur**o** |
| vos | labur**ás** |
| él, ella | labur**a** |
| nosotros | labur**amos** |
| ellos, ustedes | labur**an** |

It works for *hablar, tomar, estudiar, caminar* — every regular -ar verb. **Hacer** is not an -ar verb, so learn its three forms as they are: **hago**, *hacés, hace*.

For a porteño **la costa** is the Atlantic beaches south of the city, where you rent a **carpa** — a beach tent by the day. The other classic is **las sierras** of Córdoba: a **río** instead of the sea. A **carpa** is also a normal camping tent: *me fui al río con la carpa*.
**Confío en vos** — *I trust you*. Trust always takes **en**.

**Hacerse el** + a describing word is *to pretend, to act*: **me hice** el distraído — *I pretended not to notice*; **te hacés** el sordo — *you act like you can't hear*; **se hace** el canchero — *he shows off, he acts all cool*. **No te hagas el gil** — *don't play dumb*. A woman says **la**: *me hice **la** simpática*.

For plans, porteños use **voy a** + verb far more than the future: **la semana que viene voy a descansar**. **Pienso** + verb is also a plan: *I'm planning to*. **Tengo ganas de** is only wanting: *I feel like it*.
**Vale la pena** — *it's worth it*: worth the price, the trip or the wait.

**Como si no me viera** — *as if he didn't see me*. **El de la vidriera** — *the one in the window*; **el que quieras** — *whichever you want*. And pretending: **te hacés el dormido** — *you're pretending to be asleep*.
title_en: Como si, el de, hacerse el

body_md:
| Creo que **es** así. | No creo que **sea** así. |
| Creo que **está** en casa. | No creo que **esté** en casa. |
| Creo que **tiene** razón. | No creo que **tenga** razón. |
| Creo que **hay** tiempo. | No creo que **haya** tiempo. |

Sure → the normal verb. Doubting → the subjunctive.

The verb goes with the *thing*, not with you: **se me cayó la taza**, but **se me cayeron las llaves**; **se me quemó la comida**, **se me quemaron las tostadas**. The *me* stays put — it still happened to you.
**Entregar el proyecto** before the **plazo**; **plantear** the raise you **merecés**.

**Puede ser** — *could be* — is a common *maybe*, like **capaz**. Add *que* and the subjunctive follows: **puede ser que llueva**, **puede ser que estén cerrados**. **Es posible que** says the same, a little more carefully.

Lunfardo is Buenos Aires slang, born in the port and the tango: **morfar** (to eat), **guita** (money), **fiaca** (laziness), **pilcha** (clothes). Friends, not job interviews. **Guita** and **fiaca** are fine in any relaxed talk; **morfar** is rougher: with people you just met, say *comer*.

A **rumor** is only that until someone **confirma** it, or denies it: **el gobierno desmintió el rumor**. Before **compartirlo**, ask **¿cuál es la fuente?** A **cadena** — *a chain message* — with no source is probably **verso** — *made up*.

The family story runs in the third person plural: **se escaparon de la guerra**, **se instalaron en un conventillo** — *an old shared house where each poor family rented one room* — and **trabajaron en el puerto**. One person: **se instaló**. They left **pobreza** behind, **mantuvieron** the language and the traditions, and **guardaron** the photos of the ship. *Conservaron* says the same, but it is a written word.

**Tengo ganas de ir a la playa** — *I feel like going to the beach*. **Pienso ir** — *I'm planning to go*. Careful: **pensar** + a verb is *to plan to*, but **pensar que** is *to think that*: *pienso que tenés razón*.
**Se** + a verb says what people do in general: **acá se cena tarde** — *people have dinner late here*; **se saluda con un beso** — *you greet with a kiss*.

Porteños grade a person with two little words: **re** turns it up — *es re generosa* — and **medio** turns it down — *es medio vago*, *he's a bit lazy*. **Medio** never changes: *medio tonta*, *medio serios*. And the verb matters: **es callado** — *he is a quiet guy* — is what he is like; **está callado** — *he is quiet today* — is how he is right now. Same with **es serio** and **estás serio**.
Same **se** + the *él* form: at an asado **se trae algo** — wine, ice, dessert; **se pone la mesa** while the **asador** handles the **fuego**; **se come** when he says so, **chorizo** first.
**Recién llegué** — *I just got here*. A porteño uses *recién* with the plain past where English says *just*.
The pronoun works the same in the past: **¿Las fotos? Ya las mandé.** **¿El video? Lo vi anoche.** **¿A Sofi? La llamé ayer.** Before the verb, always — only a command takes it on the end.
Porteños call the city itself **Capital** — *Soy de Capital* — to set it apart from the suburbs around it. Not from here at all? **Soy de afuera.**

The subjunctive keeps the *yo* stem: *cierro* → **cierres**, *encuentro* → **encuentres**, *riego* → **riegues** (the **u** is only spelling: it keeps the *g* hard). The regular ones just swap the vowel: **entres**, **abras**.
**Vos** can come after the verb when you're checking who someone is: *Ah, ¿sos vos?* — *Oh, it's you?* The answer: **Sí, soy yo.** Can't believe it? **¿Posta?** — *for real?*
This is the normal way to ask for someone's number — friendly, not pushy. They may say **agendame** — *save my number* — and read it out. You answer: *te agendo*.

**-o** turns into **-a**: *brasileño, brasileña*. A consonant adds **-a**: *español, española*; *francés, francesa* (the accent goes). A word in **-e** never changes: *canadiense*, *estadounidense* — for a man or a woman.
**¿Dónde estará?** is not about tomorrow: it is *I wonder where he is*. The future guesses; **capaz** and **seguro que** do it in the present.
**Cuando llegás, me avisás** is a habit; **cuando llegues, avisame** is one future time. For what hasn't happened yet, *cuando* takes the subjunctive.

**¿Me acompañás?** — the favor is for me; **¿nos sacás una foto?** — the favor is for us. You ask with a plain present-tense question: no *can you* needed. **¿Me podrías…?** — *could you…?* — is the more careful version.

| **Lo bueno** es la gente. | The good thing is the people. |
| **Lo malo** es el tránsito. | The bad thing is the traffic. |
| **Lo mejor** fue el asado. | The best part was the asado. |
| **Lo peor** es el calor. | The worst part is the heat. |
**Lo** + adjective makes *the … thing*, and **de** says of what: **lo peor de Buenos Aires**, **lo bueno de vivir acá es que…** **Lo** never becomes la, los or las. With a plural noun, the verb is plural: **lo malo son los precios**.

**Lo que** is *what* when it means *the thing that*: **¿viste lo que pasó?**, **contame lo que pasó**. It is how every chisme starts: **no sabés lo que me contaron** — *you won't believe what they told me*. A direct question keeps **qué**: *¿qué pasó?*
**Me puse nervioso**, **me enojé**, **me asusté** — a feeling that came over you at one moment is the preterite. **Estaba nervioso** is the state you were in.
title_en: Me puse: it happened to you

body_md: People work like apartments: if you don't know whether they exist, the subjunctive. **¿Conocés a alguien que arregle bicis?** Once you've found one, it's a fact: *tengo un amigo que **sabe** arreglar bicis*.
**Tardar** is *to take (time)*: **¿cuánto tardás?** — *how long will you be?*; **el bondi tardó una hora**. Porteños are rarely **puntuales**, so *tipo ocho* already has the delay built in.
**Saber** + a verb is *to know how to*: *Nico sabe cocinar* — *Nico knows how to cook*. For *we* the form is **sabemos**: *Tranqui, sabemos llegar* — *relax, we know how to get there*.

Twice a year, in June and December, the **aguinaldo** arrives — half a month's extra pay. Every job *en blanco* pays it by law. A **licencia** is *paid leave* for a reason (sick, a new baby, exams). Your yearly holiday is **vacaciones**.

A first time is told with **nunca había** + a participle: **nunca había probado el dulce de leche** — *I'd never tried dulce de leche* (until that day). **Por primera vez** is the other half: **lo probé por primera vez en Buenos Aires**.
Spanish says you *call yourself*: **me llamo Sofi** — my name is Sofi. Asking someone else: **¿cómo te llamás?**
**Dejame las llaves** — *leave me the keys*; **te dejo** — *I'll leave you (to it)*, the porteño way of hanging up.
**Socio del club**, **hincha de toda la vida**, the **hinchada** and its **cantitos**.

Nouns: **una cosita**, **un pedacito**, **un besito**. Adjectives: **calentito** — *nice and warm*; **cortito**; **igualito a su papá**; **solito** — *all by himself* (to an adult it sounds tender or teasing, so keep it for friends). Adverbs: **tempranito**, **rapidito**. It agrees like any adjective: **una sopa calentita**.

**-ito** makes things small, and requests smaller: **un ratito** — *a little while*; **un cafecito**; **un poquito**. It sounds kind rather than childish. It softens bad news and favors too: **tengo un problemita**, **una preguntita**.
The *if* form works for every verb: take the *ellos* past and swap **-ron** for **-ra**. *Ganaron* → **si ganara**, *vivieron* → **si viviera**. Then *would*: **viviría**, **daría**, **sabría**.

**Lo que pasa es que…** — *the thing is* — explains the real reason. **Lo raro es que…** — *the weird thing is*; **lo importante es que…** — *what matters is*. A fact takes the normal verb: **lo importante es que llegaste**. Something not real yet takes the subjunctive: **lo importante es que la pases bien**.
Single or married goes with *ser* too: **soy soltera**, **son casados**. You'll also hear *estoy casado* — both are everyday Buenos Aires.
No *la* before home: **estoy en casa**, *I'm at home*. With anything else you need *el* or *la*: *en la mochila*, *en el auto*.

For anything finished, Buenos Aires uses one past: *laburé* (I worked), *laburaste* (you worked), *laburó* (he/she worked). The stress is what tells *laburo* (I work) from *laburó* (he worked) — the accent is not decoration.
title_en: The past, one person at a time

body_md: The bank has its own accidents: **se me bloqueó la tarjeta**, **se me venció la tarjeta**. Same *se me* as a dropped glass. How it happens: **puse mal la clave tres veces** — *I entered the wrong PIN three times*.
The irregular ones squeeze the verb: *hacer* → **hará**, *venir* → **vendrá**, *poder* → **podrá**, *querer* → **querrá**. The ending is always **-á** for él and ella.

**Se permite** and **se prohíbe** are sign language. Out loud people say **se puede** / **no se puede**: *acá no se puede estacionar*; *¿se puede pagar con tarjeta?* And to ask a shop: **¿hacen envíos?** — *do you deliver?*

| yo form | para que… (vos) |
| entro | para que **entres** |
| abro | para que **abras** |
| cierro | para que **cierres** |
| encuentro | para que **encuentres** |
| riego | para que **riegues** |

For *él, ella*: **para que el gato coma**. **Sin que** and **antes de que** take the same forms: *sin que se escape*, *antes de que vuelva*.
**¿Dónde queda?** — *where is it?* for a place on the map. **Me queda cerca** — *it's close to me*. Places **quedan** (or **están**); people only **están**.
**Nosotras** and **ellas** are for groups of women only. One man in the group makes it **nosotros** and **ellos**.

| yo | **tengo que** laburar |
| vos | **tenés que** practicar |
| él, ella | **tiene que** ayudar |
| nosotros | **tenemos que** estudiar |
| ellos, ustedes | **tienen que** buscar a sus hijos |

Jobs: *enfermero* → **enfermera**, *vendedor* → **vendedora**; *periodista* and *policía* stay the same.

**Cualquier duda, avisame** — *any questions, let me know* — closes half the emails in Buenos Aires. What's still to do is **pendiente**: **me quedó pendiente el archivo**. And if it needs a meeting, you **agendás** it.
**Por un lado… por otro lado** weighs two sides. **En cambio** — *but, on the other hand* — sets two people or things against each other: *yo laburo, en cambio él no*.
title_en: Por un lado, por otro lado

body_md: **Hice, vi, dije, pude, vine** — the pasts you use most carry no accent, unlike *laburé* or *comí*. **¿Qué hiciste?** — **Nada, vi una peli.**
title_en: The irregular ones have no accent

body_md:
More verbs that stretch their stem — but never with vos:
| | preferir | volver | empezar |
| yo | pref**ie**ro | v**ue**lvo | emp**ie**zo |
| vos | **preferís** | **volvés** | **empezás** |
| él, ella | pref**ie**re | v**ue**lve | emp**ie**za |
| ellos | pref**ie**ren | v**ue**lven | emp**ie**zan |
The same as *quiero, querés* and *puedo, podés*. **Nosotros** stays short too: *preferimos, volvemos, empezamos*. Add an infinitive for the plan: *¿Preferís ir al teatro?*

| yo, él, ella | **hubiera** | tomado, reservado |
| vos | **hubieras** | perdido, traído |
| nosotros | **hubiéramos** | salido, llegado |
| ellos, ustedes | **hubieran** | avisado, venido |
**Si hubiéramos salido antes, no hubiéramos perdido el vuelo.** Both halves take *hubiera*, matched to the person. **¡Hubieras reservado antes!** — *you should have booked earlier!*
**Estamos atrasados** — *we're behind*. The porteño answer: **no pasa nada, lo sacamos** — *it's fine, we'll get it done*.

**Me quedé sin batería** — *my battery died*, literally *I was left without battery*. A call, or the power at home, **se cortó** — *it cut out*. Without *sin*, **quedarse** is *to stay*: *¿te quedaste en casa?*

| **Deberías** descansar. | You should rest. |
| **Debería** llamarla. | I should call her. |
| **Estaría bueno** juntarnos. | It'd be nice to get together. |
| **Habría que** avisarle. | We ought to let him know. |

All four can take an infinitive. **Estaría bueno** — the softest porteño suggestion — also takes **que** + subjunctive: *estaría bueno que vengas*. *Tenés que* is stronger — *you have to*; *deberías* is advice.
With *ser*, a role goes straight after the verb: **Soy estudiante.** **¿Sos turista?** English says *a student*; Spanish leaves the *un* out.
**Creo que viene** — *I think he's coming* — keeps the normal verb. Doubt it and the subjunctive comes in: **no creo que venga**.
Tell a story in order with **primero**, **después**, **al final**: *Primero comimos, después vimos una película.* **Entonces** is mostly *so*: *No pude ir, entonces vi el partido en casa.*
Describe a group with **son** and a plural ending (**-s**, or **-es** after a consonant): **son re trabajadores**, **son medio distraídos**. A mixed group takes the masculine form.

| one | more than one |
| El boliche **fue clausurado**. | Los vecinos **fueron rescatados**. |
| La obra **fue clausurada**. | Las vecinas **fueron rescatadas**. |
| La ley **fue aprobada**. | Los heridos **fueron trasladados**. |

Who did it comes after **por**: *por los bomberos*.
title_en: Fue, fueron + a participle that agrees

body_md: **Si hubiera sabido, te hubiera avisado** — both halves take **hubiera**, for something that didn't happen. In speech, porteños often put the second half in the *-aba/-ía* past: **si hubiera sabido, venía** — same meaning.

Life's big steps take the pronoun, like **se casó**: **se recibió** — *graduated* (from the facu, with a title: **se recibió de abogado**) — **me recibí**, **se comprometieron** — *they got engaged* — **se jubiló** — *retired*. The sad one too: **se murió** — *died*.

| what she said | what you tell |
| «Traeme algo.» | Me pidió que le **trajera** algo. |
| «Esperen.» | Nos dijo que **esperáramos**. |
| «Dejalo acá.» | Me pidió que lo **dejara** acá. |
| «Vení.» | Quería que **viniera**. |

A request or an order told later takes the past subjunctive after **que**. News doesn't: *dijo que venía*.

When several people told you, or you'd rather not say who, use **me contaron que…** or **me comentaron que…**: *me contaron que te mudaste*. For one person: **Mati me comentó que renunció**. Porteño news travels by word of mouth and by *audio*, a WhatsApp voice message.
**No tengo señal** — *no signal*; **me quedé sin datos** — *I ran out of data*. **¿Tenés wifi?** is the first question at any bar.
At the front desk one line does it: **tengo una reserva a nombre de** … and your name. They will ask for your **pasaporte**. Staying two nights? *Dos noches.*
To say how things changed, set **antes** + the *-aba / -ía* past against **ahora** + the present: *antes era tranquilo, ahora hay mucho ruido*; *antes costaba poco, ahora es carísimo*.
Pasta is **los fideos**, always plural. Vegetables are **la verdura** or **las verduras** — both are everyday: *no le gusta la verdura*, *me gustan las verduras*.

| what she said | what you tell |
| «¿Venís?» | Me preguntó **si venía**. |
| «Sí.» | Le contesté **que sí**. |
The question comes back with **si** — *she asked me if I was coming*; the answer with **que** — *I told her yes*. What was going on slides into the imperfect: *venís* → **venía**. If it is still true now, the present can stay: *le pregunté si viene*.

**Celeste** is the light blue of the flag — for porteños a different color from *azul*: *No son azules, son celestes.* **Rosa** and **naranja** keep the *-a* for masculine too: *un pantalón rosa*, *un jean naranja*.
A request told later: **me pidió que le trajera algo**. A question: **me preguntó si venía**.
title_en: Me pidió que, me preguntó si

body_md: **Te la hago corta** — *to keep it short* — is usually followed by a long story. **La cuestión es que** — *the point is* — gets to what matters, like **el tema es que**; **en fin** closes it.

**Como si** — *as if* — always takes the past subjunctive: **habla como si supiera todo**, **como si fuera fácil**. **Como si nada** — *as if nothing had happened*. **¡Ni que fuera tan difícil!** — *it's not like it's that hard!*
**Andar** + *-ando, -iendo* is porteño for *going around doing*: **ando buscando laburo**, **¿qué andás haciendo?** It sounds looser than *estoy*.

**Enterarse** for everyone: **nos enteramos tarde** — *we found out late*; **se enteraron todos** — *everybody found out*. The one who tells it best adds **¡ni te cuento!** — *you don't even want to know*.

**Cada vez peor** and **cada vez mejor** — *worse and worse, better and better*. What's in is **de moda**; what's gone **desapareció**: **desaparecieron los almacenes** — *the corner shops disappeared*, and where the old house stood there's a **torre** — *a high-rise*. Ya no es **lo mismo** — *it's not the same anymore*.
A **secreto** stays between two people: **te guardo el secreto** — *I'll keep your secret*. And you promise it: **no se lo digo a nadie, te lo prometo** — *I won't tell anyone, I promise*.

**Metí la pata** — *I messed up, I said or did the wrong thing*. More porteño: **me mandé una macana**. A **macana** is a silly mistake; an **error** is any mistake. And when something goes wrong for someone: **¡qué macana!** — *what a shame!*

**El próximo viernes** is *next Friday* — the same as *el viernes que viene*; **el próximo finde** is *next weekend*. **La próxima** alone is *next time*: *La próxima invito yo.* **La semana que viene** — *next week*, the week that comes — is the form you will hear most.

A wish is *que* + the subjunctive: **que te vaya bien** — *good luck, hope it goes well* — is also a friendly goodbye. The answer to any wish is **gracias, igualmente** — *thanks, you too*. Afterwards you ask **¿cómo te fue?** — *how did it go?*

**Pedir** changes its vowel in some forms. Present: the *e* turns into *i* — **pido**. Past: **pedí** keeps the *e*, but for he or she it turns into *i* — **pidió**. **¿Qué pediste?** — **Pedí un bife.**

**Llevar** is *to take* — and also *to bring* when you're going somewhere: **¿qué llevo al asado?** — *what should I bring?* **Yo llevo el vino** — *I'll bring the wine*: the present does the job of *will*. To *here*, where you are, it's **traer**: **traeme pan**.
**Cargar** — *to tease*, **en joda** — *as a joke*, **me cayó la ficha** — *I finally understood* — humor, porteño style.

**De vez en cuando** is *every now and then*: **fumo de vez en cuando**. **Casi nunca** is *hardly ever*: **casi nunca manejo**. Both can be a whole answer: *¿Salís mucho? — De vez en cuando.* Your **rutina** is what you do every day.

Another life: **si hubieras estudiado, ahora serías médico**. A missed chance: **me hubiera gustado ir**, **tendríamos que haber ido**, **te lo perdiste**. And **hubieras** + participle alone is a reproach: **¡hubieras avisado!** — *you should have told me!*

| the thing | ¿El mensaje? **Lo** recibí. | ¿La foto? **La** mandé. |
| the person | ¿A Sofi? **La** llamé ayer. | ¿A Juan? **Lo** vi. |
| to him, her | **Le** di la llave. | **Les** mandé las fotos. |
| me, you | **Te** llamé. | ¿**Me** llamaste? |

Before the verb, past or present. Only a command takes it on the end: **mostrame**, **buscame**.
title_en: Lo, la, le in the past

body_md: The question at every till. With **crédito** comes a second one: *¿en cuántas cuotas?* — how many monthly payments. *En una cuota* is all at once; **sin interés** means no extra charge. Not sure they take cards? *¿Puedo pagar con tarjeta?*
**A medida que** — *as*, for two things changing together: **a medida que pasa el tiempo, te vas acostumbrando**.

*-ísimo* works on almost anything: **baratísimo**, **lindísima**, and even on *lejos*: **queda lejísimos** — *it's really far away*. It's Spanish everywhere; the everyday porteño *really* is still **re**: *re lindo*.

| | comer | vivir |
| yo | com**o** | viv**o** |
| vos | com**és** | viv**ís** |
| él, ella | com**e** | viv**e** |
| nosotros | com**emos** | viv**imos** |
| ellos, ustedes | com**en** | viv**en** |

-er and -ir are the same except for **vos** and **nosotros**, where each keeps its own vowel. The present also covers *I'm eating* and a near future: *te escribo a la noche* — I'll write to you tonight.
**Te lo presto**, **te lo paso**, **se lo digo** — person first, thing second, and *le* becomes **se**.
On the table: **chimichurri** — oil, garlic, parsley, chili — and **salsa criolla** — onion, tomato, pepper. Ketchup is a crime. The meat is cooked **a la leña** at the good places.

**Fui** is both *I went* (ir) and *I was* (ser); **fue** is both *he went* and *it was*. **Fui a la cancha** — *I went to the game*; **fue re lindo** — *it was really nice*. The sentence always tells you which.
Everything runs on WhatsApp: plans, shops, even the doctor. **Te escribo** — *I'll text you*; **mandame un mensaje**; **llamame**. On Instagram: **seguime** — *follow me*.

For where you went, porteños mostly say **fui a** or **me fui a**: *me fui a Bariloche*, *¿adónde te fuiste en enero?* **Viajar** is more about the trip itself: *viajé en micro*, *viajé sola*, *viajo mañana*. *Viajé a Bariloche* is fine too, just less everyday.
**¿Tocás la guitarra?** **¿Bailás?** And after, a **parrillada** with **chimichurri**, the **bife** bien cocido or jugoso.

| ¿**Hace cuánto** que estudiás? | How long have you been studying? |
| **Llevo** un año **aprendiendo**. | I've been learning for a year. |
| Mis amigos **llevan** meses **buscando** laburo. | My friends have been looking for work for months. |
| **Seguimos** practicando. / **Siguen** tratando. | We're still practicing. / They keep trying. |
| **Dejaron de** venir. | They stopped coming. |
| **Volví a** estudiar. | I went back to studying. |
**Desde que** llegué — *since I arrived* — counts from a moment instead.
**Fue clausurado**, **fueron rescatados**: **fue** + a participle that agrees. And on Sunday, **¿dónde votás?**
**Tampoco** is the *no* version of *también*: *Él no es de acá, y ella tampoco.* — *He's not from here, and neither is she.*
Porteños give the driver a corner, not a house number: *Voy a Thames y Gorriti.* Near the end you guide: *acá a la derecha*, **dejame acá**, *en la esquina está bien*.
**Estaba en la ducha** — the scene; **cuando sonó el timbre** — the event. If you could add *was …-ing* or *used to* in English, it's the imperfect; if it happened once and ended, it's the preterite.
Mate goes around the circle and always comes back to whoever is serving it. Saying **gracias** means *I'm done* — only say it when you don't want another round.
**Cargar** someone is *to tease, to joke with someone*: **¿me estás cargando?** — *are you joking with me?* Porteños **cargan** the people they like; being left alone is the bad sign.

The *each other* verbs take **nos** for *we* and **se** for *they*: **nos conocemos del laburo** — *we know each other from work*; **nos escribimos** — *we write to each other*; **se separaron** — *they split up*; **siempre se pelean** — *they're always fighting*.
An instrument is **tocar**: **¿tocás la guitarra?**, **mi abuelo tocaba el bandoneón en una orquesta**. **¿Cantás?** **¿Bailás tango?** — and at the milonga, **¿bailamos?**

**A esta altura** — *by now* — goes in the *now* half of the sentence: **si me hubiera mudado a Córdoba, a esta altura estaría re tranquilo**. New participles: **mudado, aprendido, dejado, invertido**.
For plans porteños say *voy a*. The future tense is for **guessing**: **¿dónde estará?** — *where can he be?*; **estará en el laburo** — *he's probably at work*.
Two pronouns go person first, thing second: **te lo devuelvo** — *I'll give it back to you*. *Le lo* never happens: it turns into **se lo**.
