To stress a promise, porteños say **me aseguró que…** — *he assured me* — or **me juró que…** — *he swore*. Then **me puso una excusa** — *he gave me an excuse* — and you learn not to **confiar en** (*trust*) the **mentiroso** (*liar*).
Three people now: **soy** de acá, **¿sos** de Capital?, **es** de afuera. Name, origin, role — *ser* carries all of them.
In Argentina the waiter is **el mozo** (or *la moza*). To call one over, *perdón* is the gentle way; *¡mozo!* is heard too. When you're done, ask for **la cuenta**.

**Sobre la hora** — *right at the deadline, at the very last minute* — is how most porteño projects get done. First a **borrador** — *a draft* — then you **corregir** it, and only then the **informe** or the **presentación**. **¿Avanzaron?** — *any progress?*
**Estamos por arrancar** — *we're about to start*. **A punto de** is a little stronger — *any second now*: **estoy a punto de terminar**.

On the bondi, getting on and off carries a *te* on the end: **subite** (get on), **bajate en la esquina** (get off at the corner). And **pará** stops anyone: *¡pará, pará!* In a car, **dejar** is *to drop off*: **dejame acá**, *te dejo en la esquina*.

**Según** — *according to* — takes papers and people: **según el diario**, **según mi mamá**, **según Nico**. **Supuestamente** and **al parecer** keep a distance from what you pass on. **Al parecer** sounds like the news; in chat people say *parece que*.

Things at home break on their own, with **se**: **se tapó el inodoro** — *the toilet's clogged*; **se trabó la puerta** — *the door got stuck* (an elevator stuck between floors **se quedó**: *se quedó el ascensor*); **se cortó el agua**. Nobody did it — it just **se rompió**. **La pileta** is the swimming pool and also the kitchen sink — **la pileta de la cocina**, or **la bacha**.
You don't just ask, you **plantear** it — *raise it, put it on the table*: **le planteé lo del aumento a mi jefa**. Then you **negociar** the **condiciones**.

To stack up reasons: **además** — *besides* — adds one more; **sobre todo** — *above all* — picks the one that counts: *me gusta, **sobre todo** por la gente*. Porteños also say **más que nada** — *mainly*.
Regular verbs make the imperfect with **-aba** (*jugaba, laburaba*) or **-ía** (*comía, salía*). Only *nosotros* takes an accent: **jugábamos**, **salíamos**.
Jobs take no *un*: **es cocinero**, **soy contadora**. The word changes for a woman — *cocinera* — except the *-ista* ones: *periodista*.
**Tarde** works the same way. **A la tarde** is *in the afternoon*; on its own **tarde** means *late*: *Es tarde.* Its opposite is **temprano** — *early*: *Es temprano.*

| a fact — normal verb | a maybe — subjunctive |
| Aunque **llueve**, entreno. | Aunque **llueva**, entreno igual. |
| Por más que me **cuesta**, sigo. | Por más que me **cueste**, sigo. |
| Aunque no **tengo** ganas, voy. | Aunque no **tenga** ganas, voy igual. |

**Aunque sea** — *even just*: *aunque sea un rato*.
Going steady is **estar de novios**. The one before is **mi ex**, and a porteño couple calls each other **amor**. When it ends badly: **me dejó** — *she left me* — or **me mintió** — *he lied to me*.
**Estaba** + *-ando, -iendo* puts you in the middle of something: **estaba durmiendo**, **estábamos cocinando**. Then the preterite cuts in: **cuando sonó el celu**, **cuando entró Juan**.
**Ir** + *-ando, -iendo* is something happening bit by bit: **voy entendiendo** — *I'm starting to get it*; **se va llenando** — *it's filling up*. **De a poco** — *little by little* — goes with it.
Someone from the city of Buenos Aires is **porteño** or **porteña** — from *puerto*, the port. People from the suburbs or the rest of the country are not.

| yo | estoy | vos | estás |
| él, ella | está | nosotros | **estamos** |
| ellos, ustedes | **están** | | |

The word for the feeling matches the people in number too:

| one man | cansad**o** | one woman | cansad**a** |
| men | cansad**os** | women | cansad**as** |

A word ending in *-e* just adds *-s*: *triste, tristes*. *Feliz* becomes **felices**. **¿Sos feliz?**, with *ser*, asks about your life in general, not just right now.

One machine **anda**, two **andan**: **no andan las pilas**. The past is irregular: **ayer anduvo bien** — *it worked fine yesterday*. **Funciona**, **funcionan** mean the same and are just as common. For *how* something works, only *funcionar*: **¿cómo funciona este control?**

The adjective copies its noun: *una campera nueva*, *un jean nuevo*, *los pantalones chicos*. **Grande** has one form for both: *una remera grande*, *las zapatillas grandes*. Adjectives usually come after the noun, not before as in English. With *¡Qué…!* both orders work: *¡Qué linda remera!*, *¡Qué campera fea!*
**Me robaron el celu**, **se rompió el calefón** — and who to call for each.
*Me gustaría* is for wishes and plans. To order or to offer, porteños use **quería** and **¿querés?**: **quería dos entradas**, **¿querés unas medialunas?**, **¿querés tomar unos mates?**
**Abrir** and **recibir** are regular: *abro, abrís, abre*; *recibo, recibís, recibe*. *¿El negocio abre a la noche?* **Recibir a** someone is to have them over: *recibo a mi suegra*.
**Acá se saluda con un beso** — *here people greet with a kiss*. **Se** + verb says what everyone does, no subject needed.

The news says **fue construido**; in conversation porteños turn it around: *construyeron el puente*, *los detuvieron*. Or they use **se**: **el puente se inauguró ayer**, **se construyó hace un siglo**. For the future the news says **será inaugurada** — *will be opened*; people say *la van a inaugurar*.

| **Me merezco** un aumento. | I deserve a raise. |
| **Me lo merezco.** | I deserve it. |
| **Te lo merecés.** | You deserve it. |
**Merecerse** usually comes with its pronoun in speech: the bare *merezco* is correct but more formal. **Valorar** is *to value*: *en mi laburo no me valoran* — *at my job they don't value me*.

**Me preocupa que trabajes tanto** — *it worries me that you work so much*. *Preocupar* and *sorprender* work like *gustar* and *molestar*: **me preocupa**, **me sorprende**, and what follows *que* goes subjunctive.

The **cuarto oscuro** — *the dark room* — is where you vote alone. In national elections since 2025 you get one **boleta** at your mesa, mark it behind a screen and put it in the **urna**. People still say cuarto oscuro, and some provinces keep the old party ballots. The **voto** is secret. If nobody wins outright, there's a **balotaje** — *a runoff*. Missed it? You have to **justificar** why.

When someone believes your joke: **¡caíste!** — *got you!* — and **qué inocente** — *you're so easy to trick*. If they complain too much: **estás exagerando** — *you're overdoing it*. **Te hacés el vivo** — *you're trying to be clever* — is for someone who tries to take advantage of others.
**Me da asco la cucaracha**, **me dan asco las cucarachas** — the verb follows the thing. In the past: **¿te dio miedo?** — **no, me dio risa**.
*Querer* and *poder* change their stem in most forms (*quiero*, *puede*) — but not with vos: **querés**, **podés**. *Ir* is fully irregular: *voy, vas, va, vamos, van*.

A request told later takes the past subjunctive: «Traeme pan» → **me pidió que le trajera pan**; «Esperen» → **nos dijo que esperáramos**. *Dijo que* + subjunctive is an order; *dijo que* + indicative is news.

**Parece que** — *it seems*, *apparently* — passes on news you are not sure of: **parece que va a llover**. *Dicen que* does the same for what people say: *dicen que va a llover todo el finde*. If it turns out to be false, **es mentira**.

**Me bajo en la próxima** — *I'm getting off at the next stop*. Don't know the stop? *¿Cuántas paradas faltan?* or simply *¿Me avisás?* In the subte, changing lines is a **combinación**, and you wait on the **andén**.
What causes the feeling follows **que** in the subjunctive: **me da bronca que no conteste**, **me da vergüenza que me vean así**.
**No sabía** — *I didn't know* — is the imperfect: a state. **Me di cuenta** — *I realized* — is the moment you finally understood. **¿Sabías que…?** opens half the gossip in Buenos Aires.
Working from home is **hacer home office**: English words, said with a Spanish accent. It never means the room: *hoy hago home office* — *I'm working from home today*.

A yes-or-no question told later hangs on **si**: «¿Venís?» → **me preguntó si venía**. *No sé si abre hoy* — *I don't know if it's open today*. **Dudo** — *I doubt it* — takes the subjunctive after **que**: *dudo que venga*.
**Deberías** for advice, **estaría bueno** for a gentle suggestion.
At the verdulería the price moves, so it's **¿a cuánto está el kilo?** — *how much is it a kilo today?* You buy **un kilo**, **medio kilo** or **una docena**.

**Había** is *there was, there were*; **hacía calor** is *it was hot*. **Estaba lloviendo** — *it was raining* — puts you in the middle of it; **llovía** says the same, and can also mean *it used to rain*. **Mientras** — *while* — joins two things going on at once.
Astor **Piazzolla** took the tango out of the **pista** — *the dance floor* — and into the concert hall. The old milongueros never forgave him.

Waking up and getting up are two verbs: **me despierto** at seven, **me levanto** at seven-thirty. With vos the stem doesn't change: **te despertás**. The little word follows the person: *me, te, se, nos* — and **se** again for *ellos*: **se levantan**, **se acuestan**.

**Pido** (I order), **pedís** (you order); in the past **pedí**, **pediste**, and — with an *i* — **pidió**. At the table: **¿Me traés la carta?** and, at the end, **la cuenta**. To get in: **Una mesa para dos, por favor.** And water is **con gas** or **sin gas**: *Para tomar, un agua sin gas.*

| a fact — normal verb | a maybe — subjunctive |
| Aunque **llueve**, vamos. | Aunque **llueva**, vamos. |
| Aunque **cuesta**, sigo. | Aunque **cueste**, sigo. |
| Aunque **estoy** cansado, voy. | Aunque **esté** cansado, voy. |

Left: it *is* raining. Right: whether or not it rains. **Igual** at the end — *anyway* — often closes it.

The *ellos* and *ustedes* form of every verb you have ends in **-n**: *quieren, tienen, laburan, viven, escriben*. *¿Quieren café?* — do you guys want coffee? Hear the *-n* and you know it's more than one.

| **Me robaron** el celu. | My phone got stolen. |
| ¿Cuánto te **cobraron**? | How much did they charge you? |
| **Dicen** que mañana llueve. | They say it'll rain tomorrow. |

The *ellos* form with nobody named is how Spanish says *it got done*: no one to blame, or no one worth naming.
Vos keeps the vowel of the infinitive and stresses it: *comer* → **comés**, *vivir* → **vivís**, *leer* → **leés**.
**Antes de que llegue** — *before he gets here* — always takes the subjunctive: it hasn't happened yet. Same person on both sides: **antes de** + infinitive — *antes de salir*.
Before the hard thing: **no te lo tomes a mal** — *don't take it the wrong way*; **con todo respeto** — *with all due respect*. After it: **no lo dije para ofenderte**.
title_en: No te lo tomes a mal

body_md: Two fixed phrases to learn whole: **a las apuradas** — *in a rush* — and **a la larga** — *in the long run*. Here *las* and *la* are just *the*, not the idiom's *la*: *salí a las apuradas y me olvidé las llaves*.
title_en: A las apuradas, a la larga

body_md: When something doesn't sit right: **me hace ruido** — *something's off about it* — and **no me cierra** — *it doesn't add up*. Porteños say both about a deal, a story, or a new boyfriend.
What everyone does at an asado: **se trae algo**, **se brinda**, **se aplaude al asador**. **Se** + the *él* form, no subject needed.

| | olvidarse | sentirse | ponerse |
| yo | **me olvidé** | **me sentí** | **me puse** |
| vos | **te olvidaste** | **te sentiste** | **te pusiste** |
| él, ella | **se olvidó** | **se sintió** | **se puso** |
| nosotros | **nos olvidamos** | **nos sentimos** | **nos pusimos** |
The pronoun always comes along. Watch *sentirse*: for él and ella the *e* turns into *i* — **se sintió**.
title_en: Me olvidé, me sentí, nos pusimos

body_md: **Me preguntó si venía** — *she asked me if I was coming*. **Le contesté que sí** — *I told her yes*. What was said slides into the imperfect.

To report it you **hacés la denuncia** at the **comisaría**, or online. The **policía** rarely finds the phone; the denuncia is for the insurance. To block the line, call your phone company. In an emergency, call **911**.
**Se casó** — *got married*, **nació** — *was born*, **me emocioné** — *I got emotional* — the news that matters.

**Por lo menos** — *at least* — finds the good side: *pagan poco, pero **por lo menos** queda cerca*. **La verdad** — *honestly* — says what you really think: ***la verdad**, no me conviene*. **Conviene** works like *gustar*: **me conviene** — *it's better for me*; **te conviene llevar paraguas** — *it's a good idea to take an umbrella*.
Same recipe as *mirá* and *vení*: drop the *-r*, stress the end. **Doblá**, **cruzá**, **caminá**, **preguntá**. *Seguir* says *sigo*, but its command is regular: **seguí**.
Two forms of *ser* so far: **soy** for yourself, **sos** for the person in front of you. *Soy Lucía, ¿y vos?* — *¿Sos turista?* The words *yo* and *vos* are optional; the verb already says who.

Start from the *yo* of the present and swap the vowel: *-ar* verbs take **e**, the rest take **a**.
| yo (now) | vos | yo, él, ella |
| llamo | **llames** | **llame** |
| vengo | **vengas** | **venga** |
| hago | **hagas** | **haga** |
| traigo | **traigas** | **traiga** |
| voy | **vayas** | **vaya** |
*Ir* is the odd one out, and its *we* is **vayamos**: *¿querés que vayamos mañana?*
Reporting a promise moves it into *would*: «voy» → **dijo que iría**; «te llamo» → **dijo que me llamaría**. Porteños also say **dijo que iba a venir** — same thing.

The **plazo** moves: they **postergaron la fecha** — *pushed the date back* — or, worse, **la adelantaron**. Then it's **horas extra** until **entregamos** — *we hand it in* (also *we handed it in*). And the boss asks: **¿ya lo entregaste?**

The thing liked is the subject; the pronoun says who likes it:
| a mí | **me** gusta nadar | **me** interesa el tenis |
| a vos | **te** gusta viajar | **te** interesan los deportes |
| a él, a ella | **le** gusta cantar | **le** interesa la música |
| a nosotros | **nos** gusta pasear | **nos** encanta la playa |
| a ellos, a ustedes | **les** gusta el fútbol | **les** encantan las series |
With a verb it stays singular: *me gusta nadar y cantar*. To name the person, put **a** in front and keep **le**: *A mi hermano le gusta nadar.* **Odiar** is a normal verb: *odio, odiás*.

In Argentina voting is **obligatorio** from 18 to 70. **¿A quién votaste?** is a real question, though many people don't answer it. **Votar a** someone: *voté a otro candidato*. **Votar por** works too: *¿por quién votás?* **Votar en blanco** is to cast a blank vote.
**Todo aumenta**, **el café subió**, **¿cuánto te cobraron?** — the small talk of prices.
**Había** + a participle is the past behind another past: **cuando llegué, ya habían comido** — *when I got there, they'd already eaten*. Buenos Aires uses this one freely.

**Me estafaron** — *I got scammed* : nobody grabs anything, they trick you. A fake call from the bank, a **billete trucho**, or the **cuento del tío**: a caller pretends to be a relative or an official and asks for money. First thing: **bloqueá la tarjeta**. Then the denuncia; if you're lucky, the street **cámaras** recorded it.
A **milonga** is both a dance hall and a faster cousin of the tango. The instrument that sighs is the **bandoneón**.
**Dejé de fumar**, **volvió a correr**, **solemos cenar tarde**.

Unlike *a menos que*, **por si** — *just in case* — keeps the normal verb. It's what people say for everyday precautions: **llevá paraguas por si llueve**; *te dejo las llaves por si llegás antes*. Short version: **por las dudas** — *llevá paraguas, por las dudas*.

In Argentina every Spaniard is a **gallego**, from Galicia or not. It is informal and friendly, but some Spaniards do not like it; the neutral word is **español**. And the great-grandparents still pay off: half of Buenos Aires is getting Italian or Spanish citizenship — **sacar la ciudadanía**. Your **raíces** — *roots* — come with a passport.
Passing on a message ends with who it's from: **saludos de parte de mi vieja**. And the classic order from home, told later: «Portate bien» → **me dijo que me portara bien**.

A document that has run out is **vencido**: *tengo el pasaporte vencido*. What comes next: **renovar** — *renew it*; **completar el formulario** — *fill in the form*; **hacer la cola** (or **la fila**) — *stand in line*; **firmar** — *sign*.

A porteño sentence breathes through its fillers: **ponele** — *let's say*; **digamos** — *sort of*; **qué sé yo** — *I don't know*; **bah** — *well, I mean*: *son las ocho, bah, ponele* — or a shrug, *oh well*. The ones you will hear most: **o sea** — *I mean*; **tipo** — *like, around*: *es tipo a las nueve*; and **viste** at the end, for *you know*: *estaba cansado, viste*.

Spanish *has* what English *is*:
| tengo hambre | I'm hungry |
| ¿tenés sed? | are you thirsty? |
| tiene frío | he's (she's) cold |
| tengo calor | I'm hot |
| tengo sueño | I'm sleepy |
| tengo miedo | I'm scared |
The same **tengo, tenés, tiene** as *tengo veinte años*.
At any **ventanilla**, open with **una consulta** — *a quick question* — and ask for the **requisitos**, *what they need*. They'll say **el original y una copia**, and they mean both.

**Me da cosa** has two uses. Doing something feels awkward: **me da cosa pedirle plata** — *I feel awkward asking him for money*. Or a thing gives you a bad feeling: **ese perro me da cosa** — *that dog makes me uneasy*. **Me pone mal** — *it makes me sad*. **Me quedé con las ganas** — *I missed out, and I still want to*.

Porteños give an address as street and number — *Corrientes 1500* — and ask **¿a qué altura?** to know which block. The number goes up about a hundred every **cuadra**. To ask the way: **¿Cómo llego a la estación?** — *how do I get to the station?*

The past has an ending for everyone: **cenamos** (we had dinner), **llegaron** (they arrived, you all arrived). *-amos* looks like the present — **anoche cenamos** tells you when — and *-aron* is only ever the past.
The same two joins as before: *a la plaza* but **al** parque, **al** hospital; *la estación **del** subte*, *la parada **del** bondi*.

The easy way to order is to ask the waiter to bring it: **¿Me traés un café?** — literally "do you bring me a coffee?". *Quiero un café* works too: **quiero**, **¿querés?** — no *ie* in the vos form. Or just name it: *Para mí, un té.* Add **por favor**.
**Funcionar** is *to work* for things: **el subte no funciona**, **los semáforos no funcionan**. In everyday talk porteños also say **andar**: *el ascensor no anda*. People *trabajan* or *laburan*.
Where English says *used to*, Spanish just uses the imperfect: **Siempre tomaba mate con mi abuela** — *I always used to have mate with my grandma*.

Tech orders are plain vos commands: **descargá la app**, **borrá las fotos**. What you already did is preterite: **la descargué**, **las borré**. Day to day people say **bajá** or **bajate** for *download*: **bajate la app, es gratis**. *Descargar* is what the screen says.

**Aparentemente** is the neutral *apparently*: **aparentemente, mañana hay paro**; **por lo visto** means the same. **Se ve que** is what you conclude from what you see: **se ve que llovió** — *it must have rained*; **se ve que está cerrado**.
**Estoy laburando** — I'm working (right now). In Argentina, *estoy llegando* can mean you're still ten minutes away.

Change, person by person: **cambiaste un montón**, **cambiaron los precios**, **el barrio mejoró**, **el servicio empeoró**. **Estás cambiado** — *you look different* — agrees like an adjective: *estás cambiada*.
**Te recomiendo que vayas** — *I'd recommend you go*. **Es mejor que** works the same way: **es mejor que pidas un taxi**.

**Ir** — *to go* — looks nothing like its forms: **voy**, **vas**, **va**, **vamos**, **van**. Spanish uses one form for *I go* and *I'm going*: *Voy a la plaza* is both. And **vamos** on its own also means *let's go*.

**Avisame** — *let me know*: **dale, avisame mañana**. **Te aviso** — *I'll let you know*. To meet up: **¿nos encontramos en la esquina?** — *should we meet on the corner?* — and **te espero** — *I'll wait for you*.

**Capaz**, **a lo mejor** and **quizás** all mean *maybe*; **seguro que** is *I bet*; **supongo que** is *I guess*; **probablemente** is *probably*. All take the plain present: **capaz está en la plaza**, **seguro que es Fede**. In Buenos Aires you will hear **capaz** much more than **quizás**.

**Me quejo** — *I complain*; **renegar** is the Argentine *to struggle with something, to grumble*. For a habit: **siempre reniego con el wifi**. For something going on now: **estoy renegando con el trámite del DNI**. Someone who's **agotado** is *exhausted*; the **estrés** is why. And the traffic? **Un caos**.

**Qué pesado** — *what a pain* — for someone who won't let it go. **Divertido** is *fun*, **tímido** *shy*. For a woman: **pesada**, **divertida**, **tímida**. With **estar** it is just for now: *Nico está pesado hoy* — *Nico's being annoying today*.

**Es cualquiera** — *that's nonsense*; **dijo cualquiera** — *he talked nonsense*; **hizo cualquiera** — *he did something stupid*. **Flasheaste** — *you're imagining things*. And a **¡qué lindo!** can be sincere, or ironic when the rain starts.

Spanish tells accidents as if they happened *to* you: **se me cayó** — *I dropped it* (it fell, and it happened to me); **se me rompió** — *it broke on me*; **se me pasó** — *I forgot* (it slipped my mind). Nobody is to blame, which is the point.

| do | don't |
| Vení. | No **vengas**. |
| Andá. | No **vayas**. |
| Decime. | No **me digas**. |
| Tocá. | No **toques**. |
| Olvidate. | No **te olvides**. |

*No* + the subjunctive (*tocar* → **toques**: the *c* turns into *qu* to keep its sound), and the pronoun moves in front: *preocupate* → **no te preocupes**. **¡No me digas!** on its own shows surprise: *no way!*

In Buenos Aires you don't google an electrician, you ask around: **¿conocés a alguien de confianza?** Same for a flatmate: *busco a alguien **ordenado**, que no **fume** y que **comparta** los gastos*.
**Y nada** is the porteño *so, yeah*: it fills the pause at the end of a story. **Al toque** — *right away*: **me contestó al toque**.
Something that isn't true now: **si tuviera plata, viajaría** — *if I had money, I'd travel*. The *si* half uses a new form, **tuviera**, **fuera**, **pudiera**.

| No **dejes** el celu en la mesa. | Don't leave your phone on the table. |
| No **saques** la billetera. | Don't take your wallet out. |
| No le **cuentes** a nadie. | Don't tell anyone. |
| No **te vayas**. | Don't go. |
| No **te pongas** nervioso. | Don't get nervous. |
| No **seas** así. | Don't be like that. |
Every *don't* grows from the *yo* of the present: *dejo* → **dejes**, *cuento* → **cuentes**, *saco* → **saques** (the *c* turns *qu* to keep its sound). *Ser* and *ir* break the rule: **seas**, like *sea*, and **vayas** (*no te vayas*).

Every new verb here is a regular -ar verb, so you already know them: *practic**o**, practic**ás**, practic**a**, practic**amos***. Learn the infinitive and the rest comes free: *necesito, usás, ayuda, enseñan*.

-ar verbs take **-ado**, the rest **-ido**: **tomado, reservado, quedado, perdido, conseguido**. *Traer* gives **traído**, with an accent. *Si hubiera tomado un taxi…*, *si me hubiera quedado en casa…*
**¿Cómo andás?** is the everyday porteño *how are you?* — you will hear it all day. The answer is short: *Bien.* or *Todo bien.* **¿Qué onda?** gets the same answer: *¿Qué onda? — Todo bien.*

People get lunfardo labels: a **chanta** talks big and doesn't deliver, a **cheto** is snobby or upper-class, and someone **piola** is cool and easy-going. **No me chamuyes** — *don't give me that* — is the subjunctive again.

To say *the black one*, drop the noun and keep **el** or **la**: *¿El negro o el azul?* — *the black one or the blue one?* *Quiero la roja* — *I want the red one*. The same works with *este* and *ese*: *Quiero este* — *I want this one*.

| | traer | querer | venir | poder |
| yo | traje | quise | vine | pude |
| vos | trajiste | quisiste | viniste | pudiste |
| él, ella | trajo | quiso | vino | pudo |
| nosotros | | | vinimos | pudimos |
| ellos | trajeron | | vinieron | pudieron |
Same endings as *hice*: *-e, -iste, -o, -imos, -ieron* — after a *j*, just *-eron*: **dijeron, trajeron**. **No vino nadie** — *nobody came*: after the verb, *nadie* still needs the *no*; in front, it doesn't: *nadie trajo hielo*.

The question at every register. **Crédito** usually means **cuotas**, and the good ones are **sin interés**. A **caja de ahorro** (*savings account* by name) is really the everyday bank account: your pay arrives there and your debit card uses it.
**Te transfiero** — *I'll transfer it to you*; with vos, **¿me transferís?** The past: **te transferí**, **¿me transferiste?** — but él changes to **transfirió**. Asking for it: **transferime**.

| Me **pone nervioso** que llegue tarde. | It annoys me when he's late. |
| Me **enoja** que me **mienta**. | It makes me angry that he lies to me. |
| Me **alegra** que vengas. | I'm glad you're coming. |
| Me da bronca que **cancele**. | It makes me mad that he cancels. |

Feeling first, then **que** + subjunctive. **Nervioso** here is often *annoyed* or *tense*, not only *nervous*. If it's you doing it, no *que*: *me enoja **llegar** tarde*.
title_en: Me pone, me enoja, me alegra

body_md: **Te estaba tomando el pelo**, **¡caíste!**, **no te piques** — teasing someone, porteño style: *I was joking with you*, *you believed it!*, *don't get offended*.

**Me mudé** — *I moved (house)*; **nos mudamos** — *we moved*. It always carries *me/te/se/nos*: **te mudaste**, **se mudó**. **Mudarse con** is *to move in with*. The **mudanza** is the move itself, and always a *quilombo* (a mess).

| 100 | **cien** — but **ciento** before more: *ciento cincuenta* |
| 200, 300, 400 | **doscientos**, **trescientos**, **cuatrocientos** |
| 500 | **quinientos** |
| 600 | **seiscientos** |
| 700 | **setecientos** |
| 800 | **ochocientos** |
| 900 | **novecientos** |
| 1000 | **mil** — never *un mil* |
Watch **quinientos**, **setecientos** and **novecientos**: they don't sound like *cinco*, *siete*, *nueve*.

Throw it back at your friend with the vos ending, **-ías**: **¿vos qué le dirías?** — *what would you tell him?* **Tendrías que** is advice with gloves on: **tendrías que llamarlo**, softer than *tenés que*.
**Nacer** — *to be born*: **¿dónde naciste?**, **el bebé nació ayer**. **Está embarazada** — *she's pregnant*.
After half past, porteños count down to the next hour: **las ocho menos cuarto** is *7:45*, *las nueve menos diez* is *8:50*. On the hour exactly: **a las diez en punto**.

**Estoy orgulloso de vos** — *I'm proud of you*. A woman says **orgullosa** and **agradecida**. **Agradecido** — *grateful*: **estoy muy agradecida**. Grateful *to* a person: **agradecido con vos**. Grateful *for* a thing: **agradecida por el regalo**.
*de + el* always becomes **del**, and *a + el* becomes **al**: *la parada del bondi*, *voy al centro*.
When someone says *gracias*, answer **de nada**. *Of course* is **claro**. And when everything is fine or agreed, porteños say **¡joya!** — *¿Todo bien? — ¡Joya!*

When the meat reaches the table, **se aplaude al asador**: *¡un aplauso para el asador!* **Se brinda** with everyone at the table. Leaving without saying goodbye to each person? Very **maleducado**. And **los ñoquis del 29**: on the 29th of each month people eat gnocchi, with money under the plate for luck.

The second verb follows the first into the past:

| now | then |
| Quiero que **vengas**. | Quería que **vinieras**. |
| Te pido que **llames**. | Te pedí que **llamaras**. |
| Me dice que **espere**. | Me dijo que **esperara**. |

The past subjunctive is the *ellos* past with **-ra**: *vinieron* → **viniera**, *hicieron* → **hiciera**. With vos: **vinieras, hicieras, llamaras**. The *yo* and *él/ella* forms are the same: **quería que viniera** — *wanted me / him / her to come*.

**¡Qué suerte que vivas cerca!**, **¡qué bueno que estemos todos juntos!** Any *qué* + reaction + *que* brings the subjunctive. **Estemos** is *we*: **-mos** on the end. About something already over, porteños just use the past: **¡qué suerte que no llovió!**

**Seguir** + *-ando / -iendo* is *still doing* or *keep doing*: **sigo laburando ahí**, **¿seguís viviendo en San Telmo?** With a noun or adjective it is just *still*: **sigo cansado**, **¿seguís con fiebre?** **Seguir sin** + infinitive is *still not*: **¿seguís sin fumar?**
Buenos Aires has more psychologists per person than almost anywhere, so **deberías ir a terapia** isn't an insult — it's what a good friend says.
**Disculpá** gets a stranger's attention: *Disculpá, ¿sos Martín?* **Permiso** is what you say to get past someone, on a full bus or in a doorway.
**Tenés que llevar una fotocopia** — *you have to*; **hace falta una fotocopia** — *a photocopy is needed*, no person named; **no hace falta** — *there's no need*.
When it lands badly: **perdoname, me expresé mal** — *I put it badly*; **quise decir otra cosa** — *I meant something else*; **no fue mi intención lastimarte**.

Opening hours are **desde** … **hasta**: *abre desde las nueve hasta las seis*. Shorter, and more common: *abre **de** nueve **a** seis*. At twelve it's **el mediodía** — and plenty of small shops **cierran** for a while right after it. With **desde**, Spanish uses the present: *estoy acá desde las ocho* = I've been here since eight.
title_en: Desde las nueve hasta las seis

body_md:
| | querer | poder | ir |
| yo | quiero | puedo | voy |
| vos | **querés** | **podés** | vas |
| él, ella | quiere | puede | va |
| nosotros | **queremos** | **podemos** | vamos |
| ellos, ustedes | quieren | pueden | van |

*e → ie* and *o → ue* everywhere except **vos** and **nosotros**. *Ir* is its own thing, and takes **a** + place (*a + el* = **al**): *voy al súper*, *voy a la facu*. **Salir** only bends in *yo*: **salgo**, *salís*, *sale*. Add an infinitive for plans: *¿Querés salir?*

Offer help with **te doy una mano**. If they try to carry the bags themselves: **dejá, dejá**. When they thank you: **no es nada** or **faltaba más** (*don't mention it*). And they may call you **querido** or **querida**.
**No me habían avisado** — *nobody had told me*; **ya lo había llamado** — *I'd already called him*. One more irregular participle: *escribir* → **escrito**.

*Amarillo* works like *rojo*: **amarilla, amarillos**. But **gris** and **marrón** are the same for *el* and *la* — *un buzo gris*, *una campera gris* — and only add *-es* for more than one: *unas zapatillas grises*.
Any verb after **no es que** goes subjunctive: **no me interese**, **no queramos**, **me caiga mal**.
title_en: No es que no me interese

body_md: Still a plain question in the present with **me** in front: **¿me acompañás?** — *will you come with me?*; **¿me llevás?** — *can you give me a ride?*; **¿me regás las plantas?** — *can you water my plants?* Asking for two of you? Swap *me* for **nos**: **¿nos llevás?** — *can you take us?*

**Saber** is to know a fact or how to do something: *sé dónde vive*. **Conocer** is to know a person or a place: **conozco a Juan**, *¿conocés Córdoba?* In the past it changes meaning: **conocí a Juan** — *I met Juan* (for the first time).

| **Se trae** algo. | You bring something. |
| **Se pone** la mesa. | The table gets set. |
| **Se brinda** con todos. | Everyone toasts together. |
| **Se aplaude** al asador. | Everyone applauds the grill master. |

**Se** + the *él* form: no subject, because it's everybody. *Acá se come tarde* works the same way. As a guest you say **llevar**: **¿qué llevo?** — *what should I bring?* The host, already there, says **traer**: **¿quién trae el vino?**
title_en: Se: what everyone does at an asado

body_md:
Words that describe someone change for a man or a woman:

| a man | a woman |
| argentin**o** | argentin**a** |
| uruguay**o** | uruguay**a** |
| porteñ**o** | porteñ**a** |
| ingl**és** | ingl**esa** |

*-o* becomes *-a*. A word ending in a consonant adds *-a*, and *inglés* loses its accent: **inglesa**.

Put **lo** before an adjective to say *the … thing*: **lo lindo** — *the nice thing*, **lo feo** — *the bad part* (same as **lo malo**), **lo único** — *the only thing*. Add **de** to say of what: **lo peor de Buenos Aires es el tránsito**. **Lo** never changes: **lo feo son los precios**.

The rest of the story is in the third person: **consiguió laburo** — *she got a job*; **renunció** — *he quit*. Nobody says *fue despedido*: it's **lo echaron** — *they fired him* — and **me contrataron** — *they hired me*.

To state a guess, porteños mostly say **debe** + infinitive: **debe estar en el laburo** — *he must be at work*; **debe tener cuarenta**; **deben ser las ocho**; to vos, **debés estar cansado** — *you must be tired*. The future is more for the question: **¿dónde estará?**, **¿qué hora será?**
The moment you snap is in the past: **me harté** — *I got fed up*; porteños say **me pudrí**: **me pudrí y me fui**. Both take **de** + infinitive: **me pudrí de esperar**. Then one word: **¡basta!**
Reported promises go into *would*: **dijo que vendría**, **me prometiste que me llamarías**. Out loud, porteños more often say **dijo que iba a venir**; *vendría* is correct but more careful.
A thing left behind is **me olvidé**: **me olvidé las llaves**. Something you did not remember to do is **se me pasó**: **se me pasó llamar a mi vieja** — or **me olvidé de llamar**.
title_en: Me olvidé or se me pasó?

body_md: **Facturas** are the pastries you buy by the dozen at the bakery — *medialunas* are the best known. The same word also means *invoice*, but at the bakery it's always pastries.
Porteños describe people by the obvious and nobody minds: **morocho** is dark-haired, **rubio** fair, **flaco** thin, **petiso** short. *Flaco* is even a nickname: *¿Todo bien, flaco?*

When someone lends you something, the conditions come fast: *te lo presto, con tal de que lo **cuides**, no lo **choques** y me lo **devuelvas entero***. The warning at the end is **si no** — *otherwise*: *si no, no te presto nada más*.
Before an interview or an exam porteños say **¡éxitos!** or **¡mucha suerte!** — and before a **parcial**, the university exam everyone dreads, both.

A taxi is black and yellow; you stop it in the street when the red *libre* sign is lit: *¿Está libre?* A **remis** is a car you book by phone at a fixed price. Most people now use an app: *pido un auto por la app*. A taxi driver is a **tachero**.

| | cenar | pagar | llegar |
| yo | cen**é** | pag**ué** | lleg**ué** |
| vos | cen**aste** | pag**aste** | lleg**aste** |
| él, ella | cen**ó** | pag**ó** | lleg**ó** |
| nosotros | cen**amos** | pag**amos** | lleg**amos** |
| ellos, ustedes | cen**aron** | pag**aron** | lleg**aron** |
*-amos* looks like the present, so the time says which: **anoche cenamos afuera**. *-aron* is only ever the past: *hablaron, tomaron*. In *yo*, *-gar* verbs add a *u* to keep the hard *g*: **pagué**, **llegué**.

The little word says who likes it; *gusta* or *gustan* matches the food:

| a mí | **me** gusta el pollo |
| a vos | **te** gusta el pescado |
| a él, a ella | **le** gusta la fruta |
| a nosotros | **nos** gustan los fideos |
| a ellos, a ustedes | **les** gustan los huevos |

*Les* is *them* or *you all*: add **a ellos** or **a ustedes** when it isn't clear.
**Tengo que laburar** is *I have to work*; **hay que** names no person — it just has to be done: **hay que sacar la basura** — *the trash has to go out*.

**Dar** has a short past with no accents: **di, diste, dio** — *le di la llave*. And *buscar* bends in *yo* to keep the hard *c* sound: **busqué** (not *buscé*). **Buscar** is *to look for* and also *to pick someone up*: *busqué la billetera*, *la busqué a Mica en la estación*.
With *-se* verbs the pronoun goes in front: *me voy* → **no te vayas**, *me puse nervioso* → **no te pongas nervioso**, *me enojé* → **no te enojes**. And the one every friend says: **no seas así**.
title_en: No te vayas, no te pongas así

body_md: After a game it's **ganamos**, **perdimos** or **empatamos** — *we* won, even if you were on the sofa. Fans always talk as part of the team: *Anoche ganamos tres a uno.*

**Me gustaría** — *I'd like* — is *gustar* in the conditional, with the same *me*: **me gustaría ir**, **¿te gustaría venir?**. **Me encantaría** is the enthusiastic yes. For more than one thing, **-ían**: **nos encantarían unas empanadas**. To order or offer something day to day, porteños say **quería** or **¿querés?**: *¿querés tomar unos mates?*
On a command the pronoun sticks to the verb: **llamame**, **mandame**, **dame**, **prestame**. Anywhere else it goes in front: **te llamo**, **¿me mandás?**
title_en: The little word goes on the end

body_md: Every club has its **ídolo**, the **jugador** whose shirt the kids wear. And every fan fears one word: the **descenso** — *relegation*.
A negative command is the subjunctive: **no te preocupes**, **no te olvides**, **no digas nada**. **Probá** becomes **no pruebes**.
A **rumor** is just that until someone **confirma**: *el club confirmó la noticia*. Or as porteños say about any rumor: **dicen que…**

**Estaba nervioso** is how you were; **me puse nervioso** is the moment it hit you. **Me sentí re mal** — *I felt awful* — is one moment too. For *us*: **nos pusimos contentos**; and **me puse colorado** is *I blushed*. About someone else: **¿cómo se sintió tu vieja?**

| yo, él, ella | **hubiera** | tomado, reservado, quedado |
| vos | **hubieras** | perdido, conseguido, traído |
| nosotros | **hubiéramos** | salido, llegado |
| ellos | **hubieran** | avisado, venido |

**Si hubiéramos salido antes, no hubiéramos perdido el vuelo.** Both halves take *hubiera*, matched to the person.

| **Cuanto antes lleguemos**, mejor. | The sooner we get there, the better. |
| **Cuanto antes reservemos**, más barato. | The sooner we book, the cheaper. |
| **Cuanto más** ganás, más gastás. | The more you earn, the more you spend. |

For what hasn't happened yet, the subjunctive; for what always happens, the normal verb.
For someone else the little word is **se**: *me llamo*, *te llamás*, **se llama**. *¿Cómo se llama él?* — *Se llama Juan.*

Nobody, nothing, no one at all — always the subjunctive, because it doesn't exist: **no conozco a nadie que hable inglés**, **no hay ningún electricista que venga el domingo**. **Algún, ningún** drop the *-o* before a masculine noun (*algún bar*, *ningún electricista*); **alguna, ninguna** for feminine ones.
With a vos command the pronoun joins the end, and there is no accent: **llamame**, **mandame un audio**, **dame**, **prestame**. *Le* and *les* are *to him, to her, to them*.
A **kiosco** is the corner shop that sells drinks, sweets and cigarettes and tops up your SUBE (the bus and subway card), often through a window onto the street. Many are open all night.

| **Voy entendiendo.** | I'm starting to get it. |
| **Vas aprendiendo** de a poco. | You're learning bit by bit. |
| **Estoy por** salir. | I'm about to leave. |
| **Está por** llover. | It's about to rain. |

**Ir** + gerund is change in progress; **estar por** + infinitive is what's about to happen.

Add **-s** after a vowel (*medialuna → medialunas*) and **-es** after a consonant. The word for "a" disappears: *una empanada*, but *dos empanadas*. **¿Cuántos?** or **¿cuántas?** matches the thing: *¿cuántas medialunas?*, *¿cuántos abuelos?*

| if (then) | now |
| Si **hubieras** estudiado medicina, | ahora **serías** médico. |
| Si me **hubiera** mudado, | a esta altura **estaría** tranquilo. |
| Si **hubiéramos** invertido, | ahora **tendríamos** ahorros. |
| Si **hubieras** aprendido inglés, | ahora **sabrías** qué hacer. |

*Hubiera* + participle for the past that went another way; the conditional for today.
**Me la jugué** — *I took the risk*; **la pifié** — *I messed up*; **la rompe** — *he's amazing*; **te las arreglás** — *you manage*. The same *la* that points at nothing.
**No doy más** — *I can't take it anymore*. **No lo aguanto** — *I can't stand him*. And when it's one thing too many: **¡es el colmo!**
Your clothing size is your **talle**: *¿Qué talle usás?* (you'll also hear *¿Qué talle sos?*) Argentine sizes run small, so ask to try it on before you pay: **¿Puedo probarme esto?**

Tell it in the past: **lo que pasó fue que se cortó la luz**. Say what you meant: **lo que quiero decir es que…**. You already know **lo que más** — *what… most*: **lo que más me molestó fue eso**. And **en el fondo** — *deep down* — for the real reason under it.
One form covers both: **él es** and **ella es**. It also works for a name: *Juan es de Rosario.*

| more than | **más** alto **que** yo |
| less than | **menos** caro **que** |
| as … as | **tan** lindo **como** |
| better, worse | **mejor**, **peor** |
| older, younger | **más grande**, **más chico** |
| really | rico → **riquísimo**, caro → **carísimo** |
The describing word still matches the person: *mi hermana es más alta que yo*. Say **mejor** for *better*; about a person, **más buena** means *nicer*. **El más chico** is *the youngest*, **el peor** *the worst*.

**Servir** is *to be of use*, and it works like *gustar*: **¿te sirven?** — *can you use them?*; **sí, me sirve** — *that works for me*. Things that are no good **no sirven**: **estas zapatillas no sirven**.
**Según el diario**, **al parecer**, **supuestamente** — passing it on without vouching for it.
**Te juro** — *I swear* — is how a porteño vouches for the story: **te juro que me dijo eso**. A long talk with a friend is **una charla**: **charlé con Sofi**.

**Tener que** changes with the person: **tenés que firmar** — *you have to sign*; **tiene que venir ella** — *she has to come*; **tienen que esperar** — *they have to wait*. **Hay que** stays the same for everyone: **hay que hacer la fila**.
title_en: Tenés que, tiene que, tienen que

body_md: **Hace un año que estudio** says the same as **llevo un año estudiando**. **Seguimos buscando** — *we're still looking*; **volví a empezar** — *I started again*.

**Gracias por todo** — *thanks for everything*; **mil gracias** — *thanks a million*; **gracias otra vez** — *thanks again*. The thanks gets bigger, the grammar doesn't change. You already know **un montón**: *gracias un montón*.

| | ser | tener | vivir | ir |
| yo, él, ella | era | tenía | vivía | iba |
| vos | eras | tenías | vivías | ibas |
| nosotros | éramos | teníamos | vivíamos | íbamos |
This past describes: how things *were*, what you *had*, where you *lived*, what you *used to* do. *Yo* and *él* share one form — the story tells you which. **De chico** is *as a kid*: **De chico vivía en Rosario.** It changes with the person: **de chica** (a woman), **de chicos** (*we*).

| him, or a masculine thing | **lo**, **los** | ¿El audio? **Lo** mando ahora. |
| her, or a feminine thing | **la**, **las** | ¿La tarjeta? **La** tengo. |
| to him, her, them | **le**, **les** | **Le** doy la llave. |
| me, you, us | **me**, **te**, **nos** | **Te** llamo mañana. |
Before a normal verb: *la tengo*. With a name you often say both: *lo llamo a Juan*, *les mando un audio a mis viejos*. Stuck to the end of a command, with no accent: **llamame**, **dame**, **mandame**, **prestame**. **Buscar** is *to look for*, and also *to pick someone up*: *te busco a las ocho* = *te paso a buscar*.
title_en: Lo, la, le — where they go

body_md: **Pronto** — *soon*; **a fin de año** — *at the end of the year*; **algún día** — *some day*. **¿Qué piensan hacer?** — **Pensamos juntar plata para viajar.** Careful: **pensar** + a verb is *to plan to*, but **pensar que** is *to think that*: *Juan piensa que tenés razón.* And the classic promise: **me anoté en el gimnasio**.
**Merecerse** — *to deserve* — comes with its pronoun: **me merezco un aumento**, **te lo merecés**. And a boss who **valora** your work says so with the sueldo.

Porteños close the thought with **igual** — *anyway*: *aunque esté cansada, voy igual*; *gracias igual* — *thanks anyway*. **De todos modos** says the same but sounds written: *salí de todos modos*. **A pesar de** takes a noun or an infinitive: *a pesar del frío*.
The subjunctive for *they* adds **-n** (**sean**, **estén**, **lleguen**); for *we*, **-mos** (**salgamos**, **hagamos**). The rule for when to use it doesn't change.
**Como si** with a *no*: **como si no pasara nada**, **como si no me viera**, **como si no le importara**. And the comeback: **¡ni que fueras mi viejo!** — *it's not like you're my dad!*
A command with *no* uses the subjunctive: *vení* but **no vengas**, *andá* but **no vayas**, *decime* but **no me digas**. The pronoun moves to the front: **no te preocupes**.

**Reírse** is *to laugh*: **me río mucho con vos** — *I laugh a lot with you*. You already know **me reí** and **nos reímos**; with *vos* in the past it is **te reíste**: **¿de qué te reíste?** **Llorar** is *to cry*: **lloré con esa película**.

You will hear these words every day — in traffic, at soccer games, between friends. Learn to understand them first. Say them only with close friends who already swear with you. Never to a stranger, at work, to someone older or to the police.

| **Tendría que haber** ido. | I should have gone. |
| **Tendrías que haber** avisado. | You should have let me know. |
| **Tendríamos que haber** salido antes. | We should have left earlier. |
| **Tendrían que haber** llamado. | They should have called. |
| **Me hubiera gustado** verte. | I'd have liked to see you. |

And the feeling: **me arrepiento**, **¿te arrepentís?**, **se arrepintió**.

Porteño thanks praise the person: **sos un genio**, **me salvaste** — *you saved me*. To a woman it is always **sos una genia**. For a present: **¡qué detalle!** — *how thoughtful!* — or **¡te pasaste!** — *this is too much, you did an amazing job!* Said in an angry voice, the same words mean *you went too far*.

The little word in front changes with the person, and so does the verb:

| yo | **me llamo** | my name is |
| vos | **te llamás** | your name is |

The question puts *cómo* first: **¿Cómo te llamás?** The vos form ends in **-ás**, with the stress on the end.

| | practicar | necesitar | ayudar |
| yo | practic**o** | necesit**o** | ayud**o** |
| vos | practic**ás** | necesit**ás** | ayud**ás** |
| él, ella | practic**a** | necesit**a** | ayud**a** |
| nosotros | practic**amos** | necesit**amos** | ayud**amos** |
| ellos, ustedes | practic**an** | necesit**an** | ayud**an** |

*Usar, buscar, preguntar, enseñar* work the same way. The vos form always carries the accent: *¿Qué buscás?*

Even when you name the person, the **le** stays: **le dije a Juan que no**, **le di la llave a Sofi**, **les mandé las fotos a mis viejos**. English says it once; a porteño says it twice. With *lo* or *la* next to it, *le* turns into **se**: *¿La foto? Ya se la mandé a Juan.*
title_en: Le di la llave a Sofi

body_md:
The same two endings as *me llamo, te llamás*, on other verbs:
| | yo | vos |
| llamarse | **me llamo** | **te llamás** |
| hablar | **hablo** | **hablás** |
| entender | **entiendo** | **entendés** |
| saber | **sé** | **sabés** |
The vos form is stressed on the end, and never changes its stem: *entiendo* but **entendés**. *Sé* is a one-off. Lost? *No entiendo. **Despacio**, por favor.*

**Soda** is fizzy water, still served from a siphon in the old cafés. It is not a soft drink — that is **gaseosa**. On a menu you will see **agua con gas** (sparkling) and **agua sin gas** (still). A **picada** is a board of cheese and cold cuts to share before dinner.

Reporting a promise: «voy» → **dijo que iba a venir**; «te llamo» → **dijo que me iba a llamar**. That is what porteños say day to day. In writing and in careful speech the same thing goes into *would*: **dijo que vendría**, **dijo que me llamaría** — learn to recognize it. Even shorter in fast speech: **dijo que me llamaba** — *he said he'd call me*.
**Se escaparon de la guerra**, **se instalaron en La Boca** — the roots of the city.

**Me arrepiento** — *I regret it*; **me arrepentí** — *I regretted it, I changed my mind*. With what you did or didn't do, **de (no) haber** + participle: **me arrepiento de no haber ido** — *I regret not going*; *no me arrepiento de haber venido*. An **oportunidad** is a chance; **aprovechar** is to make the most of it: *no aproveché la oportunidad*.
**Casarse** is *to get married*: **se casó**, **nos casamos en marzo**. The wedding is a **casamiento**, and porteño ones end at six in the morning.
Same trick as *quiero, querés*: the stem stretches in most forms — **prefiero**, **vuelvo**, **empieza** — but vos keeps it short: **preferís**, **volvés**, **empezás**.

| **Se la cree.** | He's full of himself. |
| **Me la banco.** | I can handle it. |
| **Se la bancó.** | She put up with it. |
| **Me las arreglo.** | I get by. |
| **La tenés clara.** | You know your stuff. |

The *la* stays *la* whoever you're talking about; only the verb and the first pronoun change.
title_en: A la that points at nothing

body_md: Prices **suben** — or **aumentan**, same thing — and, now and then, **bajan**. **Cobrar** has two meanings. *To charge*: **¿cuánto te cobraron?** — *how much did they charge you?* And *to get paid*: **¿ya cobraste?** — *did you get paid yet?*
**Ni ahí** — *no way, not even close* — is a strong porteño no, also to a question like **¿estás cansado?**. **Tal cual** — *exactly* — is how they agree.
**Recorrimos la Patagonia**; **¿quién ceba?** — the country and its ritual.

**Reírse** with *vos*: **¿de qué te reís?**; with *him*: **se ríe de todo**; in the past, **se rió** — *he laughed*. **¿Lloraste?** For the big laugh: **me morí de risa** — *I died laughing*. A **comedia** gets a **sonrisa**; a sad scene, **lágrimas** and **tristeza**. And people with **sentido del humor** laugh at themselves.

**Che** is how people in Buenos Aires get someone's attention — like "hey": *Che, ¿todo bien?* It comes first, often with a name: *Che, Juan, ¿un mate?* It's friendly and casual — not for formal moments.
**Con Juan fuimos a la costa** means *Juan and I went to the coast* — two people, not three. Argentines say *with Juan we…* where English says *Juan and I*: **con Sofi alquilamos una carpa**.
**Ir a** + infinitive talks about plans: *Vamos a hacer un asado.* **La semana que viene** is *next week*.

*Estar* and *tener* keep their odd stem for everyone: **estuvimos**, **estuvieron**; **tuvimos**, **tuvieron**. And a night, a party or a gig **estuvo** good or bad: **¿Cómo estuvo el recital? Estuvo increíble.**

People: **es medio vago**, **son re trabajadores**. Places: **quedan en zona norte**, **¿te queda cerca?** **Quedar** is also how clothes fit: **te queda bien**, **te queda chico**. **Te queda de paso** — *it's on your way*.
title_en: What people are like, and where places are

body_md: **¿Qué le preguntaste?** — **le pregunté si venías**. What was said steps back a tense: *podés* → **podías**, *venís* → **venías**.

| maybe nobody — subjunctive | a real person — normal verb |
| ¿Conocés a alguien que **hable** inglés? | Mi vieja **habla** inglés. |
| Busco un electricista que **venga** hoy. | El electricista **viene** hoy. |
| No hay nadie que **sepa** cocinar así. | Mi vieja **sabe** cocinar así. |

**Nadie que, ningún … que** always take the subjunctive: that person doesn't exist.
title_en: Alguien que sepa, nadie que sepa

body_md:
The rest of the family comes in the same pairs:
| man | woman |
| tí**o** | tí**a** |
| prim**o** | prim**a** |
| sobrin**o** | sobrin**a** |
| niet**o** | niet**a** |
| suegr**o** | suegr**a** |
| cuñad**o** | cuñad**a** |
*Mi* never changes: *mi tío*, *mi tía*.
A **caradura** has no shame: never pays, asks for too much, lies and doesn't feel bad about it. **¡Qué caradura!** — *you've got some nerve!* Between friends it's often a joke.
When people notice your **acento** less and less, someone will say **ya sos de acá** — *you're one of us now*. Take it: it's the highest praise the city has.

Dreaming together: **si tuviéramos plata, iríamos a Bariloche** — the *we* form carries an accent, **tuviéramos**. Asking a friend: **si pudieras, ¿dónde vivirías?** — *si pudieras* is the vos form. **Ganar** is *to win* and also *to earn*: *si ganara más* — *if I earned more*.

These verbs carry a pronoun that matches the person:
| yo | **me** levanto | **me** acuesto |
| vos | **te** levantás | **te** acostás |
| él, ella | **se** levanta | **se** acuesta |
| nosotros | **nos** levantamos | |
The pronoun goes before the verb. *Acostarse* and *almorzar* change *o → ue*, but not with vos: **me acuesto**, **almuerzo** — **te acostás**, **almorzás**.

Spanish has no *'s*. Say the thing, then **de**, then the person: *Juan's teacher* is **profe de Juan**, *Marta's student* is **estudiante de Marta**. **De** also comes after *un poco*: *un poco de inglés* — *a little English*.

**Boca** against **River** is **el superclásico**; any other big rivalry game is a **clásico**. Boca fans are called *bosteros* and River fans *gallinas*: they say it about themselves with pride, but from you it can be an insult. Which side you're on, the course leaves to you.
**Hacer las compras** is doing the food shopping; **sacar la basura** is taking the trash out.
**Interesar** works exactly like *gustar*: **me interesa el tenis**, **no me interesan los deportes**. **Odiar** doesn't — it's a normal verb: **odio madrugar**.

**No te hagas problema** — *don't worry about it* — is what a porteño says when you apologize. **No te olvides** — *don't forget*: *de* + a verb (*no te olvides de llamar*); with a thing, *de* is often dropped (*no te olvides la SUBE*).

| **me** robaron | they robbed me |
| **te** robaron | they robbed you |
| **le** robaron a mi vieja | they robbed my mom |
| **nos** robaron la bici | they stole our bike |
| **les** robaron a mis viejos | they robbed my parents |
The verb stays *robaron*; the pronoun in front says who it was taken from.

Before you **negociar**, know what you're owed. A job **en blanco** is *on the books*, with aguinaldo (an extra month's pay) and obra social (health insurance); **en negro** is *off the books*. And with inflation, the regular **ajuste** — *the pay adjustment* — is the first thing you **exigir**.

**Te reenvío el archivo** — *I'm forwarding you the file*; **cualquier duda, avisame** — *any questions, let me know*. And the story: **de golpe** — *all of a sudden*; **para colmo** — *to top it all off*; **por lo visto** — *apparently*.

The *if* half has its own form. Take the *ellos* past and swap **-ron** for **-ra**:

| tuvie-ron | **tuviera** |
| fue-ron | **fuera** |
| pudie-ron | **pudiera** |
| estuvie-ron | **estuviera** |

Then the other half takes *would*: **si tuviera tiempo, viajaría**. With vos: *si tuvieras*, *¿qué harías?*

**Elegí** is the order *choose!* and also *I chose*: **elegí el que quieras** — *pick whichever you want*; *ayer **elegí** la roja* — *yesterday I chose the red one*. The rest of the sentence tells you which.
**Disculpá que te moleste**, **¿no tendrás…?**, **quisiera** — polite without leaving vos.
Living in a building means paying **expensas** — *the monthly building fees* — to the **consorcio** — *the owners' association*. The **encargado** is the building caretaker, and knows everything.
**Estoy de acuerdo** — *I agree*. Disagreeing: **no estoy de acuerdo**, or a flat **para nada** — *not at all*. In between: **depende** — *it depends*; **en parte** — *partly*.
Scores are said with **a**: **ganamos dos a uno**, *empatamos cero a cero*. To score is **hacer un gol**: *Juan hizo dos goles*. And the field — and the whole stadium — is **la cancha**.
**¡Qué embole!** — *how boring!* — for a rainy Sunday with nothing to do. Like all of these: friends, not job interviews.
**Me debés la mitad**, **pagamos a medias**, **¿te alcanza?**. And news between friends: **me contaron que…**, **¿es cierto?**

To a friend: **elegí el que quieras**. To two friends: **elijan los que quieran**. Not chosen yet, so the subjunctive: **el que elijas**, **la que prefieras**. And when you really don't mind: **como quieras** — *whatever you like*.
Before you cross the city, you check: **fijate si abren el feriado**, **me fijo si hay turno**, **preguntale si tienen stock**. The **si** is *whether*; the verb after it stays normal.
**En cambio** sets two things against each other; **de hecho** backs up what you said; **en realidad** corrects it.

**Hacerse el** works for everyone: **te hacés el sordo** — *you act like you can't hear*; **me hice el distraído** — *I pretended not to notice*. The one who acts like he's seen it all **se hace el canchero**. To stop it: **no te hagas el gil** — *don't play dumb*.
title_en: Te hacés el, me hice el

body_md:
| Me da **bronca**. | It makes me mad. |
| Me da **vergüenza**. | I'm embarrassed. |
| Me da **lástima**. | I feel sorry (for him). |
| Me da **igual**. | I don't care. |

The cause follows **que** in the subjunctive: **me da bronca que no avise**. In the past, **me dio**: *me dio vergüenza*.
**Me da miedo** — *it scares me* — works like *gustar*; in a story it's **me dio miedo**. The reaction afterwards: **¡qué susto!**
An asado comes in order: first **chorizo** and **morcilla**, the **achuras**, then the cuts — **vacío**, tira de asado. A **choripán** is a chorizo in bread, the food of every stadium.
**Ojalá que ganemos** — *I hope we win* — *-ar* verbs swap to **e** for *we* too. For a present: **ojalá que te guste**. On a birthday: **¡feliz cumple, que cumplas muchos más!**

**No entendí** — *I didn't understand* — is what you say when you missed something just said: *Perdón, no entendí.* It is the past of *no entiendo*. For another person, *knows* is **sabe**: *Juan sabe un poco de inglés.*
**Me toca lavar los platos** — *it's my turn to do the dishes*. **¿A quién le toca?** Porteños say **me toca**, not *es mi turno*.
Meat comes **jugosa** — *rare* — **a punto** — *medium* — or well done. The **parrilla** is both the grill and the restaurant.

**El que** — *the one that* — matches what it stands for: **el que quieras**, **la que está en la esquina**, **los que vinieron**, **las que prefieras**. Not chosen yet, so the subjunctive: *el que quieras* — *whichever you want*.

**Me olvidé de su cumple** — *I forgot his birthday*. Like *me enojé* it keeps its pronoun, and takes **de** before what you forgot. Left something behind? No *de*: **me olvidé las llaves en casa**. For the others: **¿te olvidaste las llaves?**, **se olvidó de llamar**, **nos olvidamos de reservar**. Same shape: **me aburrí**, **me calmé**, **me enamoré** — of Buenos Aires, of course.

Porteños grew up on **rock nacional** — *Argentine rock* — sung in Spanish in the stadiums; the provinces on **folclore**; every party ends in **cumbia**. A **cantante** is a singer; a tango singer is often called a *cantor*.

For almost anything official you first **sacás turno** — you book an appointment online — and you bring the **DNI**, the national ID card, without which nothing happens. As a foreigner, you use your passport until you get your own DNI.
**Gardel canta mejor cada día**; the meat comes **jugosa** or **a punto**.
Porteños talk **rápido**. The line that saves you: *¿Podés hablar más despacio?* — and most people will happily slow down and **ayudar**.

With **ser** an adjective says what something is like; with **estar**, how it is right now. *Esa remera **es** linda* — it is a nice T-shirt. *¡**Estás** linda!* — you look nice today. *El café de acá **es** rico* — *este café **está** rico*. And **ser listo** is *to be clever*, while **estar listo** is *to be ready*.

*Ser* — to be — has a form for each person. So far:

| yo | **soy** | I am |
| vos | **sos** | you are |

Use **vos** with everyone: friends, the waiter, your boss. A question is the same words with a rising voice: *¿Sos Sofi?*

**Negocio** is any shop, not just a business: *el negocio de la esquina*. And porteños **comparten** everything, from an apartment to a mate. *Con mi hermano vendemos empanadas* means *my brother and I sell* — two people, not three.

*Es la una* (one o'clock), but *son las dos*, *son las siete*. Add **y media** for half past and **y cuarto** for quarter past. Other minutes go the same way: *las siete y veinte*. Past the half hour people often drop the **y**: *las ocho cuarenta*. To ask: *¿Qué hora es?* or *¿Tenés hora?* *At* a time is **a las**: *¿A qué hora?* — *A las nueve y media.* After a clock time say **de la mañana / de la tarde / de la noche**: *a las dos de la tarde*. With no clock time: **a la mañana**, *a la tarde*, *a la noche*.

The small talk of bills: **aumentaron la luz y el gas** — *electricity and gas went up*; **el boleto subió** — *the fare went up*; **no llego a fin de mes** — *I can't make ends meet*: the money runs out before the month does.

| | vos | yo, él, ella |
| ayudar | **ayudes** | **ayude** |
| esperar | **esperes** | **espere** |
| poner | **pongas** | **ponga** |
| traer | **traigas** | **traiga** |
| llevar | **lleves** | **lleve** |
| dar | **des** | **dé** |
**Necesito que**, **te pido que**, **prefiero que** and the offer **¿querés que…?** all take the subjunctive: *necesito que me ayudes*, *te pido que me esperes*, *¿querés que te lleve?* For *we*: **¿qué querés que hagamos?**

Leaving Buenos Aires you take **la autopista** (the fast road, with tolls), then **la ruta** (the ordinary road between towns). First you **cargás nafta** — *nafta*, never *gasolina* — and on the way you pay the **peaje**. **La General Paz** is the ring road between the Capital and the conurbano. Porteños *agarran* a road rather than *take* it: **agarrá la ruta**, **¿qué ruta agarramos?**
**Me molesta que llegue tarde** — *it bothers me that he's late*. *Molestar* works like *gustar*.
A goodbye is a string of wishes, all *que* + the subjunctive: **que duermas bien**, **que sigas bien**, **que llegues bien**. On the phone it ends with **besos** and **escribime**.

*No me alcanza* for you is **¿te alcanza?** — *do you have enough?*. **Cobré** — *I got paid*; **¿gastás mucho?**, **¿ahorrás algo?** — vos adds **-ás**. For everyone at work: **cobramos el lunes** — *we get paid on Monday*.
When you just say whether it has one, no *un*: *mi edificio **tiene** ascensor*, *no **tiene** terraza*. **Hay** for what's there: *en la planta baja **hay** un patio*.

The city is **la Capital** — often with no article: *vivo en Capital*. The ring of towns around it is **el conurbano**. Palermo, **San Telmo** and **La Boca** are barrios of the Capital: *Palermo está lleno de bares*, *La Boca es re turística*. The first question to any porteño: **¿en qué barrio vivís?**

Porteños say **a la noche** for *at night* or *tonight*: *A la noche estudio inglés.* *Hablamos a la noche* — we'll talk tonight. **De noche** is at night in general: *laburo de noche* (I work nights). And **¿qué hacés?** — literally *what are you doing?* — is also the everyday *how's it going?*: *Hola, ¿qué hacés?*

Nobody says *cumpleaños* in a hurry: it's **el cumple** — *¡Feliz cumple!* The verb is **cumplir**, to turn an age: *¿Cuántos años cumplís?* — *Cumplo treinta.* And *cumplís años el domingo* means your birthday is on Sunday.

| Que te mejores. | Get well soon. |
| Que te diviertas. | Have fun. |
| Que lo disfrutes. | Enjoy it. |
| Que cumplas muchos más. | I hope you have many more birthdays. |
| Ojalá que te guste. | I hope you like it. |
| Ojalá que ganemos. | I hope we win. |

The pronoun comes along into the wish: *te mejores*, *te diviertas*. For *we*, **-emos** on *-ar* verbs: *ganar* → **ganemos**. **Espero que** — *I hope* — works like *ojalá*: *espero que te guste*.

It works on adverbs too: **cerquita** — *close by*; **despacito** — *nice and slow*. **Chiquito** — *small, little*. Careful: **hablá más despacito** can mean *slower* or *quieter* — the situation tells you.
When the wanting is in the past, the second verb moves into the past too: *quiero que vengas* becomes **quería que vinieras** — *I wanted you to come*.
**Pedimos** keeps the *e*; **pidió** and **pidieron** turn it into *i*. **¿Qué pidieron?** — **Una grande de muzza y una provoleta para compartir.**
Your driver's license is the **registro** — *¿tenés registro?*. Your own or rented parking space is a **cochera**; a public paid parking lot is an *estacionamiento*.
With a *no* in front the verb stays the same and the pronoun jumps ahead: **apúrense**, but **no se olviden** — *don't forget*; **no dejen nada** — *don't leave anything*.
**Conseguí laburo** — *I got a job*. *Conseguir* is the verb for getting anything that took effort: a *turno*, a table, an apartment.
**Si hubiera ahorrado, ahora tendría…** — and the regret: **tendría que haber ahorrado**.
**Viste** is *you saw*: **¿Viste el partido?** — *Did you see the game?* Porteños also add **¿viste?** at the end of a sentence to mean *you know?*: *Es re caro, ¿viste?*
In the south, **glaciares**; in the north-east, the **cataratas** of Iguazú; in the north-west, Salta's **paisaje** of red hills.
In *yo* the spelling bends to keep the sound: *pagar* → **pagué**, *llegar* → **llegué**. At the end of the night someone says **pago yo** — and the next day, **ayer pagué yo, hoy te toca a vos**.

In the past, *gustar* and *encantar* work like any -ar verb: **me gustaba**, **me encantaba** — *I liked*, *I loved*. Several things take an **-n**: **me gustaban los dibujitos**. The same **-n** makes the *they* form of any verb: **los pibes jugaban a la pelota en la vereda**.
Like *gustar*, the scary thing is the subject. One: **me da asco la cucaracha**; more than one: **me dan asco las cucarachas**, **me dan miedo las arañas**.

Among friends it's **me afanaron** — *they stole it* (slang). It is also what you say when you were overcharged: *me afanaron con el taxi* — *the taxi overcharged me*. The **motochorro** steals from a motorbike. The confession that comes with it: **me descuidé** — *I wasn't careful*.

**Cenamos** and **salimos** look the same in the present and the past: *we have dinner* or *we had dinner*, *we go out* or *we went out*. Only -ar and -ir verbs do this; -er verbs change: **comemos** (now), **comimos** (then). A porteño never gets lost: **anoche**, **ayer**, **el sábado** — the time word does the work.
**¿Me pasás la sal?** is how you ask at the table — a question in the present. **¿Podrías…?** is softer, for a bigger favor.

| | estar | tener | pasarla |
| yo | estuve | tuve | **la pasé** |
| vos | estuviste | tuviste | **la pasaste** |
| él, ella | estuvo | tuvo | **la pasó** |
| nosotros | **estuvimos** | **tuvimos** | **la pasamos** |
| ellos | **estuvieron** | **tuvieron** | **la pasaron** |
*Estar* and *tener* get an odd stem (*estuv-*, *tuv-*) for every person, with no accent. *Pasarla* is regular: **la pasé**, **la pasó** keep the accent. **¿Cómo estuvo?** — *how was it?* — **Estuvo increíble, la pasamos bárbaro.**
**Acampamos al lado de un lago**, **hicimos dedo**; **¿te convido un mate?** — but **no hiervas el agua**. A **carpa** is a camping tent; on the beach in Mar del Plata it is also a rented shade tent.

| ¡Qué bueno que **estés** acá! | So good you're here! |
| Qué lástima que no **vengas**. | Shame you're not coming. |
| Me molesta que **llegue** tarde. | It bothers me that he's late. |

A reaction to something now or later + **que** → the subjunctive. For something that already happened, the normal past: **¡qué bueno que viniste!** **Me alegro** on its own: *I'm glad*. With more: **me alegro que** or **me alegro de que** — both are used.
To say how something was, porteños mostly use **estuvo**: *¿Cómo estuvo el partido? Estuvo bárbaro.* **Fue** works too, for events: *el recital fue bárbaro*.

A past that went differently, and what it would mean today: **si hubiera ahorrado** (then), **ahora tendría un depto** (now). The first half is **hubiera** + participle; the second is the plain conditional. **A esta altura** — *by now* — goes in the *now* half: **a esta altura estaría jubilado**.

Day to day porteños give advice with **tendrías que** more than with *deberías*: **tendrías que descansar**. Also **yo que vos** — *if I were you*: *yo que vos, iría al médico*; or a question: **¿por qué no vas al médico?**

Traditions told from back then are imperfect: **nos juntábamos**, **festejábamos**, **armábamos el arbolito** on the 8th of December. **Es costumbre…** — *it's the custom to…* — brings them into the present: *Es costumbre juntarnos en Navidad.*
**Cambiaste un montón**, **el servicio empeoró**, **cada vez peor** — and then: **me pudrí**, **¡basta!**

On a sign, **se** + verb says what is sold, rented or needed, with nobody named: **se vende** auto, **se alquila** depto, **se necesita** mozo. For more than one thing, add **n**: **se venden** bicis. The same **se** asks about rules: **¿se puede fumar acá?** — *can you smoke here?*
**Lo** + adjective is *the … thing*: **lo bueno** — *the good thing*; **lo malo** — *the bad thing*; **lo mejor** and **lo peor**. **Lo bueno de vivir acá es que…**
**Me tocó** works like *gustar*: the thing is the subject, so with two things it is **me tocaron**: *me tocaron los platos y el baño*. **Llovió** has no person at all — just *it rained*.
**Cuanto más** — *the more*: **cuanto más practicás, mejor hablás**. **Cuanto menos** — *the less*. And **cuanto antes** — *the sooner the better*: **avisame cuanto antes**.

The most natural way to say what you love about a place: **lo que más me gusta de Buenos Aires es la noche**. The opposite: **lo que menos me gusta es el ruido**. And **lo más** + adjective is *the most … thing*: **lo más lindo del barrio es la plaza**.
Nothing happens in Buenos Aires without **sacar turno** — *booking an appointment*, almost always **por internet**. Then they **piden** things: **te piden una fotocopia**, **completá esto**.

**Podríamos ir al cine** — *we could go to the movies*. **Nos convendría salir temprano** — *we'd better leave early*. Turning it down: **preferiría ir otro día**. Saying yes: between friends it is **dale** or **obvio** — **obvio, te ayudo**. **Con gusto** is the formal one, what you hear in a shop.
**Tenés razón** — *you're right*, literally *you have reason*. **No tengo tiempo** — *I don't have time*. **Tiene suerte** — *he's lucky*.

To clear it up — **aclarar**: **quiero aclarar algo**. Then: **no quise decir eso** — *I didn't mean that*; **me expresé mal** — *I put it badly*; **me entendiste mal** — *you misunderstood me*; **no lo dije por vos** — *I didn't say it about you*.
**Me llegó** — *it really touched me*: **tu mensaje me llegó un montón**. Careful: plain **me llegó tu mensaje** just means *I got your message*.

**Convidar** is *to offer, to share what's yours*: **¿te convido un mate?**, **convidame uno**. Afternoon **merienda** means mate with **bizcochitos**, or **tortas fritas** when it rains. A **matero** drinks it all day; kids get **mate cocido**, the tea-bag version. To ask for one, the question is kinder than the order: **¿me convidás un mate?** *Convidame* is for close friends.

English says *I can't see anything*; Spanish just says **no veo nada** — no word for *can*. The same with **ves**: *¿Ves?* is *can you see?* And the double negative is correct Spanish: *no* before the verb, *nada* after it.

What people are like goes with *ser*: **somos altos**, **son morochos**. The word takes an *-s* for more than one, and *-os* covers a mixed group: *mis hermanos son altos*, even if one of them is a sister.
Wishes and the future share the form: **que te diviertas**, **ojalá que ganemos**, **cuando vuelvas**, **hasta que sepa algo**. An open choice takes it too: **lo que quieras** — *whatever you want*.
Left and right both take **a la**: **a la derecha**, **a la izquierda**. To say what something is left or right of, add **de**: *la farmacia está a la derecha del banco*.
title_en: A la derecha, a la izquierda

body_md: **Me hace ruido**, **no me cierra**, **me quedé helado**, **qué alivio** — doubt, shock and relief, in porteño.

| going on — imperfect | then — preterite |
| **Estaba** en la ducha | cuando **sonó** el timbre. |
| **Volvía** a casa | cuando **empezó** a llover. |
| **Eran** las tres y no **había** luz | cuando **entró** Juan. |

**Estaba** + *-ando, -iendo* is right in the middle of it: *estaba durmiendo cuando sonó el celu.*

**Las fiestas** are Christmas and New Year together: *¡Felices fiestas!* **Navidad** falls in the heat and is celebrated the night before, on **Nochebuena** — the 24th: an *asado* or a cold spread, and at midnight **sidra**, **pan dulce** and a **brindis** — *¡salud!* — before the fireworks and **Papá Noel**.

If someone **se calentó** — *got mad* — or **se ofendió** — *took offense* — the joke went too far. **Se picó**: a game or an argument got heated. An **apodo** (*nickname*) like **el Gordo** or **el Pelado** is friendly among friends; never use one with someone you just met.
*Ir* and *ser* share their past: **fui, fuiste, fue**. *Fui a la cancha* — *I went to the stadium*; *fue bárbaro* — *it was great*. The rest of the sentence tells which.
**Hay** introduces something: *Hay un kiosco* — there's a kiosco. **Está** says where something you already know about is: *El kiosco está en la esquina.*
Swap *me* for **nos** and the whole table orders at once: **¿Nos traés la carta?** — *¿Nos traés dos vasos, por favor?*

Going on vacation? Every instruction is a **para que** + what the *other* person does: **te dejo la llave para que entres**, **para que riegues las plantas**, **para que el gato coma**. Two people, so the second verb is subjunctive.
**Deberías** — *you should* — is advice with the edges sanded off: **deberías descansar**. **Debería** is *I should* or *he should*: *debería llamar a mi vieja*.

School here is **la primaria** (six to twelve) and then **la secundaria**. In a state primary school everyone wears a white **guardapolvo** over their clothes, and the best part of the day is the **recreo**. In primaria the teacher is **la maestra** or **el maestro**; from secundaria on it is **el profesor**, **la profe**. Each year of primaria is a **grado**: *primer grado*.

**Como dice el dicho** — *as the saying goes* — and then the one that fits: **cada loco con su tema** — *to each their own*; **no hay dos sin tres** — *there's always a third time*; **el que no llora no mama** — *if you don't ask, you don't get*.

Wanting and being able are states, so back then they take the imperfect: **De chico quería ser maestro** — *as a kid I wanted to be a teacher*; **no podía salir solo** — *I wasn't allowed out on my own*. **En esa época** — *back then* — sets the whole scene. At a counter, **quería un cortado** is just a polite *I'd like a cortado*. With a person, **querer a** is *to love*: *quería mucho a mi maestra*.
With a remis, ask the price before you get in: *¿Cuánto sale hasta el aeropuerto?* In a taxi the meter decides. Paying cash, people round up: **quedate con el vuelto** — *keep the change*.
One verb for your age and for how you feel: **tengo** veinte años, **¿tenés** frío?, mi tío **tiene** sueño.

| Te lo presto, **con tal de que** me lo **devuelvas**. | on condition that |
| Te lo presto, **salvo que** lo **necesite**. | unless |
| Llevá el auto, **siempre y cuando** no lo **choques**. | as long as |
| Llevá plata **por si** la **necesitás**. | just in case |

Every condition takes the subjunctive, except **por si**. For *vos*: **devuelvas, rompas, cuides, manejes, choques**.
title_en: Con tal de que, salvo que

body_md: The future is **ir a** + verb: **voy a laburar**, **vamos a comer**. For a fixed plan the plain present works too: **viajamos el viernes**. *Viajamos* is also *we traveled*: the time word tells you which. **Que viene** after a time word is *next*: **la semana que viene**, **el año que viene**, **el finde que viene**.

| the scene — imperfect | what happened — preterite |
| **Estaba** en el subte | cuando me **llamó** Sofi. |
| **Llovía** mucho | y **llegué** tarde. |
| **Había** mucha gente | y no **pude** entrar. |

Ask: was it going on, or did it happen? Going on → *-aba, -ía*. Happened, and finished → the preterite.

| one person (vos) | more than one (ustedes) |
| probá | **prueben** |
| agarrá | **agarren** |
| tomá | **tomen** |
| no te olvides | **no se olviden** |

Also **coman**, **hagan** lugar, **vayan**, **dejen**. **Vayan** + *-ando/-iendo* is *go ahead and start*: **vayan comiendo** — *start eating*. -ar verbs **-en**, the rest **-an**. The stem is the *yo* stem: *pruebo* → **prueben**, *hago* → **hagan**, *vengo* → **vengan**. **Dejen de** + verb is *stop*: **dejen de hablar** — *stop talking*.

Many porteños have an **abuelo** or **bisabuelo** who **llegó en barco** from Italy or Spain. An Italian, or anyone with an Italian surname, is a **tano** or a **tana**: *mi abuelo era tano*. That's why a porteño talks with his hands and eats ñoquis on the 29th.
**Más caro que**, **menos lejos que** — *more expensive than*, *less far than*. **Tan lindo como** is *as nice as*. *Better* and *worse* have their own words: **mejor**, **peor**.
**Hay** introduces something: *Hay un kiosco* — there's a kiosk. **Está** says where something you already know about is: *El kiosco está en la esquina.*

To say the good and the bad together: **Buenos Aires tiene sus cosas** — *it has its issues* — like the **inseguridad** (*crime*) and the **costo de vida** (*cost of living*). But **a la vez** — *at the same time* — **no hay nada como Buenos Aires**: *there's nothing like it*.
**Paro docente**, **suspendieron las clases**, **hubo desvíos** — and the city **a pie**.

The little word in front says who likes it: **me**, **te**, **le**, **nos**, **les**. The verb is only ever *gusta* (one thing) or *gustan* (several): *le gust**a** el pollo*, *me gust**an** las medialunas*.

For produce porteños often use the singular for the whole product: **la papa está cara** — *potatoes are expensive*; **un kilo de cebolla** — *a kilo of onions*. And fruit that **está verde** is *not ripe* yet (*es verde* is the color).

For a local number you buy a **chip** — a SIM card — at a phone shop or a kiosco (take your passport: they may ask for it), and then you load **datos**: *cargar datos*, the same verb as loading the SUBE. *No tengo datos* means no internet until the next wifi.
Both start the second half: **sin embargo** — *however*, mostly in writing or formal talk — and the more spoken **así y todo** — *even so*: *hice dieta y **así y todo** engordé*.

**Como si** takes the past subjunctive: *como si supiera*. **El que, la que** — *the one that*: *la que prefieras*. **Aunque** + normal verb — *even though* (a fact): *aunque estoy cansada*; + subjunctive — *even if*: *aunque llueva*.
Hotels and hostels use the English words: **el check-in** and **el check-out**. To ask the time: *¿A qué hora es el check-out?*

The vos command is everywhere in a shop: **mirá**, **fijate**, **esperame**, **tomá** — *tomá, tu vuelto*. Drop the *-r* and stress the last vowel of the verb: *mirá*, *tomá*. With *me* or *te* added, the stress stays there: *fijate* (fi-JA-te), *esperame* (es-pe-RA-me).
The confession that comes with it: **me descuidé** — *I wasn't careful*. Porteños answer **¡qué garrón!**

| | one thing | more than one |
| to me | **se me** quemó la comida | **se me** quemaron las tostadas |
