| to you | **se te** quemó | **se te** quemaron |
| to us | **se nos** quemó | **se nos** quemaron |

The verb follows the thing: one thing **-ó**, more than one **-aron / -eron**. The middle word says who it happened to: **se me**, **se te**, **se le**, **se nos**.
title_en: Se me quemó, se me quemaron

body_md: *¿Qué hacés?* is mostly just *hi*. To ask about someone's job, say **¿De qué laburás?** or **¿De qué trabajás?** The answer takes *de* too: *Laburo de mozo.* Or with *ser*: *Soy abogada.*

**Estoy harto** — *I'm fed up*; porteños go further: **estoy podrido** — literally *rotten*. Both take **de** + a thing or an infinitive: **harta del tránsito**, **podrido del ruido**, **harta de estudiar**. Same with **me cansé de esperar** — *I got tired of waiting*. When someone or something else is doing it: **de que** + subjunctive — *estoy podrido de que el ascensor esté roto*.

All the way with you: **exacto**, **totalmente**, **obvio**, **sin duda** — and the stiffer **coincido**. All the way against: **al contrario**, **no creo**, **estás equivocado**. And for the friend who goes too far: **¡no exageres!**
**Hay que** is *it has to be done* — nobody in particular. **Tenés que** is *you have to*. **No hace falta** is *there's no need*.
title_en: Hay que, tenés que, no hace falta

body_md: Use **estar** for where someone or something is: *¿Dónde estás?* *El kiosco está acá.* It is a different verb from *ser*, which says what something is.
Now the vos side: **¿qué le preguntaste?**, **¿qué le contestaste?** — the same *-aste* as *llamaste*. And for him or her: **me explicó que…**, **me juró que…**, **me gritó**.

The little word in front of *llamar* changes with the person, just like *soy, sos, es*:

| yo | **me llamo** | **soy** |
| vos | **te llamás** | **sos** |
| él, ella | **se llama** | **es** |

*¿Quién es ella?* — *Se llama Lucía. Es una amiga.*
title_en: Me llamo, te llamás, se llama

body_md: The turn has a past: **ayer me tocó a mí, hoy te toca a vos**. **¿A quién le tocó?** Most chores are plain -ar verbs: **lavé, limpiaste, lavó**. *Sacar* changes in *yo*: **saqué** (like *busqué*). *Barrer* is an -er verb: **barrí, barriste**.
**Llevo dos años viviendo acá** — *I've been living here for two years*. Where English says *have been …ing*, Spanish stays in the present: **hace dos años que vivo acá** says the same.

| Voy, **a menos que llueva**. | unless |
| Voy, **siempre y cuando vengas**. | as long as |
| Llamame **en caso de que haya** un problema. | if, in case (formal) |
| Llevá paraguas **por si llueve**. | just in case |

The first three take the subjunctive. **Por si** is the exception: normal verb.
**Son** says what people are like: *son altos*, *son simpáticos*. **Están** says where they are: *están en la plaza*. The same people, two verbs.

Porteño advice starts with **yo que vos** — *if I were you* — and goes straight to the conditional: **yo que vos, no le diría nada**. In everyday speech you also hear the plain present: *yo que vos, no voy*.

**Me tocó** is also what you *got* without choosing: **me tocó el baño** — *I got the bathroom*; **me tocó laburar el domingo** — *I had to work on Sunday*; **me tocó un profe re copado** — *I got a really cool teacher*.
Making a plan takes three questions: **¿a qué hora?**, **¿dónde?** and **¿querés?** *Nos vemos a las nueve menos cuarto enfrente del cine, ¿podés?*

**Tener que** + an infinitive (the *-ar, -er, -ir* form) is *to have to*: *tengo que laburar* — I have to work; *¿tenés que estudiar?* — do you have to study? A different **que** joins two ideas: *tengo una jefa que habla inglés* — a boss who speaks English.
**Sesenta** (60) and **setenta** (70) are the pair everyone mixes up: **sesenta** has the **s** of *six*, **setenta** has the **t** of *seven*. And a round hundred is just **cien** — never *un cien*.

For the **residencia** you need your **antecedentes penales** — *criminal record certificate* — with the **apostilla**, the stamp that makes a foreign paper valid here, and a **certificado de domicilio** — *proof of address*. While you wait they give you the **precaria**, a temporary permit you can already work and travel with.

About what hasn't happened yet, the verb after **cuanto** goes subjunctive: **cuanto antes lleguemos, mejor**; **cuanto antes reservemos, más barato**; **cuanto más temprano empecemos, antes terminamos**. About what always happens, the normal verb: **cuanto más ganás, más gastás**.
Not only bad news: **la pizzería fue elegida la mejor del barrio**, **la ley fue aprobada**, **el chico fue elegido para el equipo**. Same pattern: **fue** + a participle that agrees.

The other team is *they*: **ganaron**, **perdieron**, **empataron**. Yours is usually *we*, from the bar or the sofa: **¡salimos campeones!** About your own team you can say either: **ganamos** (we, the fans) or **ganaron** (they, the players).
**Volver a** + an infinitive is *to do it again*: **volví a estudiar** — *I went back to studying*; **vuelvo a empezar** — *I'm starting over*.

On the shop door: **horario de atención** — *opening hours*; **abierto / cerrado**; **solo efectivo** — *cash only*; **no funciona** — *out of order*; **liquidación** — *sale*. In a building: **no se permiten mascotas**, **se prohíbe hacer ruido**.

Days take **el** for one day and **los** for every week: *el miércoles laburo* (on Wednesday), *los lunes laburo* (on Mondays). They have no capital letter. Dates work the same way, with a plain number: *el veintiuno tengo examen*. **Nos vemos** is *see you*; as a question it makes a plan: *¿Nos vemos el sábado?* — *Should we meet on Saturday?*
Nationalities are written in lowercase: *Ella es* **italiana**, never *Italiana*. Only the country takes a capital: *Brasil*, *Estados Unidos*.
Clothes go in the **lavarropas**; to **planchar** them is optional for most porteños. The floor: **barrer** with the **escoba**, then you **pasás el trapo** — the wet *trapo de piso*.
**Resulta que** — *it turns out* — is how a porteño story takes its turn. **Encima** — *on top of that* — makes it worse: **encima, llovía**. **Total** shrugs it off: **total, nadie se dio cuenta**.

| the question | asking or telling it |
| «¿Tienen stock?» | **Preguntale si** tienen stock. |
| «¿Abren el feriado?» | **Me fijo si** abren el feriado. |
| «¿Tenés turno?» | **Me preguntaron si** tenía turno. |
| «¿Está disponible?» | No sé **si** está disponible. |

**Si** is *whether*, and the verb after it is the normal one. Told later, it moves into the past: *tenés* → *tenía*. If it is still true now, the present is fine too: *me preguntaron si soy argentino*.
The porteño complaint of the WhatsApp age: **me clavó el visto** — *he read my message and didn't answer*. And the friend who forgets everything is **re colgado**.

Two pronouns together go person first, thing second: **me lo** mandás, **te la** doy. And *le* or *les* in front of *lo, la, los, las* turns into **se**: *¿le mandás el audio?* → **¿se lo mandás?**; *le doy la llave* → **se la doy**.

Prices run to thousands, so a thousand pesos has a short name: **una luca**, *diez lucas*. To **cambiar dólares**, first ask the rate: *¿A cuánto está el dólar?* And cash often gets a better price: *¿Hay descuento en efectivo?*
The name verb changes its little word with the person: **me llamo**, **te llamás**, **se llama**.

**Lo que pasó fue que**, **lo que quiero decir es que**, **lo tuyo**, **lo que sea**, **en el fondo**. And three sayings: **cada loco con su tema** — *to each their own*; **no hay dos sin tres** — *there's always a third time*; **hablando del rey de Roma** — *we were just talking about you*.

**Llegar a fin de mes** — *to make it to payday* — is the monthly sport: **no llego a fin de mes**. When the money runs short: **no me alcanza** — *it's not enough*. You cut the **gastos**, compare **marcas** at the **chino** (the corner supermarket), and notice when they **remarcaron** everything overnight.

The other way to say how you felt is **me dio** + the feeling: **me dio miedo** — *it scared me*. You will hear it with many feelings: *me dio bronca* (it made me angry), *me dio vergüenza* (I was embarrassed), *me dio lástima* (I felt sorry).

With *nosotros* and *ellos*, both verbs are complete:

| | ser | tener |
| yo | soy | tengo |
| vos | sos | tenés |
| él, ella | es | tiene |
| nosotros | **somos** | **tenemos** |
| ellos, ustedes | **son** | **tienen** |

**Ustedes** — *you all* — uses the *ellos* form. Argentina never uses *vosotros*.
title_en: Ser and tener, all of them

body_md: For *ellos* the irregular ones end in **-ieron**: **vinieron**, **hicieron**, **pudieron** — and after a *j* just **-eron**: **dijeron**, **trajeron**. **No vino nadie** — *nobody came*: after the verb, *nadie* still needs the *no*.

Argentine prices run into the thousands, so you will say **mil** all day. One thousand is just **mil** — never *un mil* — and the word does not change: *Sale mil pesos.* *¿Mil pesos? Es caro.* **Caro** and **barato** end in **-a** for a *la* word: *una gaseosa no es cara*. **¡Qué caro!** — *How expensive!*
The subjunctive after **que** for what you haven't found (*un depto que tenga balcón*) and for what makes you feel something (*me da bronca que no avise*).
For a plan, use **ir a** + the verb as it is: **voy a salir**, **¿qué vas a hacer?**, **vamos a comer**. It is how porteños talk about the future almost all the time.

**De hecho** — *in fact* — backs up what you just said: *no es caro; de hecho, es barato*. **En realidad** — *actually* — corrects it: *en realidad no es tan caro*. **Por eso** — *that's why*: *está cerca, por eso me gusta*.

The **cordillera** — *the Andes range* — runs down the whole west: **lagos** and **nieve** in the south, **bodegas** — *wineries* — in Mendoza, red **valles** in Jujuy. A **mochilero** does it all with a backpack and a **carpa** — *a tent*, down to Ushuaia.
**No dejes el celu ahí** is a warning; **es mejor que no lo dejes ahí** is advice. Both take the subjunctive.

To rent in Buenos Aires you need a **garantía** — *a guarantor*, usually a relative who owns property: *mi papá me sale de garantía* — *my dad is my guarantor*. No garantía? Foreigners often pay a **seguro de caución** — *rent guarantee insurance* — or take an **alquiler temporario amoblado** — *a furnished short-term rental*.
**Chabón** — *guy*; **mina** — *woman*; **groso** — *great*; **birra** — *beer*; **trucho** — *fake*. All among friends.

A porteño argues hard and softens it: **puede ser, pero…** — *could be, but…* **Puede ser que** + the subjunctive is *maybe*: **puede ser que tengas razón** — *you might be right*; **puede ser que llueva**.
**No es que no quiera** (subjunctive: not the real reason), **es que no puedo** (normal present: the real reason).
**Paro**, **corte**, **piquete** — and the street **está cortada**.
**¡Ojo!** — literally *eye!* — is *careful!, watch out!*: **ojo, que no es tan fácil**. **Estoy seguro** — *I'm sure*; **no estoy segura** — *I'm not sure*.
**Era, eras, éramos, eran**; **tenía, tenías, teníamos, tenían**; **jugaba, jugabas, jugábamos, jugaban**. One set of endings for *-ar*, one for *-er* and *-ir*, and *yo* and *él* always share.
**Hay** works for things you can't count, too: **hay gente** — there are people. *Gente* is singular in Spanish: *la gente está en la plaza*.
**No me alcanza** — *I don't have enough* (usually money). Word for word: *it doesn't reach for me*. **Ahorrar** is to save, **gastar** to spend: **gasté todo el sueldo**.

**Cuando quieras** — *whenever you like* — leaves an invitation open. A question with **¿cuándo?** keeps the normal verb: **¿cuándo nos vemos?** A plan with **cuando** doesn't: **cuando nos veamos, te cuento**.

A fan is **un hincha** or **una hincha**: the word is the same for a man or a woman. Say who you support with **ser hincha de**: *Mi papá es re hincha de la selección* — my dad is a huge fan of the national team.

The hardest words in any argument: **me equivoqué** — *I was wrong*. To a friend: **te equivocás** — *you're wrong*. To admit it: **reconozco que** tenés razón — *I admit you're right* — or just **te doy la razón** — *you're right*. **En eso** te doy la razón — *you're right about that* — admits only one point.

**Mejor todavía** — *even better*: **¿es gratis? Mejor todavía**; also **mejor así** — *better this way*. *Tanto mejor* says the same but sounds bookish. To **evitar** the **hora pico**, you go early; the place **se llena** fast; and leaving early, the day **rinde** — *goes further*. **Ganar tiempo** is *to save time*: **con el subte ganás tiempo**.

When you say who should do it, use **que** + subjunctive: **estaría bueno que te tomes unos días** — *it'd be good if you took a few days off*. For people in general, the infinitive: *estaría bueno **descansar***. And the push: **¡animate!** — *go for it!*

Like *vengo* and *traigo*, these verbs have an odd *I* form: **digo**, **pongo** and **veo**. With vos they are regular: **decís**, **ponés**, **ves**. *Decir* also changes **e** to **i** in **dice** and **dicen**. *—¿Qué decís? —Yo no digo nada.* To tell someone, add **le**: *¿Qué le digo a Ana?*

| | regular | shortened |
| yo, él, ella | hablar**ía**, dejar**ía**, pedir**ía**, volver**ía** | **saldría**, **tendría**, **diría** |
| vos | ir**ías** | **tendrías**, **dirías** |
| with *me* | **me quedaría** | |

**Yo en tu lugar, hablaría con él.** Vos adds **-s**: *¿vos qué le dirías?* **Tendrías que** is advice too: *tendrías que llamarlo*.

Most family words come in pairs:

| man | woman |
| herman**o** | herman**a** |
| hij**o** | hij**a** |
| abuel**o** | abuel**a** |
| novi**o** | novi**a** |
| viej**o** | viej**a** |

**Mi** — *my* — never changes: *mi hermano*, *mi hermana*. And *papá* ends in *-a* but is a man.

Said slowly, **sí, claro** means *yeah, right*. **¡Qué novedad!** — *what a surprise* — is for the bondi that's late again; **¡lo que faltaba!** — *that's all we needed* — for the rain that starts on top of it. The everyday ones: **qué raro**, said flat — *¿llegó tarde? Qué raro.* — and **mirá vos** — *well, look at that*. The **tono** — *tone* — does the work.

**Lograr** — *to manage something hard, to achieve*: **¡lo lograste!** — *you did it!* And your own line: **¡lo logré!** — *I did it!* Then **felicitaciones** — *congratulations* — or, among friends, just **¡grande!**

The first question in a new friendship. A team is a **cuadro**, and you inherit it: *Soy de Independiente, el cuadro de mi abuelo.* Answer with **soy de** or **soy hincha de**. **Hinchar por** is for one game or the national team: *Hincho por la selección.*
The verbs you use most have their own past: **hice** (I did), **vi** (I saw), **dije** (I said), **vine** (I came), **pude** (I could). No accent on any of them.

With **ir**, it grows bit by bit: **voy conociendo gente**, **el bondi se va llenando**, **me voy acostumbrando al ritmo**. It's the verb of settling in. Careful: in **andá llenando la pava**, *andá* is the command of *ir* (go): *start filling the kettle*.

The vendor always asks **¿algo más?** — *anything else?* You answer **nada más, gracias**, or keep going: **y un kilo de naranjas**. To ask a price, **¿cuánto sale?** is the everyday way — same as *¿cuánto cuesta?* For things sold by weight you already know **¿a cuánto está?**
In Buenos Aires the morning greeting is **buen día**, until lunch. After that it's **buenas tardes**, and once it's dark **buenas noches** — hello *and* goodbye. Short for any of them: **buenas**.
Change the middle word for the person: **se te cayó** — *you dropped it*; **se le rompió** — *he broke it*.
*Les* can be *them* or *you all*, so porteños often say who: **a ellos** les gusta, **a ustedes** les gusta. The same with *le*: *a ella le gusta el pescado*.

To go to **la cancha** you are usually a **socio** — *a member* — of the **club**, and you pay a monthly fee. The **popular** is the cheap standing section, where the **hinchada** sings its **cantitos** for ninety minutes under the **banderas**.
Ordering for more than one: **queremos** dos cafés. The mozo asks the table **¿qué quieren?** And for someone else: *ella **quiere** un té*. The *ie* is everywhere except *querés* and *queremos*.

**Hace** + a time is *ago*: **llegué hace una hora** — *I got here an hour ago*; **hablé con Juan hace dos días**. *Not long ago* is **hace poco**, and the question is **¿hace cuánto?** — *how long ago?*
**Ya no** — not anymore; **cada vez más** — more and more. And when it's too much: **estoy podrido**.

Holidays are told in *nosotros*: **alquilamos**, **nadamos**, **paseamos**, **sacamos mil fotos**. And the weather that ruined it: **llovió toda la semana**. In -ar verbs *nosotros* is the same now and in the past: **nadamos** is *we swim* or *we swam*; *ayer* or *en enero* tells you which.

Porteños go on **vacaciones** in January and February, and *la costa* — Mar del Plata, Pinamar — is where half of Buenos Aires ends up. A small detail: **y** turns into **e** before an *i* sound — *fuimos a la montaña e hizo mucho frío*.
A porteño **maneja** (drives) an *auto*. *Conducir* is only for forms and signs. Downtown, the **tránsito** is often **imposible**, and so is finding a place to *estacionar* (park).
**Medio** in front of an adjective softens it — *estoy medio cansado*, I'm kind of tired. It never changes: *medio cansada* too.
Stuck on a word: **¿qué significa?** Too fast? **¿Me lo repetís?** or **repetime, más despacio**. Got it wrong? **Perdón, me confundí.**

Half the time the pharmacist is your doctor: **estoy resfriado**, **tengo alergia**, **me duele el oído** — and you leave with **una curita** or **unas pastillas**. To ask: **¿Tenés algo para la alergia?** — **Necesito algo para la garganta.** A broken bone is **quebrado**: *tiene el brazo quebrado*. And when you hurt yourself: **me lastimé la rodilla**.

Paying by bank transfer is normal, in shops and between friends: **te transfiero**. You ask for the **alias**, the short name of the other person's account. Or you scan a **QR** with your phone — most people use the Mercado Pago app for it.
Most end in **-ado** or **-ido**: *comido, llegado, salido*. A few don't: **hecho**, **dicho**, **visto**, **roto**.
**Me hizo reír**, **me hace acordar**, and **cuanto más practicás, mejor**.

What he swore he'd do, told later — the everyday way: **dijo que iba a pasar**, **me aseguró que me lo iba a devolver**. More careful, and in writing: **dijo que pasaría**, **me lo devolvería**. Two have a changed stem: *poner* → **pondría**, *venir* → **vendría**.

The ATM is **el cajero**: **voy al cajero a sacar plata**. Paying a friend goes by **transferencia** to their **alias** — a few words instead of an account number: **¿a qué alias transferiste?** After it: **¿me mandás el comprobante?** The **sucursal** is the bank branch; a **comisión** is the fee a cajero charges; **las cuentas** are your bills, or your bank accounts.
**Deberíamos juntarnos**, **deberían pagarte más**, **estaría bueno que te tomes unos días**. And when they're scared: **¡animate!**
**Me quejé** — *I complained*; **¿de qué te quejás?** — *what are you complaining about?* **Reclamar** is to file a complaint, and something you do a lot with a phone company.

| Que te vaya bien. | Good luck. |
| Que la pases lindo. | Have a great time. |
| Que tengas buen finde. | Have a good weekend. |
| Ojalá que no llueva. | I hope it doesn't rain. |
| Ojalá salga todo bien. | I hope it all works out. |

A wish is **que** or **ojalá** + the subjunctive. After **ojalá**, *que* is optional: *ojalá que llueva* = *ojalá llueva*. *Tener → tengas, salir → salga*: the *g* of *tengo, salgo* comes along.

| the most | **el** barrio **más** tranquilo **de** la ciudad |
| the least | **la** calle **menos** ruidosa |
| the best, the worst | **el mejor** del mundo, **el peor** |
| really, very | lindo → **lindísimo**, barato → **baratísimo** |
| really far | lejos → **lejísimos** |

*El* or *la* matches the thing, and the group comes after **de**: *la más linda **de** la ciudad*.
The same rule as *soy profesora*: **es enfermera**, **soy contador** — no *un*, no *una*. The article only comes back when you add something: *es una periodista argentina*.

The twist arrives **de golpe** — *all of a sudden* — or **de la nada** — *out of nowhere*. **Para colmo** stacks one more thing on top, like **encima**: **para colmo, llovía**. **Por lo visto** — *apparently* — is what you say when you weren't there. When someone loses a job, people say **lo echaron**; **lo despidieron** is the word of the news and of HR.

After **como si** and **ni que**, always the *-ra* form: **como si no pasara nada** — *as if nothing were happening*; **como si no me viera** — *as if he didn't see me*; **¡ni que fueras mi viejo!** — *it's not like you're my dad!* But **hace como que** takes a normal verb: *hace como que no le importa* — *he acts like he doesn't care*.

**¡Cuidado!** — *careful!* — or the full **tené cuidado**: **tené cuidado con la billetera en el subte**. The tips that come with it: **no uses el celu en la calle**, **no tomes taxi para todo**, **es mejor que pagues en efectivo**, **te conviene reservar**.
**Vino** is wine, and it is also *he came*: **vino Juan** — *Juan came*. The sentence always tells which.

**Buscar** is *to look for* — no *for* needed: *busco una palabra*. **Preguntar** is *to ask* a question: *pregunto dónde está la parada*. With a person, though, put **a** in front: *extraño a mi familia*, *ayudamos a mis abuelos*. Only for a specific person: *busco a Sofi*, but *busco una profe*.
When you don't know the word — or don't need it — use **esto** (this thing here) and **eso** (that thing there). They never change and no noun comes after them: *Quiero eso, por favor.*

| a habit — normal verb | not yet — subjunctive |
| Cuando **vuelvo** del laburo, tomo mate. | Cuando **vuelvas**, avisame. |
| Cuando **cobro**, pago todo. | Cuando **cobre**, te invito. |
| Cuando **empiezo** a estudiar, apago el celu. | Cuando **empieces**, contame. |

**Hasta que** and **apenas** work the same way: *esperá hasta que te llame*, *apenas sepa algo, te aviso*.

The doctor's favorite order: **tenés que hacer reposo** — *you need bed rest*. And a **jarabe** for the cough. A plain **resfrío** — *a cold* — needs no doctor, just a **remedio** from the pharmacy. Anything serious, straight to the **guardia**.
**Por las dudas** — *just in case*; **de última** — *if all else fails*; **si querés** — *if you like*. Say them and you sound like you're from here.
title_en: The words that glue a conversation

body_md: Reported, *venís* becomes **venías** and *podés* becomes **podías**: *«¿Venís?»* → **me preguntó si venías**; *«No puedo»* → **me dijo que no podía**.

| if (then) | now |
| Si **hubiera ahorrado**, | ahora **tendría** un depto. |
| Si **hubiéramos** salido antes, | ya **estaríamos** ahí. |
| Si **hubiera aceptado**, | ahora **sería** otra cosa. |

*Hubiera* + participle for the past that didn't happen; the plain conditional for today.
title_en: Then, and what it means now

body_md: A scare story has its set pieces: **de repente** — *suddenly*; **me pegué un susto** — *I got such a fright*; **salí corriendo** — *I ran off* (more natural than a bare *corrí*); **casi me muero**; **pensé que era un ladrón**; and the relief: **al final no era nada**.
When the story ends badly, the answer is **¡Qué garrón!** — *how annoying!* Informal, and everywhere.

**¿Me lo podés arreglar?** — *can you fix it for me?* After the **técnico** comes: **lo arregló en cinco minutos** — *he fixed it in five minutes*. If he never comes, **hacés un reclamo** — *you file a complaint* — and **nos quejamos** all summer. The questions for the técnico: **¿tiene arreglo?** — *can it be fixed?*; **¿cuánto me sale el arreglo?**; **¿cuándo podés venir?**
**A menos que** takes the subjunctive (*a menos que llueva*); **por si** doesn't (*por si llueve*).
The answers: *de nada*, **ni hablar** — *don't mention it* — or **lo hice de onda** — *I did it to be nice*. **Te agradezco** is warmer and a touch more formal: **te agradezco de verdad**.
*Transferir* changes e to ie when the stress falls on it: yo **transfiero**, él **transfiere**. With vos the stress moves, so it stays: **transferís**.
A **chabón** is a guy, a **mina** a woman — among friends; both sound rude to strangers. Someone great at what they do is a **groso**; a **birra** is a beer.

| same person — infinitive | someone else — subjunctive |
| Estudio **para aprender**. | Te lo explico **para que entiendas**. |
| | Te lo mando **para que lo leas**. |
| | Avisame **antes de que** llegue. |

In an order, **para que** is normal even for the same person: **llevá la campera para que no tengas frío** (also right: *para no tener frío*).

**Contame** opens it; **de repente** is the twist, **por suerte** the relief, **al final** the end. **Igual** is *anyway*, *still*: *estoy cansada, pero igual voy*. **O sea** is *I mean* or *so*. **¿Qué contás?** is just a greeting: *what's new?*

The preterite says what happened; the **imperfect** says what things were like: **era** (I was / he was), **tenía** (I had), **vivía** (I lived), **iba** (I went, I used to go). *Cuando era chico vivía en Rosario* — both verbs describe, nothing *happens*.

| asking | **¿Hay** una estación **por acá**? |
| yes | Sí, **hay** una en la avenida. |
| no | No, acá no **hay** tren. |
| where | La estación **está** a dos cuadras. |

**Por acá** is *around here*. **Hay** never changes: *hay un bar*, *hay dos plazas*, *hay gente*.
**-ito** softens: **un ratito**, **un cafecito**, **cerquita**.

A machine that doesn't work **no anda**: **no anda el ascensor**, **el wifi no anda**. **Funciona** means the same and is just as common. For *how* something works, only *funcionar*: **¿cómo funciona?**

**Dormir** stretches like *poder*: **duermo**, but **dormís**. And **la siesta** after lunch is still sacred in much of the country — less so in Buenos Aires. Around five comes the fourth meal: to **merendar** — mate or coffee with something sweet.
**Me cayó la ficha** — *I finally understood* — comes from the old phone tokens that fell when the call went through. **Recién ahora me cayó la ficha** — *it only just sank in*.
**Entregamos sobre la hora**, **postergaron la fecha**; **se lo merece**, **nos lo merecemos** — *he or she deserves it*, *we deserve it*.
title_en: Sobre la hora, se lo merece

body_md:
| what she said | what you tell |
| «Comprá pan.» | Me pidió que **comprara** pan. |
| «Sacá la basura.» | Me dijo que **sacara** la basura. |
| «Lleguen temprano.» | Nos pidió que **llegáramos** temprano. |
| «Traigan algo.» | Les dijo que **trajeran** algo. |
| «Portate bien.» | Me dijo que **me portara** bien. |

Take the *ellos* past — *compraron, sacaron, trajeron* — and swap **-ron** for **-ra**: *comprara, sacara, trajera*. Nosotros adds **-ramos** with an accent: *llegáramos*.

| a masculine thing | **el que** quieras |
| a feminine thing | **la que** está en la esquina |
| more than one | **los que** vinieron, **las que** prefieras |
| a place | el bar **donde** nos conocimos |

It matches what it stands for. *El que quieras* — whichever you want — takes the subjunctive: you haven't chosen yet.

Every direction is a vos command: drop the *-r*, stress the last vowel.
| doblar | **doblá** | Doblá a la derecha. |
| cruzar | **cruzá** | Cruzá la avenida. |
| caminar | **caminá** | Caminá dos cuadras. |
| seguir | **seguí** | Seguí derecho. |
| parar | **pará** | ¡Pará! |
*Seguir* says *sigo*, but its command is regular: **seguí**. With a pronoun it joins the end: *bajarse* → **bajate**, *subirse* → **subite**.
*Salir* shortens like *tener*: **saldría**, as *tendría*. The rest just add **-ía**: **volvería**, **pediría**, **dejaría**, **buscaría**.
Most buildings have an **encargado** who lives in the building, keeps it clean and takes in your packages. He knows everything that happens on every **piso**.

Ask before you pay: *¿El desayuno está incluido?* *¿Hay wifi?* *¿Hay toallas?* An **alquiler temporario** is an apartment you rent for a few days or weeks — what the booking apps offer all over Buenos Aires.

**Ni idea** — *no idea* — is the everyday short answer when you don't know: *—¿Dónde está Nico? —Ni idea.* The full form is **no tengo idea** or **no tengo ni idea**. To say what about: *Ni idea de dónde está el cargador.*

A porteño asks with a plain question in the present: **¿me pasás la sal?**, **¿me ayudás?** — the *can you* is in the tone. **¿Podrías…?** is the extra-polite version. **¿Me pasás…?** and **¿me alcanzás…?** mean the same: *can you pass me…?*

A porteño goodbye is several: **bueno, nos hablamos**, **cuidate**, **un beso**, **que descanses** — and then another *chau* at the door. **Un abrazo** — or just **abrazo** — is the usual sign-off, especially between men: **dale, abrazo**; **chau, un abrazo**.
**¡Cuidado!** is *watch out!* — a car, a step, a wet floor. To get help fast, say what you need: *necesito un médico*, *¿hay un hospital cerca?*

**Me quedé sin batería**, **sin plata**, **sin laburo** — *I ran out of*. It is the preterite: it happened at one moment. For how things were, use **tenía** and **estaba**: *estaba en el subte*, *no tenía plata*.

**¡Más vale!** — *of course!*; **sí o sí** — *no matter what*; **ni loco** — *no way* — and a woman says **ni loca**: *¿volver con mi ex? Ni loca.* Before a verb **más vale** is *you'd better*: **más vale llevar paraguas**, **más vale que llegues temprano** (subjunctive after *que*). And when there's too much going on: **estoy a full** — *I'm really busy*.

The time in a story is always imperfect: **era la una**, **eran las tres**. The scene keeps going — **no había luz**, **hacía un calor bárbaro** — until something happens: **empezó a llover** and **llegué mojado**.
title_en: Era la una, eran las tres

body_md: **Me puse nervioso** — *I got nervous*; **se puso contenta** — *she was happy* (word for word: she got happy). The feeling changes, so it's *ponerse*, in the preterite.

**Lo de** is *the thing with*: **¿qué pasó con lo de Juan?** After **a** or **en** it is *someone's place*: **voy a lo de Sofi**, **estamos en lo de mis viejos**. And **lo de siempre** is *the usual*: at the café, at the bar, in life.

Nobody arrives on time: **si te dicen a las nueve, llegás a las nueve y media**. In the mate round **gracias** means *no more for me*: **si decís gracias, no tomás más**. Men greet each other with a kiss too. And **la propina** is about ten per cent, in cash.
Told later, the question moves into the past with its **si**: «¿Tenés turno?» → **me preguntaron si tenía turno**.

**Lo que** is *what* when it means *the thing that*: **¿viste lo que pasó?**, **no sé lo que quiere**. It can start a sentence too: **lo que pasó fue raro**. A direct question keeps **qué**: *¿qué pasó?*

*Estar* isn't only for people: things have a state right now too. **El bar está cerrado**, **el bondi está lleno**, **la cerveza está caliente**. The word matches the thing: *el bar* está llen**o**, *la plaza* está llen**a**.

The old place is imperfect, the move is preterite: **antes alquilaba en el centro** — how it was; **me mudé a Palermo** — what happened. **Extrañaba** is missing something over a period of time: *los primeros meses extrañaba mi barrio*.
**Justo** makes a complaint: **justo hoy** — *today of all days*. And **ya fue** — *forget it, it's done* — closes the subject: *¿no vino? Ya fue.*

| **Me hizo reír.** | It made me laugh. |
| **Me hizo llorar.** | It made me cry. |
| **Me hace acordar** a vos. | It reminds me of you. |

**Hacer** + infinitive is *to make someone do it*. The person goes in front: **me**, **te**, **nos**.

**Más vale pájaro en mano que cien volando** — *one sure thing is better than a hundred possible ones*; **a caballo regalado no se le miran los dientes** — *you don't complain about a gift*; **ojos que no ven, corazón que no siente** — *what you don't know can't hurt you*; **del dicho al hecho hay mucho trecho** — *easier said than done*. **El que se quema con leche, ve una vaca y llora** — *after a bad experience, you're scared of anything similar*. For someone who complicates everything: **buscarle la quinta pata al gato** — *to look for the cat's fifth leg*. And when someone walks in: **hablando del rey de Roma…** — *we were just talking about you*.

The offer is the same pattern turned around: **¿querés que te lleve?** — *do you want me to give you a ride?*; **¿querés que traiga algo?** — the guest's question before every *asado*. The *yo* form matches *él*: **lleve**, **traiga**, **ponga**.

The regret works for everyone: **tendríamos que haber salido antes**, **tendrían que haber avisado**. And the softest one of all: **me hubiera gustado** — *I'd have liked to*: **me hubiera gustado verte**.
title_en: We should have, they should have

body_md: The verb stays the same; only the little word changes with the person: **me** gusta, **te** gusta, **le** gusta, **nos** gusta, **les** gusta. *A mi hermano le gusta nadar.*
title_en: Le gusta, nos gusta, les gusta

body_md: **Y bueno** is the porteño shrug — *oh well, what can you do*: **y bueno, así es**. **Ah, me olvidaba** — *oh, I almost forgot* — adds the best part at the end. A story can be **larga** — *long* — or **corta** — *short*.
Agreeing with something positive: **A mí también.** Agreeing with something negative: **A mí tampoco.**
**Devolveme las llaves**, **dejame pasar**, **traeme el cargador** — in requests the pronoun rides on the end of the verb. Here it is *me*; for someone else it is *le*: **devolvele las llaves**.
An **alfajor** is two soft cookies stuck together with *dulce de leche*, often dipped in chocolate. Every kiosco (the corner shop) sells them, and every porteño has a favorite.
**Extraño a mi vieja** — *I miss my mom*. A person takes **a**; a thing doesn't: **extraño el mate**. Not *echar de menos*: that is Spain's, and here nobody says it.
In the story it's the past: **¿te dio miedo?** — **no, me dio risa**. **Me da vergüenza** — *I'm embarrassed* — is built the same way.

You know **queda** and **quedan** for where places are. Put the person in front to say how far it is *for them*: **¿te queda cerca la facu?** — *is college close for you?* — *el centro te queda cerca*.

Any *-ar* verb works the same way: take the *ellos* past (*compraron*), swap **-ron** for **-ra**. «Comprá pan» → **me pidió que comprara pan**; «Cerrá la puerta» → **me dijo que cerrara la puerta**; «Apagá la luz» → **que apagara la luz**.

**Me afanaron la billetera**, **me estafaron**; **se tapó la pileta**, **se trabó el ascensor** — with **me afanaron**, *they* did it and we don't say who; with **se tapó**, it happened by itself and nobody did it.

To pay, you don't say *I want to pay*: you ask them to charge you — **¿me cobrás?** The change they give back is **el vuelto**; small coins and bills are **cambio**. **Cobrar** is also *to get paid*: *¿Cuándo cobrás?* — *when do you get paid?*
**Al lado de** — *next to*: **Almagro queda al lado de Caballito**. Before *el* it shrinks: **al lado del parque**.

**¡No me digas!** and **¡callate!** both mean *no way!* — between friends *callate* isn't rude. **¡Mirá vos!** is milder: *wow, really?* By the afternoon **todo el mundo** knows, thanks to the **chusma**: the person who loves gossip.
**Te dejo la llave para que entres** — someone else's action takes the subjunctive. **Nunca había probado algo así** — one past before another.

**Hasta que** — *until* — works like *cuando*: **hasta que te mudes** looks ahead, but **hasta que conseguí laburo** is past, so the normal verb. **Para que** — *so that* — and **antes de que** — *before* — always take the subjunctive: **para que sepas**, **vení antes de que empiece**. And **que yo sepa** — *as far as I know*.
**Un toque** is *a sec, a bit*: **esperame un toque**. **De paso** is *while you're at it*: **de paso, ¿me comprás pan?**
**No hace falta que** + subjunctive is *you do not need to*: **no hace falta que vengas hoy**. With a thing, **hace falta** is *we need*: **hace falta pan**.

Nobody wants to **quedar mal** — *look rude*. So you thank them for the **invitación**, blame a **compromiso** — *other plans* — and leave the door open: **la próxima voy**, **otro día**. And if they push: **no insistas, che**. **Rechazar** needs something after it — *rechacé dos invitaciones* — and sounds formal; day to day people say **decir que no**: *me cuesta decir que no*.
**Si ganara**, **si viviera**, **si tuviéramos**: the *if* half takes *-ra*, the other half *-ía*. Politely, the *-ía* alone is enough: **¿te molestaría esperar?**

**Emocionarse** is mostly *to be moved, to get emotional* (it can also mean *to get excited*): **me emocioné en el casamiento**. **Se me puso la piel de gallina** — *I got goosebumps*. Also **me dio piel de gallina** — *it gave me goosebumps*.
**Llevo un rato esperando** — *I've been waiting a while*. **Sigo esperando** — *I'm still waiting*.

| Te aconsejo que **lleves** efectivo. | My advice: bring cash. |
| Conviene que **tomes** el subte. | Best to take the subway. |
| Es mejor que **reserves**. | Better book ahead. |
| Es importante que **uses** la SUBE. | It's important to use your SUBE card. |
| Es mejor que **salgamos** temprano. | We'd better leave early. |

Advice with **que** takes the subjunctive. In everyday speech the short way wins — no *que*, just the infinitive: *te conviene reservar hoy*, *te conviene tomar el subte*, *te recomiendo ir en subte*. *-ar* verbs take **e** (*llevar* → **lleves**), the rest **a** (*salgo* → **salgamos**).

**Este** is *this*, near you; **ese** is *that*, further away. Both match the noun: **este** café, **esa** mochila, and **estos**, **estas**, **esos**, **esas** for more than one. *Esa mochila es re linda* — **re** before an adjective is the porteño *really*.
They work like *gustar*: **me enoja que me mienta**, **me alegra que vengas**. If you're the one doing it, no *que*, just the infinitive: *me enoja **llegar** tarde*.
**-ito** and **-cito**: **fresquito**, **solcito**, **calentito**, **igualito**, **una cosita**.

You know **me acuerdo** — *I remember*. The moment something comes back is the past: **¡ah, ahora me acordé!**; **¿te acordaste del pan?** — *did you remember the bread?* To remind someone, use the command: **acordate de las llaves** — *remember the keys*.

**¿Qué hará?** — *I wonder what he's doing*; **¿cuánto saldrá?** — *I wonder how much it is* (a textbook says *¿cuánto costará?*; porteños ask prices with *salir*); **vendrá más tarde** — *she'll probably come later*. For a group: **estarán en el bar**, **serán las ocho**. To vos, the question is **¿estarás cansado?**; the statement is **debés estar cansado** — *you must be tired*. And for a plain future porteños skip this tense: **no sé si va a venir**, **seguro que no viene**.
The verb agrees with the thing: **se me cayó la taza**, **se me cayeron las llaves**. The middle word is who it happened to: **se nos acabó el café**.

Take the infinitive, drop the *-r*, and stress the last vowel:

| mirar | **mirá** |
| esperar | **esperá** |
| venir | **vení** |
| andar | **andá** |

A pronoun joins the end, and the accent goes, because the stress doesn't move: *esperá* → **esperame**. *Decir* → **decime**, *sentarse* → **sentate**. To tell someone to *go*, use **andá** — *ir* has no vos command of its own: *andá al médico*.
title_en: How a vos command is made

body_md: A porteño **despedida** — *farewell party* — ends with a toast, a **brindis**: **¡brindemos!**, **brindo por ustedes**, **¡salud!** Then **gracias por todo**, **fue un placer**, **los voy a extrañar** — and never *adiós*: you say **chau** or **hasta la próxima**, because here nobody really leaves. To leave, people say **bueno, me voy yendo** or **los dejo**; **me despido** sounds like a letter, though *me despedí de todos* — *I said goodbye to everyone* — is fine.

**Hacerse el** + a describing word is *to act, to play*: **se hace el vivo** — *he acts all clever*; **se hizo el distraído** — *he pretended not to notice*. For a woman it's **la**: **se hace la tonta**, **se hizo la distraída**.
**Lo que pasa es que**, **lo raro es que**, **lo de siempre** — and a **dicho** to close it.
A plan is closed with **¿Cómo quedamos?** — *so what's the plan?* The answer fixes the time and the place: **Quedamos tipo ocho en la esquina.** Or ask straight: *¿A qué hora nos juntamos?*

| yo | **me** despierto | **me** levanto | **me** acuesto |
| vos | **te** despertás | **te** levantás | **te** acostás |
| él, ella | **se** despierta | **se** levanta | **se** acuesta |
| nosotros | **nos** despertamos | **nos** levantamos | **nos** acostamos |
| ellos | **se** despiertan | **se** levantan | **se** acuestan |
*Despertarse* and *acostarse* stretch their stem, but not with vos or nosotros. **Me voy** works the same way: *me voy, te vas, se va*.
The errand told later: **me pidió que comprara pan**, **nos dijo que llegáramos temprano**, **les pidió que trajeran algo**. The question: **preguntale si tienen stock**.

To give your view, porteños say **para mí** or **me parece que**: *para mí conviene esperar*; *me parece que es caro*. **¿Qué opinás?** is the natural question; **opino que…** as an answer sounds stiff. **No me convence** — *I'm not sure about it* — works like *gustar*.
**Era**, **tenía**, **estaba** paint the scene — how things were. **Fui**, **tuve**, **llegó** are what happened in it. **Estaba lloviendo cuando llegó Juan.**

After *quiero que*, *necesito que*, *no hace falta que* and *para que* (so that), the verb takes the subjunctive: **quiero que me expliques** — *I want you to explain it to me*; **no hace falta que entiendas todo** — *you don't need to understand everything*; **mirá el video para que entiendas** — *watch the video so you understand*.
title_en: No hace falta que entiendas todo

body_md: Spain says *hoy he trabajado*; a porteño says **hoy laburé**. Even for today, even for something that just happened: **¿Llegaste?** — *Did you get here?*
**Resulta que** — *it turns out*; **encima** — *on top of that*; **total** — *after all, anyway* (it doesn't matter): **vamos a pie, total es cerca**.
*They* in the past: **ganaron**, **perdieron**, **empataron**. The machine that let you down: **ayer anduvo**, **hoy no anda**.

Words for people follow the person: *mi tío, mi tía*; *brasileño, brasileña*. A word in *-e* stays put: *canadiense*. A nationality ending in a consonant adds *-a*, and any accent mark goes: *francés → francesa*, *español → española*.

| yo | vos | él, ella |
| **me la banco** | **te la bancás** | **se la bancó** |
| **me las arreglo** | **te las arreglás** | **se las arregla** |

Some verbs carry *me, te, se* plus the *la*; others just the *la*: **la pifié**, **la pifiaste**; **la rompiste**, **la rompe**. The *la* never changes.
title_en: The la stays, the person changes

body_md: **No entiendo** — *I don't understand*. **¿Me explicás?** or **explicame** — *can you explain?*
**La previa** is the drinks before going out; **la sobremesa** is the long chat at the table after eating, which nobody cuts short.
When nobody's to blame: **¡qué mala suerte!** And at Ezeiza, the international airport, the board says what every porteño expects: the flight is **demorado** — *delayed*.
Every stretchy verb stays short with vos: **querés, podés, preferís, volvés**. If you hear *quieres* or *puedes*, that's not Buenos Aires.

You ask for a **turno** (an appointment), and the verb is **sacar turno**: *tengo que sacar turno con el médico*. The **guardia** is the emergency room. **Estoy engripado** — *I've got the flu* — is what gets you the day off.
Pass on news without owning it: **dicen que va a llover** — *they say it's going to rain*; **parece que Juan se mudó** — *looks like Juan moved*.
Big moments: **se recibió** — *graduated*; **se comprometieron** — *got engaged*; **se jubiló** — *retired*. And the feelings: **se emocionó** — *got emotional*; **me llegó** — *it touched me*.

**Hace calor**, **hace frío** — it's hot, it's cold. But **hay sol**, **hay viento**, **está nublado**, and **llueve** alone (for right now you'll also hear *está lloviendo*). You yourself **tenés frío**. Seasons are flipped: *el verano* runs from late December to March. **Bárbaro** means *great*, not barbaric: *¡Bárbaro!* — Great! *Hay un sol bárbaro* — it's really sunny.

**El de** is also for owners and people. With a name it is *someone's*: **el de Lucía** — *Lucía's*; **las de Santi** — *Santi's*. With people it is *the guy in, the people from*: **el de rojo** — *the guy in red*; **los de arriba** — *the people upstairs*.
title_en: El de Lucía, el de rojo

body_md: **Tener que** + infinitive says what you have to do: *Tengo que laburar*, *¿tenés que estudiar?*

For a group: **coman**, **prueben**, **sírvanse**, **no se olviden**. The *no* doesn't change the verb, only where the pronoun goes: **siéntense** → **no se sienten**; **sírvanse** → **no se sirvan**.

**Soler** is *to usually*: **suelo almorzar tarde** — *I usually have lunch late*; **¿solés venir acá?** It only ever comes with an infinitive. In speech porteños more often say **generalmente** or **casi siempre**: **generalmente almuerzo tarde**.
**Manejé**, **cargué**, **choqué**, **cobré** — *I*. **¿Manejaste?**, **¿escuchaste?** — *you*. **Leyó**, **comentó** — *he, she*. **Contaron** — *they*.

English *bring* is two verbs here. **Llevar** is to a place where you are not yet: *¿Qué llevo al asado?* **Traer** is to the place where you are now: *¿Podés traer hielo?* Going to a friend's place, always ask **¿qué llevo?** **Venir** works like *traer*: on your way to someone, say **ya voy**, not *vengo*.

**No es que** takes the subjunctive with every verb and every person: **no es que no me interese**, **no es que no me importe**, **no es que me caiga mal** — *it's not that I don't like him*; **no es que no queramos**, **no es que no podamos**.
Drop the *no* and **hace falta** says what's needed: **hace falta una fotocopia**. **¿Es obligatorio?** — *is it required?* — is a handy question at any counter.
Weather takes three verbs: **hace** calor, **hay** humedad, **está** nublado — and **llueve** on its own.
In Argentina the everyday word for "you" is **vos**, and it has its own verb forms: *vos sos* (you are). You'll hear *tú* in other countries. This course never uses it.

What you remember takes **de**: **mi abuela se acuerda de todo**; **nos acordamos de esa época**. Before **que** or **cuando**, people usually drop the **de**: *me acuerdo que íbamos a la playa*. **No me acordaba** — *I'd forgotten* — is imperfect: the not-remembering went on until someone brought it up.
The **calefón** heats the water, and breaks in July. When there's a **pérdida** — *a leak* — you call the **plomero** to **arreglar** it.
The news likes the passive: **fue** + participle. **El puente fue construido en 1900**; **la estación fue inaugurada ayer**. The participle agrees like an adjective: *construido, construida*.

**Para mí**, **me parece que**, **coincido**, **al contrario** — the whole argument. *Opino que* is for TV panels: at the table it is **para mí, el árbitro estuvo mal**. And the line that ends it: **¡no exageres!** For advice, **tendrías que** — *you should*: **tendrías que ir al médico**.
To say where someone is from, put **de** after the verb: *Soy de Rosario.* *¿De dónde sos?*

For plans, use **ir a** + a verb: *Vamos a organizar el cumple.* *¿Quién va a preparar el café?* A little word like *te* or *me* goes before it: **te voy a esperar**, *¿me vas a ayudar?* You will also hear *voy a esperarte*.

The ground floor is **la planta baja**; above it comes *el **primer** piso* (*primero* loses its *-o* before a noun). Then **segundo, tercero, cuarto, quinto**. Higher up, people often just say the number: *piso doce*. On the **timbre**, *4° B* is read **cuarto B**. **Piso** is also the floor you walk on.

Only three verbs break the pattern: *ser* (**era**), *ir* (**iba**) and *ver*, which keeps its *e*: **veía**, **veías**. Set **antes** against **ahora** and the imperfect does the rest: *antes veía dibujitos, ahora veo series.*

The other end: **no lo aguanto** — *I can't stand him*; **es insoportable**; **es re falso**. And the good end: **nos hicimos amigos** — *we became friends*. And **hay química** — *there's chemistry* — is mostly said about a couple.
In the imperfect, *yo* and *él/ella* are the same word: **era** is *I was* and *he was*. The subject — or the story — tells you which. **De chico** is *as a kid*.
title_en: Yo and él share a form

body_md: A bife comes jugoso, a punto, or **bien cocido** — *well done*; **vuelta y vuelta** is seared on each side and almost raw inside. The bill has a line for the **cubierto** — *the cover charge*: the bread and the cutlery.

| Habla **como si supiera** todo. | He talks as if he knew everything. |
| **Como si fuera** fácil. | As if it were easy. |
| Me saludó **como si nada**. | He said hi as if nothing had happened. |
| ¡**Ni que fuera** tan difícil! | It's not like it's that hard! |

**Ni que…** is a complaint: you are saying the thing is NOT true. After **como si** and **ni que**, always the *-ra* form, whatever the time.
**Voy entendiendo** — bit by bit. **Me cae bien** — I like him, as a person.
Drop the final *-r* and stress the last vowel: *mirar* → **mirá**, *venir* → **vení**. Pronouns stick to the end: **sentate**, **decime**, **esperame**.
**Ojalá** is *I hope*, and the subjunctive follows it: **ojalá que no llueva** — *I hope it doesn't rain*.

Bills come in plural, and so do the verbs: **aumentaron la luz y el gas**, **aumentan las tarifas**. The plural can also be a nameless *they*: **me aumentaron el alquiler** — *they raised my rent*. Prices that **bajaron**? Nobody remembers. Porteños keep count: *el **boleto** aumentó tres veces este año*.

In Buenos Aires prices **aumentan** so often that it is small talk: *¿viste cómo aumentó el café?* Your **aumento** — *raise* — never keeps up with the **inflación**. When something costs too much: **está por las nubes** — *sky-high*; **sale un ojo de la cara** — *it costs a fortune*.
Porteños mostly say **colegio** for school, primary or secondary: **¿A qué colegio ibas?** — *Iba a un colegio de mi barrio.* *Escuela* is understood and used too, mostly for state primary schools.

These hurt. **Pelotudo** is stronger than *boludo*; only close friends say it as a joke. A **forro** is a nasty person. An **hinchapelotas** won't stop bothering you: *¡no rompas las bolas!* — often just *¡no rompas!* **Andá a cagar** is *go to hell*: a joke between friends, a fight with a stranger. **Hijo de puta** is one of the strongest insults — but shouted at a great goal it is admiration.

| yo, él, ella | **debería** |
| vos | **deberías** |
| nosotros | **deberíamos** |
| ellos, ustedes | **deberían** |

All take an infinitive: *deberíamos juntarnos*. *En esa empresa **deberían** pagar mejor* — *that company should pay better*.
Between friends a bare vos command is polite enough: **prendé la luz**, **apagá la tele**. With a pronoun it joins the end, like *ayudame*: **acompañame**, **llevame**.
**Sigo laburando ahí** — *I still work there*. **Dejé de fumar** — *I quit smoking*. **Volvió a llamar** — *he called again*.

You rent through an **inmobiliaria** or straight from the **dueño**. Every month you pay the **alquiler** plus the **expensas** — *the building fees*. To sign the **contrato** you leave a **depósito** and show a **garantía**: someone who answers for you if you don't pay.

**Estoy saliendo con alguien** — *I'm seeing someone*. When it ends, porteños **cortan**: **cortamos** — *we broke up*. With a name they say **con Santi cortamos** — *Santi and I broke up* — and the same for a fight: **con Sofi nos peleamos**. **Nos peleamos** is *we fight* and also *we had a fight*.
**Antes alquilaba** — how it was; **me mudé** — what happened; **voy a pintar** — what's next. A porteño story moves through all three without stopping.
**¿Qué le pasará?** wonders; **a lo mejor tiene gripe** guesses; **seguro que está cansado** bets. The future can guess on its own too: **Sofi estará en el subte** — *Sofi's probably on the subway*.

| ellos (preterite) | yo, él, ella | vos |
| salieron | **saliera** | **salieras** |
| dijeron | **dijera** | **dijeras** |
| fueron | **fuera** | **fueras** |
| vinieron | **viniera** | **vinieras** · ellos **vinieran** |

Swap **-ron** for **-ra** and it works for every verb: *estudiar* → **estudiara, estudiaras**. **Fuera** is both *ser* and *ir*: *quería que fueras feliz* (be), *quería que fueras al asado* (go). **Mis viejos querían que estudiara una carrera** — the wish is in the past, so the second verb is too.
Three short commands you will hear all day: *hacer* gives **hacé**, *poner* gives **poné**, and *dar* gives **dame** — *give me*: *dame otro*. Never *haz* or *pon* — those belong to another Spanish.

**Encantado** — *delighted* — is what you say when you meet someone, and it matches whoever is speaking: a man says *encantado*, a woman **encantada**. The reply: **igualmente** — *likewise*. Day to day, most porteños just say **un gusto** or *mucho gusto*: *Soy Sofi.* — *Un gusto, Sofi.*

Porteños say **vos** to almost everyone: the shop owner, a doctor, an old man on the bus. You may still hear **usted** sometimes, but **vos** is always fine for you. The politeness lives in the words around it: **disculpá que te moleste**, **perdón por la molestia**, **muy amable**.

| El puente **fue construido** hace un siglo. | was built |
| La estación **fue inaugurada** ayer. | was opened |
| Los ladrones **fueron detenidos**. | were arrested |

**Fue** + participle, and the participle agrees like an adjective. **Detenidos** is also a noun: *hay dos detenidos* — *two people were arrested*.

| | if… | …would |
| yo, él, ella | si **ganara**, si **viviera** | **viviría**, **daría**, **sabría** |
| vos | si **pudieras**, si **tuvieras** | ¿qué **harías**? |
| nosotros | si **tuviéramos** | **iríamos**, **compraríamos** |

Any verb: the *ellos* past, **-ron** → **-ra** (*ganaron* → **ganara**). The *we* form takes an accent: **tuviéramos**.
**Además** adds a reason; **por lo menos** finds the good side; **la verdad** says what you really think.
**Me gusta el mate** means "mate pleases me". The verb matches the thing you like: *me gusta el café*, but *me gustan las facturas*.

| | jugar | salir | ver |
| yo, él, ella | jug**aba** | sal**ía** | ve**ía** |
| vos | jug**abas** | sal**ías** | ve**ías** |
| nosotros | jug**ábamos** | sal**íamos** | ve**íamos** |
| ellos, ustedes | jug**aban** | sal**ían** | ve**ían** |
*Ver* keeps its *e*: **veía**. For TV, **miraba** and **veía** both work; to see a person, only *ver*: **veía a mi abuela**. **Me encantaba andar en bici.**
Name your source first, then the news: **lo dijeron en la radio**, **lo vi en las redes**, *lo leí en el diario*, *lo vi en la tele* — or *me llamó Sofi y me dijo que…*

**Mis viejos querían que estudiara** — the wish is in the past, so the second verb is too. **Por más que me cueste** — however hard it is. Something not sure or not real yet takes the subjunctive: *por más que llueva, vamos igual*. A fact takes the normal verb: *por más que ahorro, no me alcanza*.

The family WhatsApp group sends a **cadena** — *a chain message* — every morning. **Chequeá la fuente** before you believe it — and before **compartirlo**. If it isn't true: **es mentira**, **es falso** or, very porteño, **es verso** — *it's made up*.
**Aparentemente**, **se ve que**, **lo desmintieron** — and always **¿cuál es la fuente?**

The moment a feeling hit, or a thing slipped your mind, is preterite with its pronoun: **me sentí re mal**, **me olvidé de avisarte** (a thing you left behind takes no *de*: **me olvidé las llaves**), **nos pusimos contentos**.
With weather, *very* is **mucho**, not *muy*, because *calor* and *frío* are nouns: **hace mucho calor**, **hay mucha humedad** — *mucha* because *humedad* is feminine.
On a colectivo the **boleto** — the fare — depends on how far you go, so you tell the driver first (*hasta Palermo*) and then tap. Not sure it's the right bus? *¿Va a Palermo?*
title_en: Tell the driver where you're going

body_md: With older neighbors like **don José** and **doña Marta** you still say vos, but warmly: **cómo no** — *of course*; **faltaba más** — *of course, don't mention it*; **dejá, te doy una mano** — *leave it, I'll give you a hand*.

Most work emails open with **Hola, Juan:** or **Buen día, Sofi:** and close with **Saludos**, **Abrazo** or **Un abrazo**. **Estimado Juan** / **Estimada Sofi** is the formal exception, and so is **quedo atento** (a woman: **quedo atenta**) — *I look forward to your reply*. **Te adjunto** is *I'm attaching*: *te adjunto mi CV*; **desde ya, gracias** is *thanks in advance*.

The thing that hurts is the subject: **me duele la cabeza** — *my head hurts*, **me duelen los pies** — *my feet hurt*. The *me* says whose, so Spanish uses *la*, not *mi*. For someone else, name them with *a*: **a Juan le duele la espalda** — *Juan's back hurts*.
**Hablaría**, **me quedaría** (I, he, she) · **¿qué dirías?** (vos) · **iríamos**, **podríamos** (we). Same *-ía*, then **-s** for vos and **-mos** for we.

**Lo** turns anything into *the thing*: **lo tuyo es la cocina** — *your thing is cooking*; **lo mío** — *my thing*; **lo primero** — *the first thing*; **lo justo** — *just enough*. Giving up an argument: **lo que vos digas** — *whatever you say*. **Lo que sea** — *whatever, anything*: **comemos lo que sea**.
The conditional adds **-ía** to the whole infinitive: *comprar* → **compraría**. A few shorten first: **haría**, **diría**, **tendría**, **podría**.

**Te banco** — *I'm here for you*; **no lo banco** — *I can't stand him*. One verb, opposite meanings. It also means *to wait for*: **¿me bancás acá?** — *can you wait for me here?* For things you often hear **bancarse**: *no me banco el frío* — *I can't stand the cold*.

Growing up, every wish was in the past: **mis viejos querían que estudiara** — *my parents wanted me to study*; **no querían que saliera de noche** — *they didn't want me going out at night*. The second verb follows the first into the past.
**Mis abuelos llegaron de Italia en barco** — otra **época**.
*Manejar* in the past is regular: **manejé**, **¿manejaste vos?**. **Chocar** swaps *c* for *qu* before *é*: **choqué**. Run a red light and it's **una multa**.
**Ni a palos** — *no way, not a chance*. And for a shrug: **dale que va** — *good enough, let's go*. When something's awful: **está de terror**; when it's perfect: **impecable**.
**Buen día** in the morning, **buenas tardes** later, **buenas** any time. To leave: **chau** or **hasta luego**. And after every *gracias*, a **de nada**.

| Te devuelvo **el libro**. | Te **lo** devuelvo. |
| ¿Me dejás **las llaves**? | ¿Me **las** dejás? |
| Le regalé **un libro**. | **Se lo** regalé. |

The person goes first, the thing second. **Lo, la, los, las** match the thing: *el libro* → **lo**, *las llaves* → **las**. *Le* or *les* before them becomes **se**; add **a Sofi** to say who: **se la regalé a Sofi**.
A porteño's older sister is *mi hermana **más grande***, the younger one *mi hermano **más chico***. And *-ísimo* turns anything up: **riquísimo**, **carísimo**.

A yes/no question told later uses **si** (*whether*): *¿Venís?* → **me preguntó si venía**; *¿Abre hoy?* → **no sé si abre hoy**. The verb is normal, no subjunctive. Told in the past, it usually moves back: *venís* → *venía*.

| straight | softer |
| ¿Tenés cambio? | ¿**No tendrás** cambio? |
| ¿Sabés dónde queda? | ¿**No sabrás** dónde queda? |
| Quiero un turno. | **Quisiera** un turno. |
| Perdón. | **Disculpá que te moleste**. |

**No** plus the future turns a question into a gentle one: *you wouldn't happen to…?* After **disculpá que**, the verb takes the subjunctive: *te moleste*.

After **no es que** any verb goes into the subjunctive, and you already know the forms: **sea**, **esté**, **haya**, **tenga**. *No es que sea caro, es que no tengo plata* — *it's not that it's expensive, I just have no money*. *No es que esté cansado, es que laburo temprano.*

Every porteño asks it: **¿hace cuánto que estudiás?** — *how long have you been studying?* Answer either way: **hace un año que estudio** or **llevo un año estudiando**. Or count from a moment: **desde que llegué** — *since I arrived*.
Every account has an **alias** — a few words instead of a long number — and paying a friend is **pasame el alias** and **te transfiero**. After: **mandame el comprobante**.
Everyone can keep at it: **sigo practicando**, **seguimos buscando** laburo, *mis amigos* **siguen tratando de** entenderme. And stop: **dejaron de** venir — *they stopped coming*.
**Tipo** before a time is *around*: **tipo ocho** — *around eight*, which in Buenos Aires means eight-fifteen at the earliest. **En punto** is *on the dot*, and rarer.
**Necesito que me ayudes**, **te pido que me esperes**, **¿querés que te lleve?** When the person after *que* is someone else, the verb goes subjunctive.

How a nationality changes for a woman depends on how it ends:
| a man | a woman |
| brasileñ**o** | brasileñ**a** |
| español | español**a** |
| franc**és** | franc**esa** |
| alem**án** | alem**ana** |
| canadiens**e** | canadiens**e** |
*-o* becomes *-a*; a consonant adds *-a*, and *-és* or *-án* drop the accent; *-e* stays the same.

This future is for wondering: **¿dónde estará?** — *I wonder where he is*. Same with **¿qué hora será?**, **¿tendrá cargador?**, **¿habrá café?**, **¿qué hará?**, **¿vendrá?**, **¿qué le pasará?** For *they*, add **n**: **¿dónde estarán?**, **¿de quién serán?** For plans, porteños say *voy a*.

**El que avisa no traiciona** — *don't say I didn't warn you*. You say it while you give the warning. Literally: *the one who warns you doesn't betray you*. Two more you'll hear in Buenos Aires: **sobre gustos no hay nada escrito** — *everyone has their own taste*; **el que quiere celeste, que le cueste** — *if you want something good, you have to work for it*.

The *colectivo* crosses the city; to go to another city you take the **micro** (the long-distance bus). You buy the **pasaje** at the terminal or online. A round-trip ticket is **ida y vuelta**. In Buenos Aires the micros leave from the **terminal** of Retiro, and the airports are Ezeiza (international) and Aeroparque (in the city).
The word for "the" matches its noun: **el** kiosco, **la** empanada, **los** kioscos, **las** empanadas.
**Alguien** is *someone*, **nadie** is *nobody* — and Spanish keeps the *no* as well: **no vino nadie**. If *nadie* comes first, drop the *no*: **nadie me dijo nada**.

**Lo dije en joda** — *I said it as a joke*. **Tomar el pelo** is the same game as cargar: **¿me estás tomando el pelo?** — *are you joking with me?* **¿Me estás jodiendo?** is very casual: friends only. A **broma** is a prank, or something not said seriously.
**Ya había comido** — *I had already eaten* — puts one past before another: **cuando llegaste, ya había comido**.

Each problem has its person: the **plomero** for a **canilla** that **gotea** — *a dripping faucet* — the **gasista** for the calefón, the **encargado** for the **portero eléctrico**. A **filtración** from the apartment upstairs goes to the **administración** — *the management office* — and takes months. A toilet or a faucet that leaks **pierde agua**: **el inodoro pierde agua**.

| **Me hizo** reír. | It made me laugh. |
| **Me hizo** sentir en casa. | It made me feel at home. |
| Vos **me hacés** reír. | You make me laugh. |
| **Nos hizo** llorar a todos. | It made us all cry. |

**Reírse**, now: me río, **te reís**, se ríe, nos reímos. Before: me reí, te reíste, **se rió**, nos reímos.

**Hubiera** changes with the person: **hubiera** (I, he, she), **hubieras** (vos), **hubiéramos** (we), **hubieran** (they, you all). *Si hubieras estudiado medicina, ahora serías médico. Si hubiéramos ahorrado, ahora estaríamos en Bariloche. Si hubieran construido el puente, no habría tanto tránsito.*
**¡Qué bueno que estés acá!** — reacting to something *now* takes the subjunctive. **Me alegro** — *I'm glad*; **qué lástima** — *what a shame*.
**Te debo una** — *I owe you one*. The answer is **de nada**. **No pasa nada** — *it's fine, no worries* — is the answer to *perdón*.
Porteños say a feeling *gives* them something: **me da bronca** — *it makes me mad*; **me da vergüenza** — *I'm embarrassed*; **me da lástima** — *I feel sorry*; **me da igual** — *I don't care*.
To order the same again, say **otro**: *Otro café, por favor.* For a word that takes *una*, it's **otra**: *Otra cerveza.* It already means "another", so nothing goes in front.
**Me pidió que lo llamara** — *she asked me to call him*. The same form follows an order told later: **me dijo que esperara** — *he told me to wait*.

**al lado de** (next to), **enfrente de** (across from), **atrás de** (behind), **adelante de** (in front of), **entre** (between). Careful: *enfrente* is across the street, not *in front*. Remember *de + el* = *del*: *al lado del kiosco*. With no place after them, drop the *de*: *está enfrente*, *vivo al lado*.

| one thing | more than one |
| **Se busca** perro. | **Se aceptan** tarjetas. |
| **Se permite** fumar en la terraza. | No **se permiten** mascotas. |
| **Se prohíbe** hacer ruido. | **Se hacen** envíos. |

The verb agrees with the thing: one → *se busca*, several → *se arreglan bicis*. Most real signs just say **Prohibido fumar**; **se prohíbe** is the formal version.
*Our* matches the thing, not the people: **nuestro** país, **nuestra** familia, **nuestros** hijos, **nuestras** hermanas. *Their* is still **su**: *su familia*, *sus hijos*.

**Las elecciones** — *the elections* — decide the **gobierno** and the **presidente**. Before them, the **debate** on TV; after, the **resultados**. If nobody wins outright there's a **balotaje** — *a runoff*. The course stays out of who won: the words, not the opinions.
**Te lo paso** is *I'll send it to you* — a number, a photo, a file. And a loan comes back **sin falta** — *for sure* (word for word, *without fail*).
**Pienso** + verb is *I plan to*: *pienso ir al cine*, *¿pensás salir hoy?* **Creo que** … is *I think that* …: *creo que está cerrado*, *¿creés que abre hoy?* And **no creo** is *I don't think so*.

Describing more than one person is *ser* plus a word with an *-s*:

| yo | soy alt**o** | soy alt**a** |
| vos | sos rubi**o** | sos rubi**a** |
| él, ella | es flac**o** | es flac**a** |
| nosotros | **somos** alt**os** | **somos** alt**as** |
| ellos, ustedes | **son** moroch**os** | **son** lind**as** |

A mixed group takes *-os*. A word in *-e* or a consonant just adds *-s* or *-es*: *joven* → **jóvenes**.
When the story ends well, the listener says **¡menos mal!** — *thank goodness!* — and **¡por fin!** when it took forever. **¿En serio?** keeps you talking: *really?*

**¡Mirá vos!** — *oh, really?* (mild surprise) — and **no lo puedo creer** keep the story going. Porteños also say **¡no te puedo creer!** — the same thing: *I can't believe it!* A **chusma** is someone who loves the gossip.

| what he said | what you tell |
| «Paso el martes.» | Dijo que **pasaría** el martes. |
| «Te la devuelvo.» | Me aseguró que me la **devolvería**. |
| «Lo arreglo.» | Dijo que lo **arreglaría**. |
| «Lo pongo.» | Dijo que lo **pondría**. |

The infinitive + **-ía**. A few bend the stem: *poner* → **pondría**, *venir* → *vendría*, *tener* → *tendría*.

**Buena onda** is the porteño compliment for a person: easy, warm, *nice*. **Mala onda** is the opposite. **Buena onda** and **mala onda** never change: *ella es buena onda*. **Simpático** is narrower — *friendly*, pleasant to talk to — and does change: **simpática**.
For *they*, add **-n** to the form you know: **no creo que sean**, **no creo que estén**, **no creo que tengan**, **no creo que puedan**, **no creo que lleguen a tiempo**.

| **No es que** no **quiera**, | It's not that I don't want to, |
| **es que** no puedo. | it's just that I can't. |
| **No es que** no **tengamos** ganas. | It's not that we don't feel like it. |

The reason you deny takes the subjunctive; the real one, after **es que**, the normal verb.

**A ver si** is *let's see if* — and, just as often, a hope: **a ver si nos juntamos** — *we should get together sometime*. To find something out, porteños **averiguan**. After **dudo que**, the verb goes in the subjunctive: **dudo que venga** — *I doubt he'll come*.

| **Ando buscando** laburo. | I've been looking for work. |
| **Voy conociendo** gente. | I'm getting to know people. |
| **Estamos por** arrancar. | We're about to start. |
| Estoy **a punto de** terminar. | I'm just about to finish. |

**Ando** + *-ando* is these days, on and off, not this very second; **voy** + *-ando* happens bit by bit.

| something new | something you already know |
| **Hay** un kiosco. | **El** kiosco **está** en la esquina. |
| **Hay** una parada acá. | **La** parada **está** lejos. |

**Hay** goes with *un, una*, a number or nothing at all, and never changes: *hay dos kioscos*, *¿hay agua?* **Está** goes with *el, la*.
The irregular past keeps one stem for every person: **vine, viniste, vino, vinimos, vinieron**. Learn the *yo* — **traje**, **quise**, **pude** — and the rest follows.

Sure of it? The normal verb: **seguro que abren**, **creo que viene**. Doubt it, and the subjunctive: **no creo que abran hoy**. Even the forecast gets the treatment: **el pronóstico es de lluvia, pero no creo que llueva**.

When anything stops working, porteños say it **no anda**: *no anda el wifi*, *no me anda el celu*. A machine that fails on its own takes **se**: **se apagó** — *it switched off*; **se colgó** — *it froze*. The universal fix: **apagalo y prendelo**.
**Tipo** makes a time loose: **tipo ocho** is *around eight*, and in Buenos Aires people often arrive a bit later. For exactly eight, say **a las ocho en punto**.
At work, a **proyecto** has a **plazo** — *a deadline* — and a **presupuesto** — *a budget*. You **entregás** it to the **cliente**, ideally before you're **atrasado**.
*Voy* is where you're going; **me voy** is that you're leaving: *me voy a las ocho*. *¿Te vas?* — *Sí, me voy.* And when someone is slow to leave: **¡Dale, apurate!** — *come on, hurry up!*
Two *me*s that work differently. **Me levanto**: *I* get up. **Me gusta**: it pleases *me* — so **me gustan** when the thing is plural.

Besides the public hospital and the *obra social*, lots of porteños pay a **prepaga** — a private health plan. Once a year: a **chequeo**, an *análisis de* **sangre**, **la presión** and **la vacuna** for the **gripe**.
About something that hasn't happened yet, *cuando* takes the subjunctive: **avisame cuando llegues** — *let me know when you get there*. About a habit it doesn't: *cuando llego, tomo mate*.

The morning after, the question is what still runs: **el subte funciona con normalidad**, or **suspendieron el servicio**. When the strike itself ends, the phrase is **levantaron el paro** or **se levantó el paro**. **Suspender** is for classes, an exam, a march or a service.
Many shops are their product plus **-ería**: *carne* → **carnicería**, *pan* → *panadería*. The **almacén** is the old corner shop that sells a bit of everything.

**Zona norte** — the suburbs north of the General Paz, like San Isidro and Tigre — has a name for money and **árboles**; **zona sur** — Avellaneda, Lanús, Quilmes — is, in general, cheaper. Inside the Capital, Recoleta and Belgrano are the leafy north; Caballito, Almagro and Villa Crespo sit in the middle.

Tell your life story with the past you already know: **nací** (*I was born*), **viví**, **volví**. **Me crié** is *I grew up*, and it always takes **me**: *Nací en Italia, pero me crié en Buenos Aires.* To ask: *¿Te criaste acá?*
title_en: Your story: nací, me crié, viví

body_md: **Antes era distinto** — *it used to be different*. **¡Qué épocas!** — *those were the days!* — closes it. With *ser* it is a different kind of thing: **el barrio era distinto**. With *estar* it has changed: **estás distinta** — *you look different*.
**Laburar** is the everyday Argentine word for *to work* — from the Italian *lavorare*. *Trabajar* is understood everywhere and fine too.

Where English *is*, Spanish *has*: **tengo hambre** (I'm hungry), **tengo sed** (thirsty), **tengo frío**, **tengo calor**, **tengo sueño** (sleepy), **tengo miedo** (scared). The same *tener* as your age.

**Yo en tu lugar** — *in your place, if I were you* — means the same as *yo que vos*, a little more serious. The advice after it is still *would*: **yo en tu lugar, hablaría con él**, **yo me quedaría**.
Conditions that haven't happened take the subjunctive: **a menos que llueva** — *unless it rains*; **siempre y cuando vengas** — *as long as you come*; **en caso de que** — *in case*.
title_en: A menos que, siempre y cuando

body_md: **Mejor** and **peor** never take *más*: **está mejor**, **fue peor**. Only a kind person can be **más buena** — *nicer*. For *really*, porteños say **re**: *re rico*; *-ísimo* turns it up further: **riquísimo**, **carísimo**.
The porteño *how did it go?* is **¿Cómo te fue?**, and the answer is **Me fue bien** or **Me fue re mal**.

With a verb, **gusta** and **encanta** stay singular, even for two activities: *Me gusta leer y cocinar.* With things they follow the thing: *Me encanta el fútbol*, *me encantan las series*. To agree: **A mí también** after a *yes*, **A mí tampoco** after a *no*. With a normal verb it's **yo**: *No bailo.* — *Yo tampoco.*

*Comer* and *salir* take the same endings: **comí, comiste, comió**; **salí, saliste, salió**. For *nosotros* the past looks like the present — *salimos* — and *anoche* or *ayer* says which one it is.

Months have no capital: **en marzo**, **en diciembre**. Temperature is **grados**: *hace treinta grados* is a normal January day, and porteños blame everything on **la humedad**. Argentina uses Celsius: *35 grados* is very hot (95°F), and *1 grado* is almost freezing. With **desde** or **hace** + a time, Spanish uses the present: *vivo acá hace dos meses* — I've been living here for two months.
Saying **gracias** when you hand the mate back means *I'm done*. Say it on the first one and that's your last.
**Me cayó la ficha**, **me da cosa**, **me pone mal** — feelings in porteño.
A **dicho** is a saying, and porteños drop one to close an argument: **más vale tarde que nunca**; **no hay mal que por bien no venga** — *something good can come from something bad*.
**Cocinero → cocinera**, **vendedor → vendedora**. Words in **-ista** don't change: *el periodista, la periodista*. And **policía** is the same word for both.

| | -ar | -er, -ir |
| yo, él, ella | jug**aba** | com**ía** |
| vos | jug**abas** | com**ías** |
| nosotros | jug**ábamos** | sal**íamos** |

Every verb but *ser, ir* and *ver* follows this. It's the *used to* of English: **Los sábados jugábamos a la pelota.**

A hot night, a **cucaracha** in the kitchen, and it **vuela**: **grité**, **pegué un salto** — more natural than a bare *salté* — and in the end **la maté** with an **ojota**. Every porteño has this story. The other summer visitor is the **mosquito**: **me picó un mosquito**, so nobody goes out without **repelente**.
**Limpio** is *I clean* — and also *clean*, the opposite of *sucio*: *limpio el baño* — *el baño está limpio*, *la cocina está limpia*.

Before you pass it on, ask **¿es cierto?** — *is it true?* **Cierto** changes with the noun: *la noticia es cierta*. If the answer is **es mentira** — *it's not true* — stop there. **Lo leyó en las redes** — *she read it on social media* — is not a source.
**Estricto, estricta** is *strict*. *Para salir tenía que pedir **permiso*** — *to go out I had to ask permission*. *Mi vieja **quería que volviera** temprano* — *my mom wanted me back early*.
**Si tuviera plata, viajaría.** The *if* half takes *tuviera, fuera, pudiera*; the other half takes *-ía*: *iría, haría, sería*.

| one person (vos) | more than one (ustedes) |
| pasá | **pasen** |
| esperá | **esperen** |
| vení | **vengan** |
| traé | **traigan** |
| sentate | **siéntense** |
| no te preocupes | **no se preocupen** |

-ar verbs end in **-en**, the rest in **-an**, built on the *yo* form: *vengo* → **vengan**, *traigo* → **traigan**. The pronoun is **se**, stuck on the end — and then the accent appears: **siéntense, quédense**. After *no* it goes in front: **no se preocupen**.

*Quiero que* has company: **necesito que me ayudes** — *I need you to help me*; **te pido que me esperes** — *please wait for me*. Whenever you want something from someone else, the verb after *que* goes subjunctive.
These words change with the person: **argentino** for a man, **argentina** for a woman. Same for *uruguayo / uruguaya*, *chileno / chilena*.

Porteño pizza is its own religion: **una grande de muzza**, eaten standing up by the **porción**, or **mitad y mitad** for the undecided. At a parrilla, start with a **provoleta** and a **choripán**. **Reservé para las diez** — dinner starts late.
**Mi viejo** and **mi vieja** — literally "my old one" — are affectionate Argentine words for *my dad* and *my mom*. Together: **mis viejos** — *my parents*.
The whole *gustar* pattern: **le cae bien a mi vieja**, **nos cae re bien**, **¿te caen bien mis amigos?** The person being liked is the subject: *mis amigos **te caen** bien*.

Remember **queda** for where a place *is*: **¿dónde queda Palermo?** New here is **me parece** — *I think, it seems to me*: *me parece re caro*. To ask for an opinion: **¿qué te parece el depto?** — *what do you think of the apartment?*
Your health insurance is your **obra social**; the doctor writes a **receta** and you take the **pastillas** **cada ocho horas**.

Verbs in *-ar* take **-ando**: **laburando**, **esperando**, **tomando**. Verbs in *-er* and *-ir* take **-iendo**: **comiendo**, **haciendo**. That ending never changes — only *estar* does: *Estoy comiendo.* *Está tomando un café.*

*Estar* for where things are, one or several:

| one thing | **¿Dónde está** mi celu? | **Está** en la mochila. |
| several | **¿Dónde están** mis llaves? | **Están** en casa. |
**Me cae bien** is *I like him* — as a person, not romantically. It works like *gustar*: **me cae bien Juan**, **me caen bien tus amigos**. The first impression: **me cayó mal**.
**Por acá** is *around here*, the end of every question on the street: *¿Hay un bar por acá?* *¿Hay un taxi por acá?* The answer is usually a finger and *a dos cuadras*.
**Tendría que haber** + participle is *I should have*: **tendría que haber ido**, **tendrías que haber avisado**. Porteños use it far more than any other past regret.

You can't pay the driver in cash. You tap a **SUBE** card on the reader — on buses, the subte and trains (many now take a bank card or phone too). You load it at a kiosco or a subte station: *¿Me cargás la SUBE?* When the **saldo** runs out, load it again.
**Se la cree** — *he's arrogant*; **me la banco** — *I can handle it*; **me las arreglo** — *I manage*; **la tenés clara** — *you know your stuff*. The *la* points at nothing.
title_en: Se la cree, me la banco

body_md: A word ending in **-o** is usually masculine and takes *un*: *un hermano*. One ending in **-a** is usually feminine and takes *una*: *una hermana*.

Argentines say **depto** for an apartment, **pieza** for a bedroom and **el living** for the living room. The fridge is **la heladera**. **Alquilo** on its own means *I rent my place*: *¿Dónde alquilás?*

| ¡Qué suerte que **vivas** cerca! | How lucky you live nearby! |
| Me preocupa que **trabajes** tanto. | It worries me you work so much. |
