| Me sorprende que no lo **conozcas**. | I'm surprised you don't know him. |
| ¡Qué bueno que **estemos** todos! | So good we're all here! |

A feeling about something + **que** → the subjunctive, for any person. *Me preocupa* and *me sorprende* work like *me molesta*.
**No hay nada como** — *there's nothing like*: **no hay nada como un asado con amigos**.
With your friends it's **habíamos**: **ya habíamos terminado cuando llegaste**. The whole set is now *había, habías, habíamos, habían* — and the participle never changes.

| | nacer | vivir | volver |
| yo | nac**í** | viv**í** | volv**í** |
| vos | nac**iste** | viv**iste** | volv**iste** |
| él, ella | nac**ió** | viv**ió** | volv**ió** |
| ellos, ustedes | nac**ieron** | viv**ieron** | volv**ieron** |

*Ellos* ends in **-ieron**: *comieron, salieron, vivieron*. **¿Dónde naciste?** — **Nací en Rosario.** And **no entendí** is the past too.

Argentina has its own names: **palta** is avocado, **frutilla** is strawberry. Before you buy, ask **¿están maduras?** — *are they ripe?* The opposite of *madura* is **verde**: **están verdes** — *they are not ripe yet*. (*Es verde* is the color.)

The little word matches the thing, not you: **un** té, **un** helado, but **una** torta, **una** pizza. Learn each new word with its *un* or *una* and you'll never have to guess. One twist: *agua* takes **un** — *un agua*. It is still an *una* word, though: *otra agua*.
**Listo** is *ready* — *¿estás lista?* — and on its own it closes any deal: *Listo, dale.* **Apurado** is *in a hurry*, the normal state of anyone downtown.
A porteño doesn't *have fun*, he **la pasa**: **la pasé bárbaro**, **la pasamos re bien**, **¿la pasaste bien?** The *la* never changes and never means anything — it's just part of the phrase.
Signs say what's done without saying who: **se vende** — *for sale*; **se alquila** — *for rent*; **se necesita mozo** — *waiter wanted*. More than one thing: **se venden bicis**.
When someone dies, family and friends meet at the **velorio** — *the wake*. You hug the family and say **te acompaño en el sentimiento** — *I'm sorry for your loss*.

Plans hang on *cuando* + the subjunctive: **cuando vuelvas del viaje, nos vemos**; **cuando cobre, te invito**; **cuando empieces el laburo nuevo, contame**. The other half stays normal, or a command.

**Quién** asks *who*: *¿Quién es él?* The answer drops *él* or *ella*: *Es Martín, un vecino.* Whose? Use **de**: *una amiga de Juan* — *a friend of Juan's*. A **pibe** is a young guy and a **piba** a young woman — very porteño.

**Hubiera** + participle also works alone as *would have*: **nunca lo hubiera vendido** — *I'd never have sold it*; **¿lo hubieras vendido?** — *would you have sold it?* And **ojalá hubiera** + participle is *I wish I had*: **ojalá hubiera ahorrado más**.
title_en: Would have, I wish I had

body_md: Porteños say **mi mujer** for *my wife* and **mi marido** for *my husband* — two different words, not a pair. And **bebé** is one word for a baby boy or girl: *un bebé*.

**¿Cuánto sale?** is the everyday Argentine way to ask a price — *¿cuánto cuesta?* works too. Several things **salen** or **cuestan**: *¿cuánto salen las zapatillas?* *To pay* and *to buy* follow one pattern: **pago**, **pagás**, **paga** and **compro**, **comprás**, **compra**. *¿Pagás vos o pago yo?* At the register: *¿tarjeta o efectivo?* — *card or cash?* **Mangos** is slang for pesos: *no tengo un mango* means *I don't have a peso*.

| yo | **me lo merezco** | I deserve it |
| vos | **te lo merecés** | you deserve it |
| él, ella | **se lo merece** | he, she deserves it |
| nosotros | **nos lo merecemos** | we deserve it |

Without *lo*, the thing follows: **se merece el ascenso**. The pronoun never leaves.
title_en: Se lo merece, nos lo merecemos

body_md: **Depende**, **puede ser**, **en parte** — the porteño hedge. Full agreement is **estoy de acuerdo**; full disagreement, **para nada**.

*Ser* says who you are — a name, or a role with no *un* in front:

| yo | **soy** | Soy estudiante. |
| vos | **sos** | ¿Sos turista? |


*Vos* can go before the verb or after it: *¿Vos sos Juan?* and *¿Sos vos?* are both everyday Buenos Aires.

-er verbs keep **e** and -ir verbs take **i**, but only for *vos* and *nosotros*: *vend**és**, vend**emos*** but *abr**ís**, abr**imos***. Everywhere else they match: *vendo, abro*; *lee, comparte*; *leen, escriben*. *Recibir* and *correr* follow the same pattern.
title_en: -er and -ir: different only in vos and nosotros

body_md: **Hubiera** takes the participles *había* does: **sabido, venido, ido, llamado, dicho, hecho**. **Si hubieras venido** — *if you had come*. On its own it's *would have* — *yo hubiera dicho que sí*, *I would have said yes* — or regret, *should have*: **ojalá hubiera estudiado** — *I wish I'd studied*; **¡me hubieras llamado!** — *you should have called me!*

**Ya** is *already* or *right now*; **todavía** is *still*: *Todavía estoy laburando.* *Todavía no* is *not yet*. **Casi** is *almost*. One warning: in Buenos Aires **ya estoy llegando** can mean you are still ten minutes away.
